title: Principles of Motor Learning in Treatment of Motor Speech Disorders
shortTitle: Motor Learning Principles in Motor Speech
authors: Maas, E., Robin, D. A., Austermann Hula, S. N., Freedman, S. E., Wulf, G., Ballard, K. J., & Schmidt, R. A.
summary: Seminal tutorial reviewing motor learning principles from the nonspeech literature and how they apply to treatment of motor speech disorders. The foundation for structuring motor speech practice.
researchFindings: Random and variable practice schedules produce slower initial learning but stronger long-term retention and generalization compared to blocked practice.
Reduced feedback frequency (e.g., 50% KR) outperforms 100% feedback for retention — too much feedback creates feedback dependency.
Delayed feedback and summary feedback formats (every 5 trials) enhance learning more than immediate, trial-by-trial feedback.
Errorful learning conditions (where clients make some errors) can promote deeper motor learning than error-free paradigms.
Principles interact: the same variable may have different effects depending on task complexity, client severity, and other treatment parameters.
Mental practice and attentional focus instructions can supplement physical practice in motor speech treatment.
clinicalApplication: Structure sessions to fade feedback as accuracy improves — begin with more frequent KP/KR, then systematically reduce to every 3rd or 5th trial. Use random and variable practice (vary targets, contexts, and positions within a session) rather than drilling the same target repeatedly. Avoid correction after every error; allow the client to self-monitor. For home practice, brief daily mental rehearsal of target movements supplements in-clinic work. These principles apply directly to Apraxia of Speech treatment (e.g., DTTP, RASP, MSTP) and dysarthria behavioral intervention.

sessionStats.dose: Foundational framework
sessionStats.bestFit: Apraxia of Speech, Dysarthria

bestFitCriteria: Adults with acquired or developmental apraxia of speech.
Dysarthria of any etiology where behavioral intervention is appropriate.
Any motor speech client where home practice or carryover is a treatment goal.
Clinicians designing or evaluating motor speech treatment protocols.

title: Principles of Experience-Dependent Neural Plasticity: Implications for Rehabilitation After Brain Damage
shortTitle: Neural Plasticity Principles for Rehabilitation
authors: Kleim, J. A., & Jones, T. A.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: Reviews 10 principles of experience-dependent neural plasticity and their direct implications for rehabilitation after brain damage. Essential theoretical grounding for all neurologically-based SLP intervention.
researchFindings: Use it or lose it: neural circuits that are not driven by experience will degrade — disuse accelerates deficits.
Use it and improve it: training that drives specific circuits can lead to enhancement of function beyond baseline.
Specificity: plasticity is specific to the experience — treatment must directly target the desired skill.
Repetition matters: inducing plasticity requires sufficient repetition of the targeted behavior.
Intensity matters: induction of plasticity requires sufficient training intensity; intensity and repetition interact.
Time matters: different forms of plasticity occur at different times post-injury; early intervention may capitalize on heightened plasticity windows.
Salience matters: the training experience must be sufficiently salient to engage neural circuits and drive plasticity.
Age matters: training-induced plasticity occurs more readily in younger brains; adult neuroplasticity is real but more constrained.
Transference: plasticity in response to one experience can enhance acquisition of similar behaviors.
Interference: plasticity in response to one experience can interfere with others — sequencing and scheduling of treatment targets matters.
clinicalApplication: These 10 principles argue directly for high-repetition, high-intensity, task-specific treatment delivered early post-injury. For aphasia, this means massed practice of communicative tasks (not decontextualized drills) at sufficient dose. For motor speech, specificity means targeting speech movements directly, not nonspeech oral motor exercises. Salience and time principles support motivating, ecologically valid tasks and capitalizing on subacute recovery windows. Interference has direct implications for scheduling multiple treatment targets — some combinations may interfere.

sessionStats.dose: High repetition recommended
sessionStats.bestFit: All neurological SLP populations

bestFitCriteria: Adults with acquired neurological communication or swallowing disorders.
Any SLP designing intensity, frequency, or dosage parameters for a treatment plan.
Clinicians considering early vs. delayed intervention timing.
Justifying treatment frequency and repetition to payers, teams, or caregivers.

title: Evidence-Based Practice in Communication Disorders: What Do We Know, and When Do We Know It?
shortTitle: Evidence-Based Practice in Communication Disorders
authors: Dollaghan, C. A.
summary: A foundational framework for evidence-based practice in communication disorders, defining what counts as evidence, how to appraise it, and how to integrate it with clinical expertise and patient values.
researchFindings: EBP is defined as the integration of best available research evidence with clinical expertise and client values — no single component is sufficient alone.
External research evidence must be appraised for validity, importance, and applicability before clinical application.
Clinical expertise mediates how evidence is applied to individual patients — evidence informs, but the clinician decides.
Patient values and preferences are a required component of EBP decisions, not optional considerations.
clinicalApplication: Dollaghan's framework is the conceptual foundation for why EBP-SLP exists. Every time you select a treatment approach, you are making an EBP decision: what does the research say, what does your clinical experience tell you, and what does your patient want and need? Use this article to explain EBP to students, families, or team members — and to anchor your own clinical decision-making process when research evidence is ambiguous or limited.
bestFitCriteria: Any SLP making treatment selection decisions.
Clinicians explaining their rationale for treatment choices to patients, families, or payers.
SLPs mentoring students or CFs in evidence-based clinical reasoning.
Settings where treatment approaches are being standardized or reviewed.

title: The Handbook for Evidence-Based Practice in Communication Disorders
shortTitle: Handbook for EBP in Communication Disorders
authors: Dollaghan, C. A.
summary: The definitive practical guide to implementing evidence-based practice in speech-language pathology, providing tools for critically appraising research and applying it to clinical decisions.
researchFindings: Provides a step-by-step process for formulating clinical questions using the PICO framework (Patient, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome).
Details how to search, retrieve, and critically appraise different evidence types — RCTs, systematic reviews, case studies, and expert opinion.
Addresses the hierarchy of evidence and how to interpret effect sizes, confidence intervals, and clinical significance versus statistical significance.
Offers practical tools for integrating evidence with clinical experience and patient preferences in real-world decision-making.
clinicalApplication: Dollaghan's handbook operationalizes EBP for practicing SLPs. Use the PICO framework to structure your clinical questions before searching for evidence. When evaluating a study, ask: Is the study design appropriate for the question? Are the participants similar to my patient? Is the effect size clinically meaningful? Apply critical appraisal — not just the conclusion of a paper, but the quality of its evidence — to every treatment decision. This framework underlies every article in EBP-SLP.
bestFitCriteria: SLPs seeking a practical framework for evaluating and applying research to clinical practice.
Clinical fellows and students developing evidence-based reasoning skills.
Clinicians in settings where treatment selection decisions must be documented and justified.
Any SLP who wants to move beyond "this is what we do here" toward research-informed practice.

title: Towards an International Framework for Communication Disorders: Use of the ICF
shortTitle: ICF Framework for Communication Disorders
authors: Threats, T. T.
summary: Establishes the WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) as an organizing framework for communication disorders, shifting focus from impairment alone to activity, participation, and quality of life.
researchFindings: The ICF provides a universal framework across body function/structure, activity, participation, and contextual factors — all relevant to communication disorders.
Impairment-level changes (e.g., improved naming on a standardized test) do not automatically translate to improved participation or quality of life.
Treatment goals should address all ICF levels: not just what the patient can do in the clinic, but what they do in their real life.
Environmental and personal contextual factors (caregiver support, attitudes, living situation) are recognized as variables that moderate functional outcomes.
clinicalApplication: The ICF framework is the reason EBP-SLP emphasizes functional goal targets over impairment-level metrics alone. When writing goals, ask: does this goal address body function (e.g., naming accuracy), activity (e.g., ordering at a restaurant), or participation (e.g., returning to work)? The strongest clinical plans address all three levels. Use the ICF to justify goal breadth in documentation, to frame progress for families, and to advocate for continued treatment when impairment plateaus but participation goals remain unmet.
bestFitCriteria: Any adult with a communication or swallowing disorder where quality of life and functional participation are treatment goals.
SLPs writing goals that need to address real-world participation beyond the clinical setting.
Settings where treatment justification requires demonstrating functional impact.
Clinicians advocating for continued care when standardized test scores have plateaued.

title: Intensity of Aphasia Therapy, Impact on Recovery
shortTitle: Aphasia Therapy Intensity and Recovery
authors: Bhogal, S. K., Teasell, R., & Speechley, M.
summary: Systematic review demonstrating that intensive aphasia therapy (~9 hrs/week) produces significantly better outcomes than low-intensity therapy (~2 hrs/week), regardless of total treatment duration.
researchFindings: Positive studies (showing treatment effect) provided 8.8 hrs of therapy per week for 11.2 weeks — approximately 98 total hours.
Negative studies provided only 2 hrs per week for 22.9 weeks — approximately 44 total hours.
Hours per week (not total duration) was significantly correlated with improvement on the PICA (p = 0.001) and Token Test (p = 0.027).
Total therapy hours also correlated with better PICA (p < 0.001) and Token Test outcomes.
Total treatment duration was inversely correlated with hours/week — stretching treatment over more weeks with fewer hours/week predicts worse outcomes.
Conclusion: intensive short-course therapy outperforms dilute long-course therapy for aphasia recovery.
clinicalApplication: Use this evidence when advocating for aphasia treatment intensity at care-planning meetings. The benchmark is approximately 8–9 hours per week of direct speech-language therapy. In acute or IPR settings, this means daily treatment is not only appropriate but evidence-supported. In SNF or outpatient, use this to justify 3–5 sessions/week over 8–12 weeks rather than 1–2 sessions/week spread over months. When payer limits restrict frequency, prioritize total hours delivered early rather than spacing sessions out. Document intensity as a clinical rationale in your treatment plans.

sessionStats.dose: ~98 total hours for significant recovery
sessionStats.bestFit: Acute, IPR, subacute aphasia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with post-stroke aphasia in the acute or subacute phase.
Any aphasia client where treatment frequency or intensity is being discussed with the team or payer.
Clinicians needing evidence to justify daily treatment or increased session frequency.
Care planning for IPR, acute care, SNF, or intensive outpatient aphasia programs.

title: Improving Language in Individual Conversation-Level Therapy: Group and Individual Results of ECoLoGiC Treatment for People With Moderate and Severe Aphasia
shortTitle: ECoLoGiC Conversation-Level Aphasia Treatment
authors: Elman, R. J., & Bernstein-Ellis, E.
summary: ECoLoGiC targets real-world conversational communication in moderate-to-severe aphasia. Participants (n=10) showed an average 11.31-point WAB-R gain; 7 of 10 shifted to a less severe severity category.
researchFindings: Participants (n=10) with moderate-to-severe aphasia showed an average 11.31-point increase on the Western Aphasia Battery – Revised (WAB-R) following ECoLoGiC treatment.
7 of 10 participants shifted to a less severe aphasia category on the WAB-R post-treatment.
Generalization was observed across multiple measurement types beyond the primary outcome measure.
ECoLoGiC (Expanding Communication and Language Opportunities Generated in Conversation) directly targets conversational competence rather than isolated language drills.
Treatment is delivered in individual format but draws on conversation-based principles derived from group aphasia treatment literature.
Clinically meaningful gains were observed even in participants with more severe profiles who typically show limited response to impairment-based approaches.
clinicalApplication: ECoLoGiC is particularly well-suited for moderate-to-severe aphasia clients where functional conversational outcomes are the primary treatment target. Unlike impairment-focused drills, ECoLoGiC structures sessions around real conversational exchanges, maximizing ecological validity and generalization. Use this approach when WAB-R severity ratings, functional communication scales (ASHA-FACS, CETI), or caregiver report indicate that conversation in daily life is the key gap. The conversation-first framing also supports shared decision-making with clients who want to "talk better" — not just name pictures. The model can be implemented in both individual and group formats.

sessionStats.dose: Treatment course varies; typically 12–20 sessions
sessionStats.bestFit: Moderate–severe chronic aphasia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with moderate-to-severe aphasia (any etiology) where conversational participation is the primary functional goal.
Clients who have plateaued with impairment-based therapy and need a functional, conversation-focused approach.
Situations where caregiver-reported communication breakdown in daily conversation is documented.
IPR, outpatient, or community re-entry settings where participation-level outcomes are prioritized.

title: The Efficacy and Utility of Constant Therapy in Poststroke Aphasia Rehabilitation
shortTitle: Constant Therapy Digital App for Post-Stroke Aphasia
authors: Kurland, J., Liu, A., & Stokes, P.
journal: Perspectives of the ASHA Special Interest Groups
summary: Pilot trial providing Level II evidence that the Constant Therapy app is effective for post-stroke aphasia rehabilitation. Supports use between sessions and at home to extend treatment intensity.
researchFindings: Constant Therapy (a commercially available digital therapeutic app) produced clinically meaningful improvements in post-stroke aphasia on standardized language measures.
Study provides Level II evidence per the authors — pilot design with sufficient rigor to support clinical adoption pending larger RCTs.
The app delivers structured, adaptive language exercises across multiple domains (naming, comprehension, reading, writing) with performance tracking.
Participants were able to use the app independently at home, extending the effective dose of therapy beyond clinic sessions.
App-based delivery supports telehealth and home program integration — clinicians can monitor performance data remotely through the clinician dashboard.

Digital therapeutic approach addresses the intensity gap: clients needing 8–9 hrs/week of aphasia therapy rarely receive it in standard care; between-session app use supplements clinic-based treatment.
clinicalApplication: Prescribe Constant Therapy as a structured home program supplement to in-clinic aphasia treatment — not as a replacement for skilled SLP services. Use the clinician dashboard to assign specific task domains aligned with current treatment targets (e.g., naming tasks if anomia is the focus), and review performance data at each session to guide clinical decision-making. The app is most valuable for clients who are motivated to practice independently and have family or caregiver support for setup. Given the intensity evidence (Bhogal et al., 2003), any tool that reliably extends weekly dose is clinically meaningful. Particularly useful in SNF and outpatient settings where session frequency is constrained.

sessionStats.dose: Adjunct to standard SLP treatment schedule
sessionStats.bestFit: Motivated clients with home support

bestFitCriteria: Adults with post-stroke aphasia who are medically stable and able to engage with an iPad or tablet independently or with caregiver assistance.
Clients receiving outpatient, SNF, or home health aphasia treatment where session frequency is below 5x/week.
Any aphasia client where extending weekly treatment dose beyond in-clinic hours is a goal.
Telehealth aphasia caseloads where remote monitoring of practice data adds clinical value.

title: Efficacy of swallowing rehabilitative therapies for adults with dysphagia: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
shortTitle: Network Meta-Analysis: Adult Swallowing Rehab
authors: Lee, C. L., Banda, K. J., Chu, Y. H., Liu, D., Lee, C. K., Sung, C. M., Arifin, H., & Chou, K. R.
summary: First network meta-analysis comparing swallowing rehabilitative therapies. Combined approaches — especially CTAR + traditional dysphagia therapy — showed very large to huge effect sizes and topped rankings for function and aspiration reduction.
researchFindings: First network meta-analysis to compare multiple swallowing rehabilitative therapies head-to-head using RCT data (25 RCTs, n=1,020 adults).
Combined therapy approaches produced the largest effect sizes: CTAR + traditional dysphagia therapy (TDT), EMST + TDT, and Shaker + TDT all showed very large to huge effects.
CTAR (Chin Tuck Against Resistance) + TDT was the top-ranked intervention for swallowing function and aspiration reduction.
Standalone EMST (Expiratory Muscle Strength Training) and Shaker exercise also outperformed sham or no treatment, but combinations were consistently superior.
Effect sizes: CTAR + TDT showed the largest pooled effect for penetration-aspiration scale improvement.
Network meta-analysis methodology allowed indirect comparisons across trials that never directly compared the same interventions — increasing the clinical applicability of findings.
clinicalApplication: Prioritize combination swallowing therapy over single-modality approaches when treating adults with oropharyngeal dysphagia. CTAR (chin tuck against resistance using a ball or resistance device) is easy to implement and well-supported as an add-on to traditional dysphagia therapy (thermal-tactile application, effortful swallow, Mendelsohn, etc.). When EMST equipment is available, consider EMST as a complementary approach especially for clients with respiratory muscle weakness, neurological dysphagia, or chronic aspiration. Use the Shaker (head lift) exercise selectively for clients with upper esophageal sphincter dysfunction and adequate cervical spine tolerance. Document combination rationale in treatment plans — this NMA provides direct 1a-level justification for multi-modal dysphagia treatment design.

sessionStats.dose: CTAR: 3 sets × 10 reps; EMST: 5 sets × 5 reps at threshold; Shaker: per protocol
sessionStats.bestFit: Oropharyngeal dysphagia, neurological

bestFitCriteria: Adults with oropharyngeal dysphagia of neurological etiology (stroke, TBI, PD, ALS, MS) where swallowing rehabilitation is appropriate.
Clients with confirmed penetration or aspiration on instrumental assessment (MBSS or FEES) who are candidates for rehabilitation rather than compensation only.
Patients where cervical spine status allows head-lift or chin-tuck maneuvers (screen appropriately for Shaker and CTAR candidacy).
Treatment planning for any dysphagia rehab program where evidence-based exercise selection and combination therapy rationale is required.

title: Voice Therapy, Vocal Hygiene Education, and Self-Study in Women with Phonotraumatic Vocal Fold Lesions
shortTitle: VP Therapy vs. Vocal Hygiene in Phonotrauma
authors: Behrman, A., Rutledge, J., Hembree, A., & Sheridan, S.
summary: RCT (n=62) comparing voice production (VP) therapy to vocal hygiene education (VHE) in women with phonotraumatic vocal fold lesions. VP therapy produced larger VHI reductions; adherence was the critical mediator of outcome.
researchFindings: VP therapy produced significantly greater reductions in Voice Handicap Index (VHI) scores than VHE from baseline to end of study.
Treatment effect size was large for VP group and small for VHE group.
More participants adhered to VP than to VHE across the 6-week treatment + 4-week self-study period.
Only adherent participants in either group achieved significant improvement — non-adherent participants showed minimal change.
Only adherent VP participants continued to improve during the 4-week self-study phase.
Over two-thirds of the VP group achieved final VHI scores within normal limits, compared to approximately one-third of the VHE group.
clinicalApplication: Prioritize voice production therapy (resonant voice, semi-occluded vocal tract exercises, flow phonation, or similar approaches) over vocal hygiene counseling alone for clients with benign phonotraumatic lesions. Vocal hygiene is an appropriate supplement but insufficient as a primary treatment. Critically, adherence is the single strongest predictor of outcome — build adherence strategies into treatment from session one: brief daily home practice, motivational follow-up, and clear self-monitoring tools. The self-study data suggest that a structured home practice phase after active therapy can extend and consolidate gains if the client is adherent.

sessionStats.dose: 6 weeks active + 4 weeks self-study
sessionStats.bestFit: Mild–Moderate phonotrauma

bestFitCriteria: Adult women (study population) with benign, bilateral phonotraumatic vocal fold lesions (nodules, polyps, edema).
Voice clients with measurable VHI elevation at baseline.
Any voice client where adherence to home practice is a clinical concern.
When choosing between vocal hygiene counseling and direct voice production therapy as a primary approach.

title: Constraint-induced therapy of chronic aphasia after stroke
shortTitle: Constraint-Induced Language Therapy (CILT)
authors: Pulvermüller, F., Neininger, B., Elbert, T., Mohr, B., Rockstroh, B., Koebbel, P., & Taub, E.
summary: Landmark RCT showing that Constraint-Induced Language Therapy (CILT) — 3 hrs/day for 10 days — produced significantly greater language gains than conventional therapy, even in chronic aphasia.
researchFindings: CILT participants received 3 hours/day of intensive communicative language therapy for 10 consecutive weekdays (30 total hours).
CILT group showed significantly greater improvements on the Aachen Aphasia Test compared to the conventional therapy group.
Gains were clinically meaningful and observed even in participants with chronic aphasia who had been stable for years.
CILT constrains compensatory communication strategies (gesture, writing, drawing) and requires verbal output exclusively — forcing the impaired language system to engage.
The principle of massed practice + behavioral constraint mirrors constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) for limb rehabilitation.
Effect sizes were large; improvements were maintained at 6-month follow-up.
clinicalApplication: CILT directly operationalizes neural plasticity principles — constraint forces the impaired language system to work rather than allowing intact systems to compensate. In practice, sessions consist of structured communication games (barrier tasks, requesting, describing) where only verbal responses are accepted; compensatory strategies are blocked. The 10-day/30-hour model is best suited for intensive aphasia programs (IPR, intensive outpatient). In standard outpatient settings, apply CILT principles by selectively constraining compensation during some activities and maximizing verbal trial volume. Best evidence is for clients who can produce some verbal output and may be using gesture or writing as primary strategies.

sessionStats.dose: 30 hrs total over 10 days
sessionStats.bestFit: Chronic aphasia with some verbal output

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia (>6 months) who have a verbal communication mode, even if limited.
Clients who rely heavily on compensatory strategies (gesture, writing) and where the goal is to rebuild verbal output.
Intensive aphasia programs (IPR, intensive outpatient) where high treatment dose is achievable.
Clients who are behaviorally able to follow the constraint rule and tolerate communicative challenge.

title: A meta-analysis of clinical outcomes in the treatment of aphasia
shortTitle: Meta-Analysis: Aphasia Treatment Outcomes
authors: Robey, R. R.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: Foundational meta-analysis demonstrating that treated aphasia recovers approximately twice as much as untreated aphasia, with acute-phase treatment and sufficient intensity producing the largest effects.
researchFindings: Treated aphasia recovered approximately twice as much as untreated aphasia across all outcome measures and phases.
Effect sizes for treatment initiated in the acute phase (within 1 month post-onset): large (d ≈ 0.79).
Effect sizes for treatment initiated in the chronic phase (>1 year post-onset): moderate — still statistically and clinically meaningful.
Treatment dose (total hours) was positively correlated with outcome; more intensive treatment produced better results.
Spontaneous recovery accounts for some improvement, but treated recovery consistently and substantially exceeds untreated recovery.
No statistically significant evidence that any one treatment approach was superior to others — quantity and timing of treatment were the dominant predictors.
clinicalApplication: Use Robey (1998) alongside Bhogal et al. (2003) to make the case for early, intensive aphasia treatment in care-planning discussions. The 2x recovery finding is compelling for justifying aphasia treatment to payers and medical teams who may view aphasia as a naturally resolving condition. The dose-response relationship supports increasing session frequency when possible, especially in the acute and subacute phases. The finding that chronic-phase treatment still produces meaningful effect sizes is important for justifying continued outpatient services beyond typical payer caps.

sessionStats.frequency: As often as feasible (acute phase especially)
sessionStats.dose: Higher total hours = better outcomes
sessionStats.bestFit: All aphasia phases; strongest case in acute

bestFitCriteria: Any adult with post-stroke aphasia where treatment frequency or continuation is under discussion.
Clinical advocacy with payers, insurers, or medical teams skeptical of aphasia treatment benefit.
Justifying continued treatment for clients in the chronic phase.
Treatment planning discussions about optimal timing and dose of aphasia services.

title: Speech and language therapy for aphasia following stroke
shortTitle: Cochrane Review: SLT for Post-Stroke Aphasia
authors: Brady, M. C., Kelly, H., Godwin, J., Enderby, P., & Campbell, P.
summary: Most comprehensive systematic review of SLT for post-stroke aphasia — 57 RCTs, 3,002 participants. SLT significantly improves functional communication, receptive and expressive language over no treatment; intensity is a key moderator.
researchFindings: SLT significantly improved functional communication compared to no treatment (high-quality evidence across 57 RCTs).
SLT also improved receptive and expressive language, and reading outcomes compared to no treatment or social support only.
Intensive SLT (more hours/week) produced significantly better outcomes than conventional-intensity SLT for functional communication.
No significant difference in outcomes between delivered-by-SLP and trained volunteer/carer-delivered SLT for some outcomes — with implications for augmenting dose.
Unclear evidence on optimal content or timing of SLT; intensity and dose remain the most consistently positive moderators.
No evidence that SLT causes harm; dropout rates were similar across groups.
clinicalApplication: Brady et al. (2016) is the highest-level single evidence source for aphasia SLT — cite it when making the global case for aphasia treatment with insurers or medical teams. The intensity finding is consistent with Bhogal (2003) and Robey (1998) and supports maximizing session frequency. The volunteer-delivery finding is clinically relevant: trained communication partners (family members, volunteers) delivering structured tasks between sessions can extend effective dose without requiring additional SLP time — a practical tool in settings with access limitations.

sessionStats.dose: More sessions/week = better outcomes (evidence-consistent finding)
sessionStats.bestFit: All post-stroke aphasia

bestFitCriteria: Any adult with post-stroke aphasia at any stage of recovery.
Cases where treatment justification for payers, teams, or families requires the highest-level global evidence.
Treatment planning conversations about frequency, partner involvement, and dose.

title: Rehabilitation of Swallowing by Exercise in Tube-Fed Patients with Pharyngeal Dysphagia Secondary to Abnormal UES Opening
shortTitle: Shaker Exercise for UES Dysfunction / Dysphagia
authors: Shaker, R., Easterling, C., Kern, M., Nitschke, T., Massey, B., Daniels, S., Grande, B., Kazandjian, M., & Dikeman, K.
summary: Original RCT establishing the Shaker head-lift exercise as an effective rehabilitation approach for pharyngeal dysphagia caused by impaired upper esophageal sphincter (UES) opening, resulting in deglutitive aspiration elimination and decannulation of PEG in some participants.
researchFindings: The Shaker exercise (sustained isometric + isokinetic head lifts against gravity in supine) significantly increased the anteroposterior diameter of UES opening compared to sham exercise.
Exercise group showed significantly reduced aspiration and penetration on videofluoroscopic swallow study post-treatment.
A subset of participants who were PEG-tube dependent at baseline achieved oral feeding after the 6-week exercise program; no sham participants did.
Suprahyoid muscle strengthening via head lift exercise directly targets the mechanical component of UES dysfunction — the biomechanical rationale is well-established.
Protocol: 3 sustained 1-minute head raises + 30 repetitive head raises, 3x/day for 6 weeks.
No adverse events; the exercise is suitable for motivated patients with adequate cervical spine tolerance.
clinicalApplication: Prescribe the Shaker exercise as a targeted rehabilitation approach for clients with confirmed UES dysfunction on MBSS or FEES (specifically: reduced anteroposterior UES opening, post-swallow residue in the pyriform sinuses, overflow aspiration). Screen for cervical spine contraindications (RA, cervical stenosis, recent cervical surgery) before initiating — the exercise requires sustained cervical extension against gravity. The exact protocol from the study: sustained holds of 60 seconds, 3x; followed by 30 rapid head lifts, 3x daily. This is a home exercise program between sessions, not an in-session activity. Pair with direct swallowing therapy targeting the same biomechanical deficit.

sessionStats.dose: 3 × 60-sec sustained lifts + 30 repetitive lifts per session; 6-week program
sessionStats.bestFit: UES dysfunction confirmed on instrumental assessment

bestFitCriteria: Adults with oropharyngeal dysphagia and confirmed impaired UES opening on MBSS or FEES.
Post-swallow pyriform sinus residue with overflow aspiration as the primary pattern on instrumental assessment.
Clients with adequate cervical spine mobility and no contraindications to sustained cervical extension.
PEG-dependent patients in rehabilitation settings where return to oral feeding is a goal.

title: Aspiration and Swallowing in Parkinson Disease and Rehabilitation with EMST: A Randomized Trial
shortTitle: EMST for Swallowing in Parkinson's Disease
authors: Troche, M. S., Okun, M. S., Rosenbek, J. C., Musson, N., Fernandez, H. H., Rodriguez, R., Romrell, J., Pitts, T., Wheeler-Hegland, K. M., & Sapienza, C. M.
summary: RCT demonstrating that Expiratory Muscle Strength Training (EMST) significantly improved swallowing safety and reduced aspiration in individuals with Parkinson's disease — with the mechanism tied to improved hyolaryngeal excursion.
researchFindings: EMST group (4 weeks, 5 days/week, threshold device at 75% maximum expiratory pressure) showed significantly reduced penetration-aspiration scale scores vs. sham group on VFSS.
EMST produced significant improvements in hyolaryngeal excursion during swallowing — the biomechanical mechanism linking expiratory muscle strength to swallowing safety.
Suprahyoid muscle activation (essential for laryngeal elevation and UES opening) improved with EMST, explaining the swallowing benefit from a respiratory exercise.
Participants in the EMST group also showed improved cough effectiveness — an important secondary benefit for airway protection.
Sham group (device with no resistance) showed no significant changes, confirming resistance-based training was essential.
Protocol: 5 sets × 5 reps at 75% maximum expiratory pressure (MEP), 5 days/week for 4 weeks.
clinicalApplication: EMST is particularly well-supported for Parkinson's disease dysphagia, where both swallowing and cough effectiveness are impaired. The threshold device (available commercially — Threshold PEP/IMT device or Power Breathe) provides resistance-based training that the client can perform at home with minimal supervision. Calibrate to 75% MEP — you'll need to measure MEP with a handheld manometer at baseline and adjust the device accordingly. The dual benefit for cough and swallow is clinically important in PD: improved cough helps clear material that does penetrate, even if some aspiration still occurs. Coordinate with the neurology team and document the intensity rationale.

sessionStats.dose: 4-week program; recalibrate device as strength improves
sessionStats.bestFit: Parkinson's disease dysphagia with aspiration

bestFitCriteria: Adults with Parkinson's disease and confirmed aspiration or penetration on instrumental swallowing assessment.
PD patients with reduced voluntary cough effectiveness in addition to dysphagia.
Clients in outpatient or home health settings where a structured daily home exercise program is feasible.
Dysphagia of neurological etiology where respiratory muscle weakness is a contributing factor (ALS, MS, post-stroke also possible).

title: Pragmatic randomised controlled trial of swallowing therapy in acute stroke patients
shortTitle: Intensive Dysphagia Therapy in Acute Stroke
authors: Carnaby, G., Hankey, G. J., & Pizzi, J.
summary: Three-arm RCT comparing intensive dysphagia therapy, standard dysphagia therapy, and no dysphagia therapy in acute stroke patients. Intensive therapy produced the best functional swallowing outcomes and lowest chest infection rates.
researchFindings: Three groups: intensive SLT dysphagia therapy (daily treatment targeting swallowing), standard SLT therapy (weekly/biweekly), and social stimulation (no swallowing treatment).
Intensive group had the highest rate of return to normal diet at 6 months and the lowest rate of chest infections.
Standard SLT group outperformed the social stimulation group on most swallowing outcomes, confirming treatment benefit over no treatment.
Intensive therapy was associated with reduced dependency on modified textures at 6-month follow-up.
No significant difference in mortality between groups.
Findings directly support daily dysphagia treatment in the acute stroke phase — consistent with intensity principles from the plasticity literature.
clinicalApplication: Use this evidence when designing dysphagia treatment schedules in acute care and IPR. Daily dysphagia treatment in acute stroke produces meaningfully better outcomes than standard weekly/biweekly scheduling. In practice: prioritize daily contact with acute stroke patients who have confirmed dysphagia on bedside or instrumental assessment; even brief daily sessions (20–30 min) targeting swallowing maneuvers, texture advancement trials, and compensatory strategy training outperform less frequent approaches. Document treatment frequency as a clinical rationale, and use the chest infection rate data when communicating dysphagia risk to the medical team.

sessionStats.bestFit: Acute stroke with confirmed oropharyngeal dysphagia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with acute post-stroke oropharyngeal dysphagia in inpatient acute care or IPR settings.
Cases where treatment frequency for dysphagia is under discussion with the team or rehabilitation manager.
Clients at high risk for aspiration pneumonia where evidence-supported treatment intensity can be justified.

title: Three treatments for teachers with voice disorders: a randomized clinical trial
shortTitle: Three Voice Treatments for Teachers RCT
authors: Roy, N., Weinrich, B., Gray, S. D., Tanner, K., Toledo, S. W., Dove, H., Corbin-Lewis, K., & Stemple, J. C.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: Three-arm RCT (n=64 teachers) comparing resonant voice therapy, vocal hygiene instruction, and voice amplification. Resonant voice therapy produced the greatest VHI reductions and vocal symptom improvement.
researchFindings: Three-arm RCT with 64 teachers randomly assigned to: resonant voice therapy (RVT), vocal hygiene education (VHE), or voice amplification device.
Resonant voice therapy produced significantly greater reductions in Voice Handicap Index (VHI) scores than vocal hygiene or amplification.
VHI improvement: RVT group showed approximately 10-point greater reduction in total VHI than either comparison group.
Voice amplification reduced vocal demand but did not produce equivalent therapeutic benefit — the device compensates rather than rehabilitates.
Vocal hygiene showed the smallest effects, consistent with Behrman et al. (2008) finding that hygiene alone is insufficient as a primary treatment.
All three interventions were relatively brief (8 sessions); RVT achieved the strongest outcomes in this limited dose.
clinicalApplication: For teachers and other professional voice users with hyperfunctional voice disorders or phonotraumatic lesions, resonant voice therapy (forward-focused tone production using resonant voice strategies) is the most evidence-supported direct voice treatment. SOVT (semi-occluded vocal tract) exercises, lip trills, straw phonation, and humming are common resonant voice tools. Vocal hygiene is a useful supplement but should not stand alone as a primary treatment — pair it with direct voice production work. Voice amplification may be appropriate as a workplace accommodation to reduce vocal demand, but should be prescribed alongside, not instead of, voice therapy.

sessionStats.dose: 8 sessions (study protocol); clinical programs often extend to 12–16
sessionStats.bestFit: Professional voice users, hyperfunctional voice disorders

bestFitCriteria: Adult professional voice users (teachers, singers, clergy, call center workers) with hyperfunctional voice disorders or vocal fatigue.
Benign phonotraumatic lesions (vocal nodules, polyps, edema) in adults with high vocal demand occupations.
Voice clients where treatment selection between resonant voice therapy, hygiene counseling, and environmental modification is under consideration.
Any voice client where VHI is used as a primary outcome measure to track progress.

title: Efficacy of Vocal Function Exercises as a method of improving voice production
shortTitle: Vocal Function Exercises (VFE) Efficacy
authors: Stemple, J. C., Lee, L., D'Amico, B., & Pickup, B.
summary: Foundational controlled trial establishing VFE as an effective voice treatment, showing significant improvements in maximum phonation time, semitone pitch range, and airflow in participants completing the program.
researchFindings: VFE group showed significant improvement in maximum phonation time (MPT) at completion versus controls — a direct indicator of improved breath support and laryngeal efficiency.
Significant improvement in lowest and highest sustainable notes (semitone pitch range) in the VFE group, indicating improved laryngeal muscle flexibility and coordination.
Mean airflow rate improved significantly in VFE participants, reflecting more efficient laryngeal valving.
VFE (four exercises: sustained /i/, gliding pitch slides, sustained /o/ at various pitches) targets muscular strength, coordination, and flexibility of the laryngeal mechanism.
The exercise rationale parallels strength and conditioning principles from physical rehabilitation — specificity, progressive loading, and repetition.
VFE is widely adopted in clinical practice for hypofunctional voice disorders, aging voice, and as maintenance for professional voice users.
clinicalApplication: VFE is a simple, well-structured home practice program well-suited for clients who need a repeatable, low-cost daily voice exercise regimen. The four exercises take approximately 10 minutes when practiced correctly. Assign as a home program alongside in-clinic voice production work — use clinic time for cueing, biofeedback, and adjusting targets; use VFE for the daily repetition dose that drives laryngeal muscle conditioning. VFE is particularly useful for presbyphonia, post-surgical voice (post-thyroplasty maintenance), hypofunctional voice disorders, and professional voice users during maintenance phases. Periodically verify home technique with a session recording or real-time feedback.

sessionStats.dose: Ongoing; 4–8 weeks for measurable objective change
sessionStats.bestFit: Hypofunctional voice, presbyphonia, professional voice

bestFitCriteria: Adults with hypofunctional voice disorders (reduced MPT, bowing, breathiness, glottal incompetence).
Older adults with presbyphonia where progressive exercise is a priority.
Post-surgical voice clients (thyroplasty, vocal fold augmentation) during maintenance phase.
Professional voice users needing a structured conditioning regimen between performance periods.

title: Intensive voice treatment (LSVT LOUD) for patients with Parkinson's disease: a 2-year follow up
shortTitle: LSVT LOUD for Parkinson's Disease — 2-Year Follow-Up
authors: Ramig, L. O., Sapir, S., Countryman, S., Pawlas, A. A., O'Brien, C., Hoehn, M., & Thompson, L. L.
summary: RCT with 2-year follow-up demonstrating that LSVT LOUD (intensive loudness training, 16 sessions/1 month) produced durable improvements in vocal loudness and intelligibility in Parkinson's disease, with gains maintained at 2 years.
researchFindings: LSVT LOUD group maintained significantly greater vocal sound pressure level (loudness) at 2-year follow-up compared to baseline and compared to a comparison treatment group.
Improvements in vocal loudness, pitch variability, and voice quality were maintained at 2 years — unprecedented durability in a PD voice/speech treatment study.

LSVT targets the internal amplitude calibration deficit in PD: clients with PD perceive their reduced loudness as normal, leading to under-scaling of effort. LSVT trains "LOUD" as the therapeutic target.
Protocol: 16 individual sessions, 4 sessions/week for 4 weeks, each session ~60 min of intensive vocal exercise including sustained phonation, pitch glides, and functional speech practice.
Carryover to conversational speech loudness was documented — not just sustained phonation tasks.
LSVT is now available as LSVT LOUD (voice/speech focus) and LSVT BIG (limb movement focus) — both delivered under the same intensive protocol principles.
clinicalApplication: LSVT LOUD is the most evidence-based behavioral treatment specifically for hypokinetic dysarthria in Parkinson's disease. The 4-week/16-session intensive protocol is essential to the treatment — do not dilute by spreading sessions over a longer period. The key clinical principle is amplitude recalibration: train the client to produce what feels "too loud" in the clinic, then transfer "loud" into daily communication. Pair with a structured home practice program (sustained /ah/ and pitch glides daily). LSVT certification is recommended for fidelity. Caregiver education is essential — caregivers must reinforce "loud voice" and avoid communicating for the client, which reduces practice opportunities.

sessionStats.dose: 16 sessions over 4 weeks (protocol-critical)
sessionStats.bestFit: Hypokinetic dysarthria in Parkinson's disease

bestFitCriteria: Adults with Parkinson's disease presenting with hypokinetic dysarthria: reduced loudness, monopitch, hypernasality, or reduced intelligibility in conversational speech.
PD clients whose medication is optimized and whose motor status is stable enough for 4x/week treatment.
Early to mid-stage PD where cognitive demands of the protocol are manageable.
Outpatient or IPR settings where 4-week intensive scheduling is feasible.

title: Treatment Guidelines for Acquired Apraxia of Speech: Treatment Descriptions and Recommendations
shortTitle: AOS Treatment Guidelines Systematic Review
authors: Wambaugh, J. L., Duffy, J. R., McNeil, M. R., Robin, D. A., & Rogers, M. A.
summary: Systematic review synthesizing and evaluating all available evidence for acquired apraxia of speech treatment. Identifies Sound Production Treatment (SPT), DTTC, and motor learning-based approaches as having the strongest evidence bases.
researchFindings: Sound Production Treatment (SPT) had the most replicated evidence base across multiple participants and study designs.
Dynamic Temporal and Tactile Cueing (DTTC) showed strong efficacy, particularly for severe AOS with co-occurring aphasia.
Motor learning principles (variable practice, feedback fading, random practice) are consistently present in the most effective AOS treatment protocols.
Melodic Intonation Therapy (MIT) has evidence primarily for severe non-fluent aphasia with AOS — evidence base is smaller but clinically meaningful.
Non-speech oral motor exercises (NSOMEs) were not supported as effective for improving speech production in AOS.
Intensity and practice volume emerged as critical variables across all approaches — underdosed AOS treatment does not produce clinically meaningful change.
clinicalApplication: Use this systematic review to guide AOS treatment selection based on severity and co-occurring deficits. For mild–moderate AOS: SPT (targeting phoneme clusters with modeling, repetition, and feedback fading) is well-supported. For severe AOS (especially with significant aphasia): DTTC (tactile, temporal, and simultaneous production cuing) addresses motor execution at a deeper level. MIT (melodic intonation) may unlock output in severely non-fluent clients when direct speech production approaches have been exhausted. Avoid dedicating session time to NSOMEs — the evidence does not support their use for improving speech. Apply motor learning principles to all approaches: fade feedback systematically, vary practice conditions, ensure sufficient trial volume.

sessionStats.dose: 100+ trials per session recommended for motor learning
sessionStats.bestFit: Mild–severe acquired AOS, any etiology

bestFitCriteria: Adults with acquired apraxia of speech secondary to stroke, TBI, or neurodegenerative disease.
AOS with or without co-occurring aphasia (treatment selection varies by severity and aphasia profile).
Clinicians selecting between AOS treatment approaches or justifying treatment choices to the team.
Treatment planning for AOS when standardized treatment data, motor learning application, and treatment intensity all need to be documented.

title: Evidence-Based Cognitive Rehabilitation: Updated Review of the Literature From 2003 Through 2008
shortTitle: Evidence-Based Cognitive Rehabilitation Guidelines
authors: Cicerone, K. D., Langenbahn, D. M., Braden, C., Malec, J. F., Kalmar, K., Fraas, M., Felicetti, T., Laatsch, L., Harley, J. P., Bergquist, T., Azulay, J., Cantor, J., & Ashman, T.
journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
summary: Comprehensive systematic review and evidence-based practice guidelines for cognitive rehabilitation after TBI and stroke — categorizing interventions as Practice Standards, Guidelines, or Options across all cognitive domains.
researchFindings: Attention training (direct attention training and metacognitive strategy training) in the post-acute phase of TBI is a Practice Standard — the highest level of recommendation.
Compensatory memory strategy training using internal strategies and external aids is supported for mild memory impairment as a Practice Guideline.
Training of metacognitive strategies (self-monitoring, self-regulation) for functional task performance post-TBI is a Practice Guideline.
Comprehensive holistic neuropsychological rehabilitation programs for post-acute TBI are a Practice Standard.
Computer-based cognitive rehabilitation for attention post-stroke is a Practice Recommendation.
SLPs are directly implicated in delivering attention, memory, communication, and executive function interventions — the guidelines span the full scope of cognitive-communication practice.
clinicalApplication: Use the Cicerone practice standards hierarchy when making treatment decisions in cognitive-communication: prioritize Practice Standards (direct attention training, holistic rehabilitation) over lower-evidence options. For TBI clients: direct attention training (e.g., APT-3, structured hierarchical tasks) in the post-acute phase has the strongest evidence. For memory: external aid training (smartphones, memory notebooks, digital reminders) outperforms attempts to improve memory impairment directly — match aid complexity to the client's cognitive and technological capacity. Document which Cicerone evidence level supports each treatment target in your session notes — this strengthens medical necessity documentation substantially.

sessionStats.dose: Domain-specific; attention training typically 20–30 sessions
sessionStats.bestFit: Post-acute TBI, post-stroke cognitive deficits

bestFitCriteria: Adults with TBI or stroke presenting with deficits in attention, memory, executive function, or communication at the post-acute stage.
Clinicians selecting cognitive rehabilitation targets or approaches in acute, IPR, outpatient, or community re-entry settings.
Documentation of medical necessity for cognitive rehabilitation services citing the highest-level available evidence.
Interdisciplinary teams (OT, PT, neuropsychology, SLP) developing coordinated cognitive rehabilitation programs.

title: Evidence-Based Systematic Review: Effects of External Aids on Individuals With Moderate-Severe Traumatic Brain Injury
shortTitle: External Aids for TBI: Systematic Review
authors: Kennedy, M. R. T., Coelho, C., Turkstra, L., Ylvisaker, M., Moore Sohlberg, M., Yorkston, K., Chiou, H. H., & Kan, P. F.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: Systematic review establishing strong evidence that external memory and cognitive aids (notebooks, electronic devices, structured cueing systems) improve functional outcomes for adults with moderate-to-severe TBI.
researchFindings: External cognitive aids (memory notebooks, paging systems, smartphones, structured cueing hierarchies) have strong evidence for improving everyday functional task completion in moderate-to-severe TBI.
Errorless learning is the most consistently supported training approach for helping individuals with TBI learn to use external aids effectively.
Electronic devices (pagers, smartphones, reminder apps) had growing evidence at time of publication — the evidence base has continued to grow since 2008.
External aids are more effective than attempting to remediate memory impairment directly in moderate-to-severe TBI — the impairment may not be reversible, but the function can be compensated.
Systematic instruction (structured, repetitive training with the aid) is necessary — simply providing a device or notebook is insufficient.
Caregiver training in aid use and prompting strategies significantly improves generalization and maintenance.
clinicalApplication: For moderate-to-severe TBI clients: prioritize external aid training over attempts to improve memory directly — the evidence does not support that the underlying impairment is substantially modifiable, but compensatory function is achievable. Select aids appropriate to the client's technology literacy, severity of impairment, and daily routine (e.g., smartphone reminders for tech-savvy clients, structured memory notebook for those who are not). Use errorless learning for aid training: model correct use → guided practice → fading support → independent performance. Train caregivers to prompt aid use without doing the task for the client. Document specific aid targets, training steps, and generalization data.

sessionStats.dose: Systematic training typically 15–25 sessions before independent use
sessionStats.bestFit: Moderate-severe TBI with memory/executive function impairment

bestFitCriteria: Adults with moderate-to-severe TBI presenting with memory impairment that limits independent daily functioning.
Clients who have not made functional gains with direct memory remediation — shifting to compensatory aid-based approaches.
TBI rehabilitation at IPR, outpatient, or community re-entry level where functional independence is the primary goal.
Families and caregivers who are actively involved in supporting aid use at home.

title: Stuttering Treatment Research 1970–2005: Systematic Review Incorporating Trial Quality Assessment of Behavioral, Cognitive, and Related Approaches
shortTitle: Stuttering Treatment Systematic Review 1970–2005
authors: Bothe, A. K., Davidow, J. H., Bramlett, R. E., & Ingham, R. J.
summary: Comprehensive quality-weighted systematic review of 35 years of stuttering treatment research. Smooth speech (prolonged speech) and related fluency-shaping approaches had the most consistent evidence; cognitive and acceptance-based approaches had emerging support.
researchFindings: Smooth speech / prolonged speech approaches (slowed rate, gentle onset, continuous airflow) had the largest and most consistent evidence base across the 1970–2005 period.
Fluency-shaping techniques produced large effect sizes for reducing stuttering frequency, with good carryover in studies using real-world generalization measures.
Stuttering modification approaches (cancellation, pull-outs, preparatory sets) had a smaller evidence base but clinically meaningful outcomes for clients who value naturalness over fluency.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adjuncts reduced anxiety and negative attitudes about stuttering, but showed less consistent evidence for reducing stuttering frequency directly.
Electromyographic (EMG) biofeedback and other instrumental approaches had limited but positive evidence for select populations.
Trial quality varied substantially — many older studies lacked randomization, blinding, and adequate follow-up, limiting the strength of conclusions from that era.
clinicalApplication: For adult stuttering treatment, select the approach based on the client's personal goals: clients who prioritize fluency → fluency-shaping (smooth speech, prolonged speech, rate control, gentle onset); clients who prioritize naturalness and acceptance → stuttering modification (Mayo Clinic model, ACT-based approaches). Most adults with persistent developmental stuttering benefit from a hybrid approach: fluency tools for high-stakes situations + modification tools for daily communication + cognitive work on communication attitudes. Do not promise fluency — the evidence supports significant reduction, not elimination, and spontaneous relapse without ongoing practice is common. Monitor generalization explicitly: in-clinic fluency ≠ real-world fluency.

sessionStats.frequency: 2–3x/week active treatment; fade to monthly maintenance
sessionStats.dose: Fluency-shaping programs: typically 8–20 sessions intensive or 20–40 outpatient
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with persistent developmental stuttering

bestFitCriteria: Adults with persistent developmental stuttering presenting for outpatient or intensive treatment.
Clients who want to improve functional communication — whether through fluency or acceptance goals.
Clinicians selecting between fluency-shaping vs. stuttering modification vs. hybrid approaches.
Documentation of evidence-based stuttering treatment selection for authorization or program development.

title: Communicative Competence for Individuals who require Augmentative and Alternative Communication: A New Definition for a New Era of Communication?
shortTitle: Communicative Competence Framework for AAC
authors: Light, J., & McNaughton, D.
summary: Foundational framework redefining communicative competence for AAC users across four knowledge/skill domains — linguistic, operational, social, and strategic — updated for modern technology and expanded participation goals.
researchFindings: Communicative competence for AAC users is defined across four domains: linguistic competence (language knowledge), operational competence (device/system use), social competence (communication interaction), and strategic competence (compensatory strategies for barriers).

A fifth domain — psychosocial competence — is proposed in this updated framework: confidence, resilience, and a positive communication identity are essential outcomes, not just byproducts of treatment.
The framework emphasizes participation as the ultimate goal — not just producing messages, but engaging meaningfully in life roles and relationships.
Modern AAC technology (high-tech SGDs, apps, tablets) has expanded participation possibilities and demands updated competency targets, particularly in operational and social domains.
Goal setting for AAC intervention should be driven by the individual's participation priorities, not by arbitrary developmental sequences or device hierarchies.
The framework has informed AAC assessment, intervention planning, and outcome measurement across the lifespan.
clinicalApplication: Use the Light & McNaughton framework to structure AAC goal setting across all four domains — not just operational goals (turning on the device, navigating to vocabulary). For each AAC client, assess: linguistic (does vocabulary match communication needs?), operational (can they access the device efficiently in real-life contexts?), social (are they initiating, maintaining, and repairing in real conversations?), and strategic (do they have effective strategies when the device fails or communication breaks down?). The psychosocial domain is often neglected — address communication identity and confidence explicitly, especially for acquired AAC users post-stroke or TBI who may experience grief around AAC adoption. Participation goals should drive device selection and vocabulary organization.

sessionStats.bestFit: Any adult AAC user across settings and diagnoses

bestFitCriteria: Adults who use AAC (any modality — high-tech SGD, low-tech, multimodal) for primary communication.
Clinicians conducting comprehensive AAC assessment or updating a client's intervention plan.
Goal-setting for AAC users where participation-level outcomes need to be clearly defined and documented.
Adults who have recently acquired the need for AAC (post-stroke, ALS, TBI) and are adjusting to AAC as a communication system.

title: Treating Agrammatic Aphasia within a Linguistic Framework: Treatment of Underlying Forms
shortTitle: Treatment of Underlying Forms (TUF) for Agrammatism
authors: Thompson, C. K., & Shapiro, L. P.
summary: Describes the Treatment of Underlying Forms (TUF) approach for agrammatic aphasia, grounded in linguistic complexity theory — treating complex syntactic structures drives generalization to simpler untreated structures.
researchFindings: TUF operationalizes the Complexity Account of Treatment Efficacy (CATE): treating complex syntactic structures (e.g., object-moved wh-questions, passives) induces generalization to simpler syntactic structures not directly treated.
Treating simpler structures first does not induce generalization to more complex untreated structures — making complexity-first treatment more efficient.
TUF has been replicated across multiple participants with agrammatic aphasia in single-subject experimental designs with positive effects.
The approach is grounded in linguistic theory (Government Binding / Minimalist program) — treatment targets specific syntactic movement operations, not surface forms.
Generalization to untreated sentences of the same or simpler syntactic type is the primary evidence of therapeutic learning.
TUF is particularly appropriate for clients with non-fluent, agrammatic aphasia who produce simplified sentence structure (telegraphic speech, omitted functors and verb morphology).
clinicalApplication: TUF is the most theoretically grounded approach for agrammatic aphasia with sentence-level production deficits. Treatment targets complex sentence types (wh-movement, passives, object relatives) using a structured sequence: clinician production → repetition → picture description → unprompted production. The key clinical principle is to start with complex structures — do not warm up with simple sentences first, as this wastes treatment time and does not drive generalization in the right direction. TUF requires some background in syntactic structure to implement with fidelity; consult the treatment manual or Thompson Lab resources for stimulus sets. Most appropriate in outpatient settings with clients who have conversational goals around producing grammatical sentences.

sessionStats.dose: Typically 15–30 sessions before generalization is measurable
sessionStats.bestFit: Agrammatic non-fluent aphasia (Broca's, transcortical motor)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with agrammatic aphasia producing telegraphic or simplified sentences with omitted function words and verb morphology.
Clients whose sentence production goals involve producing grammatically complete utterances in conversation.
Outpatient or chronic aphasia settings where longer-term syntactic treatment is feasible.
Clinicians with some background in syntactic theory or access to TUF training/stimulus materials.

title: Training Volunteers as Conversation Partners using "Supported Conversation for Adults with Aphasia" (SCA): A Controlled Trial
shortTitle: Supported Conversation for Adults with Aphasia (SCA)
authors: Kagan, A., Black, S. E., Duchan, J. F., Simmons-Mackie, N., & Square, P.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: Controlled trial demonstrating that training volunteers in Supported Conversation for Adults with Aphasia (SCA) significantly improved the communicative competence of both partners — enabling more equitable conversations and increasing participation for people with aphasia.
researchFindings: Volunteers trained in SCA techniques showed significantly greater ability to acknowledge and reveal the competence of adults with aphasia in conversation compared to untrained volunteers.
Adults with aphasia had significantly more opportunities to communicate their thoughts, feelings, and knowledge when conversing with trained partners.

SCA trains partners to use acknowledgment techniques (confirming competence) and revelation techniques (creating opportunities for expression through multimodal supports like writing, gestures, and drawing).

The intervention targets the conversation partner, not the person with aphasia — recognizing that communication barriers often reside in the environment and partner behavior, not solely in the person with aphasia.
SCA principles align with the Life Participation Approach to Aphasia (LPAA) and WHO-ICF participation domain.
Gains in partner skill were maintained at follow-up assessment, suggesting training was durable.
clinicalApplication: Implement SCA training as a component of aphasia treatment, particularly for clients in the subacute or chronic phase where maximizing daily communication participation is a goal. Train family members, care staff, or volunteers using SCA principles: (1) acknowledge communicative competence verbally and nonverbally; (2) use multimodal supports (writing key words, gesture, drawing, pointing to pictures) to reveal what the person is trying to say. SCA is especially valuable in SNF, long-term care, and home health settings where the client's daily communication partners have more influence on quality of life than the SLP does. Document partner training as a skilled SLP service (it is) and track partner use of SCA strategies as an outcome measure.

sessionStats.frequency: Partner training: 2–4 group or individual sessions
sessionStats.dose: Structured training program; typically 6–10 hrs total for volunteers
sessionStats.bestFit: Any aphasia severity where partner skill is a barrier

bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia of any severity where daily communication quality is limited by partner skills and behaviors.
Clients in settings with consistent communication partners (family, care staff) who are willing to receive training.
Aphasia treatment programs with a Life Participation Approach orientation.
SNF, long-term care, or home health settings where maximizing communication participation is the primary goal.

title: Semantic Feature Analysis Treatment for Anomia in Two Fluent Aphasia Syndromes
shortTitle: Semantic Feature Analysis (SFA) for Anomia
authors: Boyle, M.
summary: Demonstrates that Semantic Feature Analysis (SFA) — a structured naming treatment using semantic feature maps — improves trained and untrained naming in fluent aphasia syndromes, with generalization to connected speech.
researchFindings: SFA produced significant improvements in naming accuracy for trained items in both participants with fluent aphasia syndromes (anomic and Wernicke's aphasia).
Generalization to untrained semantically related items was observed — evidence that SFA activates semantic networks beyond treated items.
Improvements extended to connected speech measures (information units in picture description), not just confrontation naming.
SFA procedure: for each target, the client generates or is cued to identify semantic features (group, action, properties, location, association) using a structured feature map.
The self-cueing process embedded in SFA — working through feature categories to access a word — is thought to strengthen semantic-lexical connections.
SFA is widely adopted in clinical practice for anomia across aphasia types; the evidence base across multiple studies (Boyle & Coelho, Wambaugh, others) is strong.
clinicalApplication: SFA is one of the most clinically accessible and widely-used naming treatments in aphasia practice. Use a feature map template with semantic categories (What group? What does it do? What does it look like? Where do you find it? What do you associate with it?) as a structured self-cueing framework. Begin with personally relevant, high-frequency vocabulary — items the client wants to use in daily communication, not random picture sets. As accuracy improves for trained items, monitor for generalization to semantically related untrained items and to connected speech. SFA can be easily adapted to app-based or paper-based home practice, and works well as a structured partner-assisted exercise for family members to facilitate at home.

sessionStats.dose: Typically 8–20 sessions for measurable naming gains
sessionStats.bestFit: Anomic, Wernicke's, Broca's aphasia with word retrieval deficit

bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia whose primary functional deficit is word retrieval (anomia) in conversation, picture description, or functional communication tasks.
Any aphasia type — SFA evidence spans fluent and non-fluent syndromes.
Clients in the subacute or chronic phase where naming treatment is a sustained treatment focus.
Home program integration: SFA feature maps can be facilitated by trained family members or aides between sessions.

title: Oral Reading for Language in Aphasia (ORLA): Evaluating the Efficacy of Computer-Delivered Therapy in Chronic Nonfluent Aphasia
shortTitle: ORLA: Oral Reading for Language in Aphasia
authors: Cherney, L. R.
summary: Describes and evaluates ORLA (Oral Reading for Language in Aphasia), a treatment in which clients repeatedly read aloud sentences and paragraphs aloud with the clinician and then independently — producing improvements in reading, expressive language, and sentence production.
researchFindings: Participants with chronic non-fluent aphasia showed improvements in oral reading accuracy and expressive language measures following ORLA treatment.
ORLA is based on principles of intensive massed practice: repeated oral reading of sentences and functional paragraphs aligned with the patient's daily life.
Computer-delivered ORLA (using the ORLA software) was as effective as clinician-delivered ORLA in producing reading and language gains, with implications for dose extension.
Treatment effects extended beyond reading to measures of expressive language and connected speech in some participants.
The neurological rationale for ORLA involves repeated auditory-articulatory coupling during oral reading, hypothesized to strengthen connections between auditory input and speech motor output.
ORLA is compatible with high-dose, intensive delivery and with home practice when the client has adequate reading ability as a starting point.
clinicalApplication: ORLA is particularly well-suited for non-fluent aphasia clients who have some preserved reading ability and want to improve spoken language fluency. Develop scripts from personally relevant, high-frequency content — appointment conversations, phone calls, family interactions. Sessions involve: (1) chorally reading with the clinician; (2) reading slightly after the clinician; (3) reading simultaneously; (4) reading independently. Systematic fading of the clinician's voice mirrors motor learning feedback-fading principles. The computer-based version (ORLA software, Rehabilitation Institute of Chicago) enables home practice and self-administered sessions, which is an important dose extender. Track progress with oral reading accuracy, reading rate, and connected speech samples.

sessionStats.dose: Minimum 10–20 sessions; home practice critical for dose
sessionStats.bestFit: Non-fluent aphasia with functional reading as a foundation

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic non-fluent aphasia (Broca's, transcortical motor) who have at least single-word reading ability as a foundation.
Clients where improving oral language production fluency (not just word retrieval) is a treatment priority.
Settings where home practice or computer-based self-administration can extend treatment dose.
Clients whose daily communication involves predictable, recurring conversational scripts that can be targeted directly.

title: Therapy for Naming Disorders: Revisiting, Revising, and Reviewing
shortTitle: Naming Therapy in Aphasia: Review of Approaches
authors: Nickels, L.
summary: Comprehensive systematic review of naming treatments for aphasia, comparing phonologically based, semantically based, and combined approaches. Finds that both semantic and phonological cuing treatments are effective, with client and deficit profile determining best fit.
researchFindings: Both semantically based treatments (SFA, semantic cuing hierarchies) and phonologically based treatments (phonemic cuing, word-sound cuing) produce naming improvements in aphasia.
No single treatment approach is universally superior — the optimal approach depends on the locus of the naming deficit (semantic access vs. phonological encoding vs. word form retrieval).
Phonological cuing treatments are most effective for clients with phonological encoding deficits; semantic treatments are most effective for clients with semantic access deficits.
Assessment of the naming deficit's cognitive locus (using error analysis and cueing hierarchies) should guide treatment selection — not arbitrary protocol assignment.

Maintenance and generalization vary across approaches: some treatments produce strong item-specific learning (trained items improve) with limited generalization; others show broader semantic network effects.
Self-cuing strategies embedded in treatment are a useful long-term approach for chronic anomia — clients can apply a personal cuing sequence independently in daily communication.
clinicalApplication: Use error analysis to profile each client's naming deficit before selecting a treatment approach. Semantic errors (naming related items) → semantic-level impairment → SFA or semantic cuing treatment. Phonological errors (sound-level errors, neologisms, no-response with good semantic knowledge) → phonological encoding deficit → phonemic cuing, word-sound similarity training. Mixed errors → combined approach. For clients with severe anomia across all cuing conditions, consider communication-strategy approaches (circumlocution, multimodal communication) rather than expecting item-specific naming recovery. Build self-cuing sequences into treatment early — teach the client a personal strategy to use in daily conversation, not just a set of trained words.

sessionStats.bestFit: Any aphasia type with word retrieval impairment

bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia of any type where naming deficit is the primary or co-occurring functional impairment.
Clinicians selecting between semantic vs. phonological naming treatment approaches based on error analysis.
Any aphasia client where treatment planning requires matching treatment to the underlying locus of deficit.

title: A Randomized Study of Three Interventions for Aspiration of Thin Liquids in Patients with Dementia or Parkinson's Disease
shortTitle: Three Interventions for Thin Liquid Aspiration: RCT
authors: Logemann, J. A., Gensler, G., Robbins, J., Lindblad, A. S., Brandt, D., Hind, J. A., Kosek, S., Lundy, D., McGarvey-Toler, S., Rademaker, A. W., Sharma, G., Sessler, C., Miller, R., & Panther, K.
summary: Large multi-site RCT (n=711) comparing chin-down posture, nectar-thick liquids, and honey-thick liquids for thin liquid aspiration in dementia and Parkinson's disease. Chin tuck had the fewest side effects; no significant difference in pneumonia rates at 3 months.
researchFindings: Three-arm RCT (n=711) comparing chin-down posture, nectar-thick liquids, and honey-thick liquids for thin liquid aspiration in dementia (n=351) and Parkinson's disease (n=360).
No significant difference in 3-month pneumonia incidence between the three interventions — all three produced comparable pneumonia rates.
Honey-thick liquids produced the best immediate in-study aspiration reduction during fluoroscopy; however, this did not translate to fewer pneumonia events at follow-up.
Participants assigned to honey-thick liquids were significantly more likely to be dehydrated at 3 months — an important safety and quality-of-life consideration.
Chin-down posture had the best side-effect profile and was preferred by participants and caregivers.
The study challenges the assumption that reducing aspiration frequency necessarily reduces pneumonia risk — other factors (oral hygiene, immune status, aspiration volume) are critical.
clinicalApplication: This landmark RCT should inform how you counsel patients and families about aspiration management options. The lack of a clear pneumonia-reducing winner between the three interventions means clinical decision-making must weigh individual factors: cognitive ability to use chin-down posture, palatability and compliance with thickened liquids, hydration status, and quality of life. For dementia patients: chin-down posture may be difficult to maintain independently; honey-thick liquids risk dehydration. Oral hygiene is likely a more powerful pneumonia-prevention lever than liquid modification alone — include oral care in every dysphagia management plan. Document your reasoning for texture/liquid recommendations in terms of the full risk-benefit picture, not just aspiration reduction in isolation.

sessionStats.bestFit: Dementia or PD with thin liquid aspiration confirmed on instrumental assessment

bestFitCriteria: Adults with dementia or Parkinson's disease and confirmed thin liquid aspiration on MBSS or FEES.
Decision-making about compensatory liquid modification strategies vs. postural compensation.
Clinical counseling conversations with families and caregivers about aspiration risk, pneumonia, and hydration tradeoffs.
Ethics and goals-of-care discussions where quality of life and aspiration risk must be balanced.

title: Predictors of Aspiration Pneumonia: How Important Is Dysphagia?
shortTitle: Predictors of Aspiration Pneumonia
authors: Langmore, S. E., Terpenning, M. S., Schork, A., Chen, Y., Murray, J. T., Lopatin, D., & Loesche, W. J.
summary: Landmark prospective study identifying the most powerful predictors of aspiration pneumonia. Oral hygiene and dependency for feeding were stronger independent predictors than dysphagia alone, reframing how pneumonia risk should be managed.
researchFindings: Dysphagia was a significant but not the dominant predictor of aspiration pneumonia — oral hygiene status was an equally powerful independent predictor.
Poor oral hygiene (dental plaque, periodontal disease, high oral bacterial counts) was the single most powerful modifiable risk factor for aspiration pneumonia.
Dependency for oral care (inability to clean one's own teeth/mouth) was a strong independent risk factor — largely a proxy for severity of physical and cognitive impairment.

Tube feeding did not protect against aspiration pneumonia; PEG-tube patients still developed pneumonia at comparable rates — microaspiration of oropharyngeal secretions persists regardless of oral intake status.
Multiple risk factors interact: dysphagia + poor oral hygiene + dependency + respiratory compromise = highest pneumonia risk.
The study reframes aspiration pneumonia from a "swallowing problem" to a multi-factorial medical risk requiring a team-based prevention approach.
clinicalApplication: Oral hygiene is as important as dietary modification in aspiration pneumonia prevention — and often more actionable. Include specific oral hygiene recommendations in every dysphagia treatment plan: tooth brushing 2x/day (even for patients on tube feeding), removal of dentures at night, professional dental care, and nursing/caregiver training in oral hygiene protocols. Communicate directly with nursing staff in inpatient settings about oral care as a medical necessity.
