summary: Controlled comparison demonstrating that internet-delivered stuttering treatment (smooth speech program) produced equivalent outcomes to telephone delivery, with both telehealth formats achieving similar fluency gains to clinic-based treatment — supporting telehealth as a viable delivery mode for stuttering.
researchFindings: Internet-delivered and telephone-delivered smooth speech stuttering treatment produced equivalent outcomes on percent syllables stuttered (%SS) and speaking rate at post-treatment and follow-up.
Both telehealth formats produced outcomes comparable to published results from face-to-face delivery of the same smooth speech program.
Telehealth delivery significantly reduces barriers to stuttering treatment for adults in rural or underserved areas, or those with work/family scheduling constraints.

Generalization tasks completed in the client's real-world environment (rather than the clinic) are a natural advantage of telehealth — clients practice in the actual speaking contexts they want to improve.
Client satisfaction with telehealth delivery was high; technical issues (connectivity) were the primary reported limitation at the time of the study.
Outcome generalization from the treatment room to daily life is a consistent challenge in stuttering treatment — telehealth delivery may offer an inherent ecological advantage.
clinicalApplication: Telehealth is a well-supported delivery mode for stuttering treatment — not a second-tier option. For adults with persistent developmental stuttering, offer telehealth as a primary delivery option when clinic access is limited, when work or family obligations limit attendance, or when the client is geographically distant. The smooth speech / fluency-shaping format used in the O'Brian studies is highly compatible with video-based telehealth: clinicians can monitor rate, airflow, and onset via video as effectively as in person. Assign real-world practice tasks during telehealth sessions that leverage the client's home and community environments — the in-home setting eliminates the "transfer out of clinic" problem that often limits stuttering treatment generalization.

sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with persistent stuttering in any geographic setting; rural and underserved populations

bestFitCriteria: Adults with persistent developmental stuttering who have scheduling, geographic, or access barriers to in-person clinic attendance.
Any stuttering treatment program offering telehealth as a delivery mode.
Fluency-shaping treatment programs (smooth speech, prolonged speech) where online delivery is planned.

title: Anxiety and Stuttering: Continuing to Explore a Complex Relationship
shortTitle: Anxiety and Stuttering: Clinical Implications
authors: Iverach, L., & Rapee, R. M.
summary: Review establishing that social anxiety disorder co-occurs in approximately 40% of adults who stutter — significantly higher than population norms — with clinical implications for integrated treatment of stuttering and anxiety.
researchFindings: Adults who stutter have significantly elevated rates of social anxiety disorder (SAD) compared to the general population — approximately 40% meet diagnostic criteria for SAD.
Social anxiety in people who stutter is often specifically triggered by speaking situations — not a general anxiety disorder — making it directly relevant to stuttering treatment.
Avoidance behaviors (avoiding calls, presentations, job interviews, social situations) driven by anxiety about stuttering significantly compound the disability beyond the disfluency itself.
Stuttering-specific anxiety is often under-treated in speech therapy because SLPs may not screen for it, and mental health providers may not address the speech-specific dimension.
Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for social anxiety, combined with speech treatment, produces better outcomes than speech treatment alone for adults with co-occurring stuttering and anxiety.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) applied to stuttering addresses experiential avoidance and psychological flexibility — with promising emerging evidence for reducing stuttering-related suffering.
clinicalApplication: Screen every adult who stutters for social anxiety and avoidance using tools like the Overall Assessment of the Speaker's Experience of Stuttering (OASES) and a simple anxiety screener (GAD-7 or PHQ-9). When elevated anxiety or avoidance is identified, the treatment plan should explicitly address both the fluency and the anxiety dimensions. Options: integrate CBT techniques (cognitive restructuring, graduated exposure to feared speaking situations) directly into fluency treatment; refer to a psychologist for concurrent CBT/ACT; or use ACT-based fluency treatment (Acceptance and Commitment Therapy approaches adapted for stuttering). Do not assume that achieving better fluency will automatically reduce anxiety — for some clients, the opposite is needed first.

sessionStats.bestFit: Adults who stutter with elevated social anxiety, avoidance, or psychological distress

bestFitCriteria: Adults who stutter presenting with avoidance of speaking situations, social anxiety, or significant emotional distress related to stuttering.
Stuttering treatment programs where the gap between in-clinic fluency and real-world communication participation is large — anxiety and avoidance may be the limiting factor.
Cases where referral for concurrent psychological treatment (CBT, ACT) is clinically appropriate.

title: AAC for Adults with Acquired Neurological Conditions: A Review
shortTitle: AAC for Adults with Acquired Neurological Conditions
authors: Beukelman, D. R., Fager, S., Ball, L., & Dietz, A.
summary: Comprehensive review of AAC for adults with acquired neurological conditions including ALS, TBI, stroke/aphasia, and other degenerative diseases — covering device selection, implementation, and outcome evidence for each population.
researchFindings: AAC for acquired neurological conditions requires population-specific approaches: ALS needs proactive timing and voice banking; aphasia requires vocabulary organization matching language deficits; TBI requires cognitively accessible design.
For ALS: AAC introduction should be proactive — before intelligibility is severely compromised — and voice banking should begin while speech is still adequate for high-quality recording.
For aphasia: high-tech AAC (speech-generating devices, apps) combined with multimodal communication (gesture, writing, drawing) produces better functional outcomes than either alone.
For TBI: AAC system complexity must be matched to the client's cognitive and linguistic profile — overly complex systems are abandoned; simple, accessible systems are used.
Abandonment of AAC devices is a persistent clinical problem — careful matching of device features to user needs and robust training are the primary prevention strategies.
The evidence base for AAC in acquired populations is growing but remains smaller than for developmental AAC — more RCT evidence is needed across all acquired neurological conditions.
clinicalApplication: Match AAC system design to the specific acquired neurological condition and its trajectory. For progressive conditions (ALS, PD, MS): plan proactively and sequence AAC supports ahead of functional decline — waiting until speech is unintelligible results in rushed decisions under crisis conditions. For static acquired conditions (stroke, TBI): AAC may serve different roles over time — initial compensatory communication → rehabilitation scaffold → long-term communication system. Abandonment prevention requires comprehensive training for both the client and communication partners, ongoing technical support, and regular system updates as needs change. Document AAC trials, rejection rationale, and final recommendations with the specificity needed for insurance authorization.

sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with acquired neurological conditions affecting speech and language

bestFitCriteria: Adults with ALS, TBI, stroke, aphasia, or other acquired neurological conditions where speech is insufficient for daily communication needs.
Clients in the early stages of progressive disease where proactive AAC planning is clinically indicated.
AAC evaluation and trial for any acquired communication disorder where high-tech or low-tech augmentative communication is being considered.

title: The Societal Role of AAC: How Does it Affect the Social Participation of Adults with Complex Communication Needs?
shortTitle: AAC and Social Participation for Complex Needs
authors: Baxter, S., Enderby, P., Evans, P., & Judge, S.
summary: Systematic review examining the evidence for AAC improving social participation in adults with complex communication needs — finding consistent positive effects on participation, quality of life, and communication effectiveness across multiple populations and device types.
researchFindings: Systematic review of 30 studies examining AAC outcomes in adults with complex communication needs (ALS, aphasia, TBI, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy, and other conditions).

AAC consistently improved communication effectiveness and social participation across included studies — positive effects were found across high-tech SGD, low-tech symbol systems, and multimodal communication.
Quality of life improvements were documented alongside communication outcomes in studies measuring both.
The greatest participation gains were seen when AAC systems were matched to the individual's specific communication needs and participation goals, rather than generic device assignment.
Partner training and environmental support were identified as critical mediators of participation outcomes — AAC technology alone is insufficient without social and environmental accommodations.
Evidence quality varied; many studies used small samples and pre-post designs — larger RCTs are needed, but the consistent direction of findings supports AAC as participation-improving.
clinicalApplication: Use this systematic review evidence when justifying AAC for adults with complex communication needs to payers or medical teams who question whether AAC "works." The evidence consistently shows participation and quality of life benefit across populations and device types. Critically, match the AAC system to individual participation goals — what specific activities and relationships does the client want to engage in, and what does their communication need to do to support those? Document participation-level goals (attending family events, using the phone, returning to work) alongside device-level goals in AAC treatment plans. Partner and environmental support are not optional — include them in the AAC plan as essential components, not add-ons.

sessionStats.sessionLength: AAC evaluation: 2–4 hrs; training and follow-up: 10–20+ sessions
sessionStats.bestFit: Any adult with complex communication needs requiring AAC

bestFitCriteria: Any adult with complex communication needs where AAC justification is needed for payer or team.
AAC evaluation cases where participation-level goals need to be explicitly defined and measured.
Adults with acquired or congenital communication needs in any medical or community setting.

title: The iPad and Mobile Technology Revolution: Benefits and Challenges for Individuals who require Augmentative and Alternative Communication
shortTitle: iPad and Mobile Technology for AAC
authors: McNaughton, D., & Light, J.
summary: Examines the benefits and clinical challenges of iPad and mobile technology as AAC tools, establishing frameworks for evidence-based integration of apps into AAC practice — addressing both the promise of accessible, low-cost AAC and the risks of unsupported device adoption.
researchFindings: Mobile devices (iPad, Android tablets, smartphones) have dramatically increased access to AAC technology by lowering cost barriers — high-quality AAC apps are available at a fraction of the cost of dedicated SGDs.
The social acceptability of mobile devices is significantly higher than dedicated AAC devices — reducing stigma concerns for adults and adolescents.
The proliferation of apps requires clinicians to apply rigorous evaluation frameworks — not all apps with "AAC" labeling are clinically appropriate, and app quality varies enormously.
Customization, vocabulary organization, symbol systems, and motor access must be evaluated for each client — a specific app may be ideal for one client and inappropriate for another.
Frame shifts: mobile technology has shifted AAC from specialist-only equipment to a mainstream technology accessible to clients, families, and SLPs without high-tech equipment procurement barriers.
Ongoing training, follow-up, and system updating remain critical — clients who receive a device or app without comprehensive implementation support have poor outcomes.
clinicalApplication: When considering AAC apps for adults with acquired communication needs, apply a systematic evaluation framework: does the app support the client's vocabulary needs? Is the access method appropriate (touch, switch, eye gaze)? Is the symbol system or text-based layout suitable for the client's language and literacy profile? Test multiple apps in trial periods before final recommendation. For insurance purposes, determine whether an app on a consumer device constitutes a covered SGD — this varies by payer. Document app features, vocabulary organization rationale, and access method in the AAC evaluation. Critically, prescribe training alongside the app — the evidence consistently shows that unsupported app adoption leads to abandonment.

sessionStats.bestFit: Any adult requiring AAC where mobile technology is an appropriate access modality

bestFitCriteria: Adults with acquired communication needs where iPad or mobile device-based AAC is being considered.
AAC evaluations where low-cost, socially acceptable AAC technology is a priority.
Clinicians evaluating communication apps for clinical recommendation — applying evidence-based selection criteria.

title: Promoting Acceptance of Augmentative and Alternative Communication by Adults with Acquired Communication Disorders
shortTitle: AAC Acceptance in Adults with Acquired Disorders
authors: Lasker, J., & Bedrosian, J.
summary: Addresses the significant clinical challenge of AAC acceptance in adults with acquired communication disorders — distinguishing device-level barriers from psychological adjustment barriers, and providing frameworks for facilitating genuine AAC adoption.
researchFindings: Adults with acquired communication disorders (ALS, stroke, TBI) frequently resist AAC introduction — resistance stems from device-level factors (usability, acceptability) AND psychological factors (identity, grief, denial of communication decline).
For ALS patients: AAC acceptance is closely tied to psychological adjustment to the disease — clients who have not accepted their diagnosis often refuse AAC regardless of communication decline.
Communication identity — how a person views their voice and communication style as part of their self-concept — is a powerful psychological barrier to AAC acceptance in acquired disorders.
Partner involvement is a critical mediator of acceptance: partners who are also resistant to AAC significantly reduce the likelihood of client adoption.
Staged counseling approaches, peer support from AAC users with similar diagnoses, and gradual introduction of low-tech tools before high-tech SGDs can reduce acceptance barriers.
Voice banking before loss of natural voice supports AAC acceptance by preserving a personalized voice quality in the SGD — reducing the sense of identity loss.
clinicalApplication: Address AAC acceptance as a clinical goal alongside device selection and training. For ALS clients: start the AAC conversation early and frame it as preserving communication control — not replacing speech. Involve the AAC community (peer support groups, AAC user networks) alongside clinical services. For stroke/aphasia clients: acknowledge the grief of losing natural voice and the identity implications of AAC use; do not rush adoption. Use graduated low-tech tools first (alphabet boards, communication books) to build comfort and partner familiarity before introducing high-tech SGDs. Partner counseling around communication identity and acceptance is skilled SLP work — document it as such. Voice banking (ModelTalker, VocaliD) for ALS is a powerful acceptance facilitator when started early.

sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with acquired communication disorders where AAC resistance or delayed adoption is a clinical barrier

bestFitCriteria: Adults with ALS who are resistant to AAC introduction despite declining speech intelligibility.
Adults with aphasia or TBI for whom psychological adjustment to acquired communication impairment is delaying functional AAC use.
Any AAC evaluation where the client or communication partner expresses resistance, grief, or identity-based concerns about AAC adoption.
ALS clients who are candidates for voice banking — early acceptance work enables better voice banking outcomes.

title: Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System for Voice Therapy: Application to Everyday Clinical Care
shortTitle: RTSS Framework Applied to Voice Therapy
authors: Wolfberg, J., Whyte, J., Doyle, P., Gherson, S., Muise, J., Petty, B., Tolejano, C. J., Hillman, R. E., Stadelman-Cohen, T., & Van Stan, J. H.
summary: Applies the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System (RTSS) to voice therapy to improve treatment precision, reproducibility, and research translation. A practical framework for structured clinical decision-making across voice disorders.
researchFindings: The Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System (RTSS) provides a structured framework to explicitly define what a treatment is doing, to what target, and through what mechanism.
Applying RTSS to voice therapy reveals that many treatments share active ingredients (e.g., increasing respiratory support, altering vocal tract shape) even when they carry different procedure names.
RTSS separates treatment ingredients from the procedures used to deliver them — allowing clinicians to identify which component of a treatment is doing the therapeutic work.
The framework improves reproducibility of clinical decisions and documentation, and supports translation of research findings to practice.
Case examples across common voice disorders (hyperfunctional voice, phonotrauma, neurogenic voice disorders) demonstrate RTSS application in everyday clinical care.
RTSS-structured reporting in voice therapy research would allow better synthesis across studies and more precise clinical recommendations.
clinicalApplication: Use the RTSS framework to make your voice therapy more intentional and documentable. When selecting a voice technique (e.g., resonant voice, SOVT exercises, flow phonation, vocal function exercises), explicitly identify: (1) the therapeutic target (e.g., reducing laryngeal tension, increasing subglottal pressure), (2) the active ingredient (e.g., altered vocal tract impedance), and (3) the mechanism of change (e.g., reduced collision forces on vocal folds). This precision is especially useful when explaining treatment rationale to the interdisciplinary team, documenting skilled care for payers, or adapting techniques when a client is not responding as expected. The RTSS lens also helps you recognize when two different-sounding techniques are actually targeting the same mechanism — and when to switch to something genuinely different.

sessionStats.dose: Framework applies across treatment durations
sessionStats.bestFit: Any voice disorder population

bestFitCriteria: Any adult voice disorder client where treatment selection rationale needs to be explicitly documented (payer justification, IPR team communication, supervision).
Clinicians building or refining voice therapy programs who want to audit which active ingredients their treatment is delivering.
Voice therapy cases with plateau or poor response where re-analysis of treatment targets is needed.
SLPs completing CEU learning or clinical fellowship supervision in voice disorders who want a structured framework for treatment reasoning.

title: Using Spaced-Retrieval as an Intervention During Speech-Language Therapy
shortTitle: Spaced Retrieval Training for Dementia and MCI
authors: Brush, J. A., & Camp, C. J.
summary: Foundational paper establishing spaced retrieval training (SRT) as an SLP intervention for individuals with dementia. SRT leverages preserved procedural memory through gradually expanding recall intervals — enabling functional new learning even in moderate-stage dementia.
researchFindings: Spaced retrieval training works by having the client successfully recall target information at gradually increasing time intervals — starting at 30 seconds and doubling with each successful recall.
The approach harnesses procedural (implicit) memory, which is relatively preserved in Alzheimer's disease compared to episodic (declarative) memory.

Participants with dementia successfully learned and retained functional information (clinician names, safety procedures, swallowing compensatory strategies) using SRT — information they could not retain with conventional practice.
If a recall attempt fails, the interval is shortened by half and the information is represented — minimizing errors and frustration (errorless learning principle).
Spaced retrieval gains have been maintained at follow-up across multiple studies, demonstrating durable retention, not just in-session performance.
Clinical targets demonstrated in the original work include: learning a therapist's name, recalling one personally important fact, and retaining a dysphagia compensatory maneuver.
clinicalApplication: SRT is one of the most clinically practical memory interventions in the SLP scope for dementia and MCI. The protocol: (1) identify a personally relevant target (caregiver name, medication time, chin tuck technique, safety procedure); (2) present the target and immediately test recall; (3) if correct, double the interval; (4) if incorrect, shorten by half and represent. Begin at intervals matched to the client's current retention ability — severely impaired clients may start at 15–30 seconds. Keep sessions focused on 3–5 high-priority targets rather than a broad list. SRT can be embedded within standard SLP sessions and taught to caregivers or nursing staff for daily practice between sessions. Dysphagia application: SRT is particularly powerful for teaching clients with dementia to use compensatory swallowing techniques (chin tuck, small sips) at meals — a Medicare-billable skilled SLP intervention when documented with functional dysphagia goals.

sessionStats.dose: 3–5 target items per session; 4–8 week training blocks
sessionStats.bestFit: Mild–moderate dementia or MCI with functional memory or dysphagia goals

bestFitCriteria: Adults with MCI or mild-to-moderate dementia where functional memory goals are appropriate (names, schedules, safety procedures, compensatory strategies).
Patients with sufficient sustained attention to engage in brief structured recall practice.
Dysphagia treatment in dementia: teaching and reinforcing compensatory swallowing techniques when motor learning is impaired.
Any dementia client where caregiver training in a structured, evidence-based memory technique is a component of the intervention plan.

title: Cognitive Stimulation to Improve Cognitive Functioning in People With Dementia
shortTitle: Cognitive Stimulation Therapy for Dementia: Cochrane Review
authors: Woods, B., Aguirre, E., Spector, A. E., & Orrell, M.
summary: Cochrane systematic review of 15 RCTs showing cognitive stimulation therapy (CST) significantly improves cognition and quality of life in mild-to-moderate dementia — and enhances the effects of cholinesterase inhibitor medication. The only non-pharmacological dementia intervention recommended by UK NICE guidelines.
researchFindings: Meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found CST produced statistically and clinically significant improvements in cognitive function compared to control conditions.
Quality of life also improved significantly with CST — making CST one of the few non-pharmacological dementia interventions with concurrent evidence for both cognition and QoL.
CST enhanced the effects of acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (AChEI) medications — participants on AChEIs who also received CST showed greater cognitive gains than those on medication alone.
Standard CST protocol: 14 twice-weekly sessions in groups of 5–8 participants, each 45 minutes, structured around themed activities (current affairs, word association, categorization, sensory tasks).
Benefits were found across dementia etiologies and mild-to-moderate severity levels.
Maintenance CST (weekly follow-up sessions beyond the 14-session program) has been shown to sustain and extend initial cognitive and QoL gains.
clinicalApplication: CST is the highest-level non-pharmacological cognitive intervention for dementia within SLP scope. The 14-session twice-weekly group format is feasible in SNF, adult day programs, outpatient memory clinics, and community settings. SLPs are particularly suited to lead CST groups given the communication-rich format — sessions use verbal discussion, categorization, word tasks, reminiscence, and group interaction to stimulate cognitive processing. Beyond cognition and QoL, SLPs can simultaneously track communication participation outcomes (turn-taking, topic maintenance, initiation) within each session. After the 14-session program, schedule maintenance CST (weekly sessions) to sustain gains. Pair with individual spaced retrieval training (Brush & Camp) for clients who also need specific functional memory goals alongside group stimulation. Document CST as skilled SLP service targeting cognitive-communication deficits and group participation.

sessionStats.dose: 14 sessions (7 weeks); then maintenance CST ongoing
sessionStats.bestFit: Mild–moderate dementia; group-capable patients in SNF, day programs, or memory clinics

bestFitCriteria: Adults with mild-to-moderate dementia (any etiology) who are able to engage in a small group setting.
SNF, adult day programs, memory clinics, or outpatient settings where group cognitive programming is feasible.
Dementia patients on cholinesterase inhibitor medication where augmenting pharmacological treatment with behavioral intervention is a goal.
Any dementia client where cognitive functioning, quality of life, and social engagement are treatment priorities.

title: Algorithmic Spaced Retrieval Enhances Long-Term Memory in Alzheimer Disease: Case-Control Pilot Study
shortTitle: Algorithmic Spaced Retrieval for Alzheimer's Disease
authors: Niu, Y., Zhang, Q., Liu, J., & Chen, H.
summary: A machine-learning algorithm that adapts spacing intervals based on individual memory performance significantly enhanced long-term retention compared to fixed-interval spaced retrieval in adults with AD.
researchFindings: Algorithmic spaced retrieval produced significantly greater long-term retention than fixed-interval practice in participants with mild AD.
The adaptive algorithm adjusted recall intervals based on each individual's real-time performance, reducing failed retrieval attempts.
Gains in target information retention were maintained at 4-week follow-up in the algorithmic group but not in the control group.
Participants and caregivers reported high acceptability and low burden for the app-delivered training format.
clinicalApplication: Spaced retrieval training (SRT) is already an established SLP technique for memory compensation in MCI and dementia — this study supports using adaptive, performance-based spacing rather than fixed intervals. In practice, this means starting with shorter recall intervals (e.g., 30 seconds) and systematically increasing them only when the patient demonstrates successful retrieval. Apps that automate this spacing can supplement clinical sessions. Target personally relevant information: caregiver names, medication schedules, daily routines, or safety procedures. Pair with errorless learning principles to minimize frustration during failed retrievals.

sessionStats.dose: 5–10 target items per session
sessionStats.bestFit: Mild–moderate AD or MCI

bestFitCriteria: Adults with mild cognitive impairment or early-to-mid stage Alzheimer's disease.
Patients with functional memory goals (remembering names, schedules, routines, safety information).
Patients with adequate attention to engage in structured recall practice.
Caregivers available to assist with home practice between sessions.

title: The "Counseling+" Roles of the Speech-Language Pathologist Serving Older Adults With Mild Cognitive Impairment and Dementia From Alzheimer's Disease
shortTitle: Counseling+ Roles of SLP in MCI and Dementia
authors: Bourgeois, M. S., & Hickey, E. M.
journal: Perspectives of the ASHA Special Interest Groups
summary: Defines the expanded scope of the SLP working with MCI and early dementia — beyond direct impairment treatment to include caregiver coaching, life participation support, and psychosocial counseling.
researchFindings: SLPs are uniquely positioned to address both the communication and cognitive-linguistic needs of individuals with MCI and dementia.
The "Counseling+" framework includes informational counseling, supportive counseling, caregiver training, and advocacy beyond direct skill training.
Early SLP involvement in MCI may slow functional decline by establishing compensatory strategies before impairment is severe.
Caregiver communication training is among the most evidence-supported SLP interventions for maintaining quality of life in dementia.
clinicalApplication: This article establishes the clinical rationale for SLPs to take an active role early in the MCI/dementia trajectory — not just when communication is severely impaired. In practice, SLPs working with this population should incorporate: (1) early counseling about anticipated communication changes, (2) memory aid training before severe impairment sets in, (3) structured caregiver communication coaching, and (4) life participation goal-setting that addresses what matters most to the patient. Use validated tools like the Functional Linguistic Communication Inventory (FLCI) and Dementia Rating Scale to track progress.

sessionStats.bestFit: MCI or early-stage dementia

bestFitCriteria: Adults newly diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer's disease.
Patients and families seeking guidance on what to expect and how to prepare.
Caregivers struggling with communication breakdown or behavioral changes.
Patients motivated to establish compensatory strategies while insight is intact.

title: Living Successfully With Chronic Aphasia: Outcomes and Program Improvement After 5 Years of Operations
shortTitle: Living Successfully With Chronic Aphasia: 5-Year LPAA Outcomes
authors: Martin, N., Drager, K., & Snider, S.
summary: A 5-year follow-up of an aphasia center program using Life Participation Approach values shows sustained improvements in quality of life and communication participation, supporting LPAA as a long-term clinical framework.
researchFindings: Participants in an LPAA-based aphasia center program maintained or improved quality-of-life scores over 5 years on the SAQOL-39.
Sustained engagement in meaningful communication activities was associated with better long-term outcomes than impairment-focused treatment alone.
Caregiver well-being also showed improvement, suggesting benefits extend beyond the person with aphasia.
Program adaptations over 5 years based on participant feedback improved adherence and perceived benefit.
clinicalApplication: The Life Participation Approach to Aphasia (LPAA) shifts focus from reducing impairment to re-engaging patients in the communicative activities that matter most to them. In practice, this means starting each episode of care by identifying the patient's participation priorities — returning to a hobby, communicating with grandchildren, resuming volunteer work — and building treatment goals around re-enabling those activities. Supported conversation techniques, multimodal communication, and caregiver coaching are core LPAA tools. This study supports continuing LPAA-based programming even into the chronic phase of aphasia, where impairment-based gains may plateau but participation can still improve.

sessionStats.bestFit: Chronic aphasia (6+ months post-onset)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic aphasia (any severity) who have plateaued in impairment-based treatment.
Patients expressing frustration with social isolation or loss of meaningful activities.
Patients with communicative partners (family, caregivers) willing to participate in treatment.
Any post-stroke aphasia patient where quality of life and life participation are the primary goals.

title: Endoscopic and Videofluoroscopic Evaluations of Swallowing for Dysphagia: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: FEES vs. VFSS for Dysphagia: Systematic Review
authors: Dinis, R., Fernandes, A., & Costa, M.
summary: A 2025 systematic review finds FEES has slightly superior sensitivity for detecting pharyngeal residue and aspiration compared to VFSS, but both tools provide comparable diagnostic accuracy overall — supporting clinical selection based on patient factors and setting availability.
researchFindings: FEES demonstrated higher sensitivity for detecting pharyngeal residue, penetration, and aspiration compared to VFSS across included studies.
FEES showed slightly better detection of premature spillage into the pharynx before the swallow trigger.
No significant differences were found between FEES and VFSS for overall diagnostic accuracy of dysphagia.
Clinical selection of the appropriate instrumental assessment should be based on patient tolerance, setting resources, and the specific swallowing behaviors in question.
clinicalApplication: This review supports using clinical judgment and patient/setting factors when choosing between FEES and VFSS rather than defaulting to one tool universally. FEES may be preferable when pharyngeal residue or silent aspiration is the primary concern, when the patient cannot tolerate fluoroscopy positioning, or when bedside access is needed (e.g., ICU). VFSS remains valuable for visualizing the oral preparatory phase, esophageal function, and swallowing biomechanics across all phases. Use this evidence to justify your instrumental assessment choice in documentation and to guide interprofessional conversations about referral pathways.

sessionStats.bestFit: Neurogenic or structural dysphagia requiring instrumental assessment

bestFitCriteria: Adults with suspected neurogenic dysphagia (stroke, ALS, PD, TBI) requiring instrumental swallowing evaluation.
Patients with clinical signs of silent aspiration where bedside evaluation is insufficient.
Settings where both FEES and VFSS are available and the clinician is determining which is most appropriate.
Documentation or team communication situations requiring justification of instrumental assessment choice.

title: A Systematic Review on Dysphagia Treatments for Persons Living With Dementia
shortTitle: Dysphagia Treatment in Dementia: Systematic Review
authors: Rogus-Pulia, N., Malandraki, G. A., & Johnson, S.
summary: This systematic review synthesizes the evidence for dysphagia interventions in people living with dementia — a high-need, underresearched population — and identifies which approaches have the strongest support.
researchFindings: Compensatory strategies (texture modification, postural adjustments, pacing) have the most consistent evidence for reducing aspiration risk in persons with dementia.
Direct rehabilitative swallowing exercises have limited evidence in dementia due to motor learning challenges, though modified approaches show promise.
Environmental modifications — reduced distractions, optimized positioning, smaller bites — significantly improved meal safety and intake.
Caregiver and nursing staff training in dysphagia management was among the most impactful interventions given reliance on care partners at mealtimes.
clinicalApplication: When treating dysphagia in a patient with dementia, prioritize compensatory strategies and environmental modifications over exercise-based rehabilitation, as the capacity for new motor learning is reduced. Key clinical strategies include: texture-modified diets using IDDSI standards, upright positioning during all oral intake, limiting distractions at mealtimes, cueing sequences for swallowing initiation, and training all care partners (family and nursing staff) on safe feeding techniques. Document caregiver training thoroughly as it is often the intervention with the highest impact. Reserve direct swallowing exercises for patients in earlier stages with sufficient cognitive engagement.

sessionStats.bestFit: Mild–severe dementia with dysphagia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with any stage of dementia presenting with dysphagia or reduced oral intake.
Patients with recurrent aspiration pneumonia or unexplained weight loss.
Patients requiring mealtime support from caregivers or nursing staff.
Settings where caregiver or staff training is feasible and appropriate.

title: Behavioral Treatment for Speech and Language in Primary Progressive Aphasia and Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: Behavioral Treatment for Primary Progressive Aphasia
authors: Wauters, L. D., Croot, K., Dial, H. R., Duffy, J. R., Grasso, S. M., Kim, E., Schaffer Mendez, K., Ballard, K. J., Clark, H. M., Kohley, L., Murray, L. L., Rogalski, E. J., Figeys, M., Milman, L., & Henry, M. L.
summary: Systematic review of behavioral treatment for all PPA variants and primary progressive apraxia of speech. Word-finding and naming treatment show the strongest evidence — effects are real and item-specific — establishing that treatment is not futile even in a progressive condition.
researchFindings: Behavioral speech and language treatment produces meaningful, measurable gains in PPA — treatment is not futile despite the progressive nature of the condition.

Word-finding and naming treatment (semantic and phonological approaches) showed the most consistent evidence across PPA variants — effects are typically item-specific (trained items improve more than untrained).
Script training and conversational approaches showed evidence for improving functional communication in personally relevant, targeted contexts.
Treatment effects were found across all three PPA variants (nonfluent/agrammatic, semantic, logopenic), though optimal approaches differ by variant.
For nonfluent/agrammatic PPA and primary progressive apraxia of speech: motor speech and proactive AAC interventions alongside language treatment are important given the speech production component.
Maintenance of treated items over time was variable — spaced review and overlearning strategies may support longer-lasting retention in a progressive condition.
clinicalApplication: PPA is not a contraindication to SLP treatment. Tailor the approach to the PPA variant: for semantic variant PPA, prioritize personally relevant word-finding therapy targeting high-value vocabulary that the client is losing; for nonfluent/agrammatic PPA, address both language and motor speech components and introduce AAC proactively; for logopenic PPA, target sentence-level production and memory support strategies given the working memory component of this variant. Use overlearning and spaced review to maximize retention of treated items given progressive memory impairment. Introduce AAC early in the disease trajectory — not only when communication breaks down — so the patient can contribute to system design and practice while insight and motor control are preserved. Document rationale for treating a progressive condition explicitly: SLP services maintain functional communication as long as possible, delay dependence on alternative communication, and support the patient and family during a difficult diagnostic journey.

sessionStats.dose: Ongoing; reassess goals every 3–6 months as condition progresses
sessionStats.bestFit: All PPA variants; early-to-mid stage of progression

bestFitCriteria: Adults with any variant of primary progressive aphasia (semantic, nonfluent/agrammatic, logopenic) or primary progressive apraxia of speech.
Patients and families seeking evidence that SLP treatment is beneficial and appropriate despite a progressive diagnosis.
Clinicians planning proactive AAC introduction alongside continued behavioral language treatment.
Cases requiring documentation of SLP treatment rationale for a progressive neurological condition for payer or medical team.

title: Melodic Intonation Therapy on Non-Fluent Aphasia After Stroke: A Systematic Review and Analysis on Clinical Trials
shortTitle: Melodic Intonation Therapy for Nonfluent Aphasia
authors: Tarng, W. W., Lin, C. W., & Ou, K. L.
summary: Systematic review of MIT for nonfluent post-stroke aphasia. Consistent positive effects on repetition, naming, and functional communication were found — MIT is most evidence-supported for chronic Broca's aphasia with severely limited verbal output.
researchFindings: MIT produced consistent positive effects on repetition across included clinical trials — the most reliably improved outcome measure.
Naming and responsive speech also improved with MIT compared to control conditions, with functional communication gains documented across multiple studies.
MIT targets right-hemisphere language networks by using melodic contour and rhythmic tapping to support verbal production when left-hemisphere language networks are damaged.
The original MIT protocol progresses through levels: intoning high-frequency phrases with hand-tapping → repeated attempts with fading melodic support → production with natural prosody.
Intensive delivery (high session frequency and within-session trial volume) is a shared feature of the most effective protocols — aligning with Kleim & Jones neural plasticity principles.
Methodological quality across studies varied; sample sizes were generally small — the evidence base supports clinical use but larger controlled trials are warranted.
clinicalApplication: MIT is best suited for clients with chronic Broca's aphasia — nonfluent with relatively preserved auditory comprehension — who have severely limited verbal output. The protocol progresses through structured levels from fully intoned phrases with hand-tapping to natural speech production with fading melodic support. Target high-frequency, personally meaningful phrases (greetings, wants and needs, daily routine expressions) rather than abstract drill material — this supports generalization and salience. MIT is not appropriate as a primary approach for fluent aphasia (Wernicke's), severe comprehension impairment, or apraxia of speech that does not respond to melodic cuing. Pair MIT with motor learning principles: vary target phrases within sessions, fade the melodic cue systematically as accuracy improves, and use home practice recordings of target phrases. Document the specific communication functions being targeted and measure progress on both trained and untrained items.

sessionStats.dose: Intensive blocks of 15–20 sessions; advance through MIT levels as proficiency improves
sessionStats.bestFit: Chronic nonfluent aphasia (Broca's) with preserved comprehension and severely limited verbal output

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic Broca's aphasia (nonfluent, agrammatic) with at least functional auditory comprehension.
Clients with severely limited verbal output where impairment-focused naming therapies have plateaued.
Clients who demonstrate at least minimal response to melodic or sung cuing during informal probing.
Settings where intensive treatment frequency (3–5x/week) is achievable — MIT effects are unlikely to generalize from low-dose treatment alone.

title: Assessing Functional Communication in Persons With Aphasia: A Scoping Review of Formal and Informal Measures
shortTitle: Functional Communication Assessment in Aphasia: Scoping Review
authors: Kagan, A., Simmons-Mackie, N., & Threats, T.
summary: A comprehensive scoping review of 67 studies identifies the landscape of formal and informal functional communication measures for aphasia, highlighting a shift toward real-world, participation-based assessment.
researchFindings: Sixty-seven studies met inclusion criteria, revealing a broad range of measures from standardized tests to naturalistic conversation sampling.
Informal assessments emphasizing life participation, conversational discourse, and real-world communication are increasingly used alongside standardized tests.
No single measure captures all dimensions of functional communication in aphasia — a multi-measure approach is recommended.
AAC strategy use, communicative partner interaction quality, and community participation were identified as underassessed but clinically important domains.
clinicalApplication: This review provides a roadmap for choosing functional communication measures in aphasia practice. Rather than relying solely on standardized language tests (e.g., WAB, BNT), SLPs should incorporate measures that capture real-world performance: the Functional Assessment of Communication Skills (FACS), Communicative Effectiveness Index (CETI), or structured conversation sampling. Naturalistic observation during activities the patient values (phone calls, family dinners, hobby participation) captures dimensions that standardized tests miss. Use this evidence to justify a multi-measure assessment battery in documentation and to build goals that reflect functional, participation-based outcomes.

sessionStats.bestFit: Any person with aphasia requiring outcome measurement

bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia of any etiology or severity requiring formal assessment or outcome measurement.
Patients transitioning from acute to chronic care where functional communication goals need to be reestablished.
SLPs seeking to justify or diversify their assessment battery beyond standardized impairment measures.
Clinical settings focused on demonstrating treatment outcomes for payer or program evaluation purposes.

title: Treatment of Aphasia in Linguistically Diverse Populations: Current and Future Directions
shortTitle: Aphasia Treatment in Linguistically Diverse Populations
authors: Hula, W. D., Kellough, S., & Doyle, P. J.
summary: This review addresses the critical gap in aphasia treatment evidence for multilingual and culturally diverse adults, offering guidance for clinical practice when research representation is limited.
researchFindings: The majority of aphasia treatment research has been conducted with monolingual English-speaking White adults, limiting generalizability.
Established aphasia treatments (e.g., SFA, VNeST, CILT) have limited evidence in non-English or multilingual speakers.
Language selection for treatment in bilingual/multilingual aphasia requires individualized assessment of language use history, dominance, and patient goals.
Culturally responsive practice — including involving interpreters, bilingual SLPs, and community liaisons — improves engagement and outcomes in diverse populations.
clinicalApplication: When serving multilingual patients with aphasia, avoid defaulting to the dominant or "first" language without assessing the patient's actual communication needs and goals. Conduct or obtain a language history to understand premorbid language use across contexts. When possible, assess in all relevant languages using multilingual-adapted tools or with interpreter support. For treatment, prioritize the language(s) most important for the patient's daily functioning and relationships. Document your language selection rationale explicitly. Use this article as a reference when advocating for interpreter access or culturally adapted materials in your setting.

sessionStats.bestFit: Multilingual or culturally diverse adults with aphasia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia who are bilingual, multilingual, or speak a language other than English as a primary language.
Patients from culturally diverse backgrounds where standard assessment norms may not apply.
SLPs working in diverse urban or community health settings.
Clinical situations requiring interpreter involvement or culturally adapted treatment materials.

title: A Meta-Analysis and Systematic Review of the Effects of Sensory Modulation Treatments for Neurogenic Oropharyngeal Dysphagia
shortTitle: Sensory Modulation for Neurogenic Dysphagia
authors: Dai, M., Cheng, I., Sasegbon, A., Li, W., & Hamdy, S.
summary: This meta-analysis of 16 RCTs (620 participants) found that oropharyngeal sensory stimulation significantly improved swallowing function in neurogenic dysphagia (SMD = 0.80). Pharyngeal electrical stimulation (PES) showed clear, consistent benefits; gustatory stimulation (capsaicin) showed a trend but inconclusive results. Adverse effects were minimal across all included studies.
researchFindings: Oropharyngeal sensory stimulation significantly improved neurogenic dysphagia overall (SMD [95% CI] = 0.80 [0.41, 1.20], p < 0.001) across 16 RCTs with 620 participants.

Electrical stimulation subgroup showed robust, significant effects (SMD = 0.79 [0.36, 1.23], p < 0.01); gustatory stimulation (capsaicin) showed a non-significant trend (SMD = 0.76, p = 0.31) with very high heterogeneity.
Sensory stimulation significantly improved readiness for decannulation in tracheostomised patients (OR = 6.47 [1.10, 38.04]), suggesting utility in the most severe neurogenic dysphagia cases.
clinicalApplication: SLPs working with patients with post-stroke, Parkinson's, MS, or ALS-related dysphagia should consider referral to or collaboration with teams providing pharyngeal electrical stimulation (PES), which has the clearest evidence base among sensory modulation approaches. Most PES protocols in the included trials used 10 minutes of stimulation per session over 3 consecutive days. Capsaicin-based gustatory stimulation remains experimental -- there is biological plausibility (TRPV1 receptor activation) but RCT evidence is currently insufficient to guide routine practice. Key contraindications include cardiac pacemakers. For tracheostomised patients with severe neurogenic dysphagia, PES may be especially worth pursuing given the significant improvement in decannulation outcomes.

sessionStats.dose: 3 consecutive days (most common protocol)
sessionStats.bestFit: Neurogenic dysphagia (stroke, Parkinson's, MS, ALS)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with neurogenic oropharyngeal dysphagia confirmed on FEES or VFSS.
Post-stroke patients represent the most studied population -- strongest evidence applies here.
Tracheostomised patients with severe dysphagia may benefit particularly (decannulation outcomes).
Gustatory stimulation (capsaicin) not recommended for routine use pending larger RCT evidence.
Caution with electrical stimulation in patients with cardiac devices or oral/pharyngeal surgical history.

title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Application of Thickened Liquids to Treat Adults With Neurogenic Dysphagia
shortTitle: Thickened Liquids for Neurogenic Dysphagia
authors: Li, W., Cheng, I., Sasegbon, A., Dai, M., & Hamdy, S.
summary: This meta-analysis of 16 studies found that thickened liquids reduce aspiration events and improve penetration-aspiration scale (PAS) scores in adults with neurogenic dysphagia, but at the cost of significantly increased pharyngeal and oral residue. The authors caution that the evidence base is predominantly non-RCT, and clinicians must weigh aspiration risk reduction against residue-related consequences when prescribing thickeners.
researchFindings: Thickened liquids significantly reduced aspiration events in RCTs (OR = 0.49 [0.28, 0.88], p = 0.02) and non-RCTs (OR = 0.31 [0.13, 0.71]), and improved PAS scores (mean difference = -1.99, p < 0.00001).
Thickened liquids did NOT significantly reduce penetration events (OR = 0.40, p = 0.11, I2 = 88%), indicating incomplete airway protection benefit.

Thickened liquids significantly increased both pharyngeal residue (OR = 1.57, p = 0.001) and oral residue (OR = 2.87, p < 0.0001) -- a clinically meaningful trade-off that increases post-swallow aspiration risk and reduces hydration efficiency.
clinicalApplication: The key clinical takeaway is not that thickeners are ineffective, but that they involve a genuine trade-off: reduced aspiration risk versus increased residue (which can itself cause post-swallow aspiration, reduced oral intake, and dehydration). SLPs should: (1) document the clinical rationale for thickener recommendations; (2) counsel patients and families on the residue trade-off and the importance of clearing residue with dry swallows; (3) revisit thickener prescriptions regularly and consider trials of compensatory strategies where aspiration has resolved; and (4) use instrumental assessment (FEES or VFSS) rather than clinical swallow exam alone to guide consistency decisions given the non-significant effect on penetration.

sessionStats.sessionLength: N/A -- dietary modification, not discrete therapy sessions
sessionStats.dose: Continuous as prescribed; reassess every 3-6 months
sessionStats.bestFit: Neurogenic dysphagia with confirmed aspiration on thin liquids

bestFitCriteria: Adults with neurogenic dysphagia and confirmed aspiration of thin liquids on FEES or VFSS.
Patients where aspiration pneumonia risk outweighs the trade-off of increased residue and reduced oral intake.
Not appropriate as a standalone solution for patients with severe pharyngeal residue -- the residue increase will compound dysphagia severity.
Reassess regularly: thickener need may diminish with spontaneous recovery or therapy-driven improvement.

title: The Benefits of Conversation Group Treatment for Individuals With Chronic Aphasia: Updated Evidence From a Multisite Randomized Controlled Trial on Measures of Language and Communication
shortTitle: Conversation Group Treatment for Chronic Aphasia
authors: Hoover, E., Szabo, G., Kohen, F., Vitale, S., McCloskey, N., Maas, E., Kulkarni, V., & DeDe, G.
summary: This multisite RCT randomized 104 people with chronic aphasia to large-group conversation treatment, dyad conversation treatment, or delayed control (1 hour, twice weekly, 10 weeks). Large-group conversation treatment produced meaningful benefits on language and communication measures compared to the delayed control, while the dyad condition showed weaker effects. Group therapy at scale may be a cost-effective option for chronic aphasia.
researchFindings: Large-group conversation treatment (3+ participants) produced significant gains on language and communication measures compared to the delayed control; the dyad condition did not reach significance in the same comparisons.
Treatment was delivered 1 hour twice weekly over 10 weeks across multiple clinical sites, supporting real-world feasibility and generalizability.
The omnibus intent-to-treat analysis did not show overall significant effects across all conditions, highlighting that group format (large vs. dyad) moderates outcomes.
clinicalApplication: SLPs designing group therapy programs for chronic aphasia should prioritize large-group formats (3+ participants) over dyads based on this evidence. The 10-week, 2x/week protocol is directly replicable in outpatient and community settings and suits people with chronic aphasia who have plateaued in individual impairment-based therapy. Conversation group treatment targets social communication and participation -- outcomes often not addressed in individual treatment -- and can be delivered cost-effectively at scale. SLPs should document baseline communication participation and use functional communication measures (e.g., ASHA-FACS, CETI) as primary outcomes for this intervention rather than standardized language tests.

sessionStats.dose: 10 weeks
sessionStats.bestFit: Chronic Aphasia (6+ months post-stroke or acquired brain injury)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic aphasia (at least 6 months post-onset) who have reached a plateau in impairment-based individual therapy.
Sufficient communicative ability to participate meaningfully in group conversation (all aphasia severity levels were included).
Large-group format (3+ participants) preferred over dyad based on this trial's findings.
Best positioned as a complement or follow-on to individual therapy rather than a replacement.

title: Music-Based Interventions for Nonfluent Aphasia: A Systematic Review of Randomized Control Trials
shortTitle: Music-Based Interventions for Nonfluent Aphasia
authors: Koshimori, Y., Akkunje, P. S., Tjiandri, E., Kowaleski, J. B., & Thaut, M. H.
journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
summary: This systematic review of 10 RCTs examined music-based interventions -- including Melodic Intonation Therapy (MIT), Modified MIT, and singing-based approaches -- for nonfluent aphasia recovery. MBIs showed particular promise for enhancing repetition and naming, even compared to standard speech therapy. However, most studies exhibited moderate to high risk of bias, and functional communication outcomes were examined in only 2 of 10 RCTs.
researchFindings: Across 10 RCTs, music-based interventions showed consistent benefit for repetition and naming abilities in nonfluent aphasia -- improvements were notable even when compared directly to speech-language therapy rather than a no-treatment control.
MIT and Modified MIT were the most studied approaches; singing-based methods showed promise for specific speech fluency outcomes with a smaller evidence base.
The evidence carries significant limitations: moderate-to-high risk of bias across studies, highly heterogeneous outcome measures, and functional communication outcomes measured in only 2 of 10 RCTs.
clinicalApplication: MIT remains the most evidence-supported music-based intervention for Broca's and other nonfluent aphasias. The typical MIT approach uses intoned speech with hand-tapping rhythm to leverage right-hemisphere musical processing and support verbal output -- SLPs can implement this directly without specialized music therapy credentials. This review confirms that MIT can be at least as effective as standard speech therapy for repetition and naming in nonfluent aphasia, which is clinically meaningful for patients who have not responded to conventional approaches. The weak functional communication evidence means MIT should be tracked with real-world measures (e.g., conversation sampling, CETI, goal attainment scaling) rather than naming probes alone. Consider MIT when: (1) patient has nonfluent aphasia with relatively preserved melodic/prosodic processing, (2) standard word retrieval approaches have plateaued, or (3) patient shows positive response to rhythmic or musical input during initial assessment.

sessionStats.frequency: Daily (most effective MIT protocols are intensive)
sessionStats.dose: 3-4 weeks intensive, then maintenance
sessionStats.bestFit: Nonfluent aphasia (Broca's, global, or transcortical motor aphasia)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with nonfluent aphasia (Broca's, global, or transcortical motor) post-stroke or acquired brain injury.
Patients who have not achieved adequate verbal output gains through conventional impairment-based treatments.
Relatively preserved auditory processing and rhythm perception (assessed during initial trial sessions).
Consider Modified MIT for patients with severe motor speech involvement who may struggle with standard MIT prosody demands.

title: Evaluating Behavioural Interventions for Oropharyngeal Dysphagia in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Swallowing Manoeuvres, Exercises, and Postural Techniques
shortTitle: Behavioral Swallowing Interventions: Maneuvers, Exercises & Posture
authors: Adzimova, S., Speyer, R., Cordier, R., Windsor, C., Korim, Z., & Tedla, M.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies evaluated the most commonly used standalone behavioral interventions for oropharyngeal dysphagia: chin tuck, effortful swallow, Mendelsohn maneuver, modified jaw opening exercise, volitional laryngeal vestibule closure, and the Shaker exercise. Most studies reported positive outcomes. Meta-analysis was only feasible for chin tuck (moderate positive effect). Overall, the evidence is preliminary and should be interpreted cautiously due to small samples and high heterogeneity.
researchFindings: Seventeen studies evaluated six behavioral interventions -- all showed positive outcomes in at least one study, but evidence for each is limited by small sample sizes and significant heterogeneity across populations and outcome measures.
Meta-analysis was only feasible for chin tuck due to insufficient study homogeneity across other interventions; chin tuck showed a moderate positive effect size across 5 studies.

Evidence is preliminary across all interventions: predominantly mixed-diagnosis populations (mostly post-stroke) and varied outcome measures limit definitive conclusions about which intervention is best for which patient.
clinicalApplication: This review provides a useful current synthesis of standalone behavioral dysphagia intervention evidence. Key takeaways: (1) Chin tuck has the strongest quantitative evidence among standalone maneuvers -- moderate positive effect confirmed via meta-analysis, though primarily from biomechanical studies rather than patient-centered outcomes. (2) Effortful swallow and Mendelsohn maneuver have positive supporting studies but insufficient pooled data -- use clinical judgment and instrumental assessment to guide selection. (3) The Shaker exercise has mechanistic and early clinical support but remains under-studied as a standalone intervention. Use these techniques as components of a comprehensive dysphagia program supported by FEES or VFSS findings -- not as generic standalone prescriptions. Track both instrumental measures (airway protection, residue) and functional outcomes (diet texture level, patient-reported swallowing quality of life).

sessionStats.dose: 4-8 weeks (varies by intervention)
sessionStats.bestFit: Oropharyngeal dysphagia in adults (post-stroke most studied)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with oropharyngeal dysphagia confirmed by FEES or VFSS, with specific biomechanical deficits identified.
Chin tuck: best supported for patients with reduced tongue base retraction or premature spillage.
Mendelsohn maneuver: appropriate when reduced laryngeal excursion and incomplete UES opening are identified.
Shaker exercise: appropriate for patients with reduced anterior laryngeal excursion and hyoid movement.
All maneuvers require sufficient cognition and motor learning ability for consistent performance.

title: Lee Silverman Voice Treatment to Improve Speech in Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: LSVT LOUD Meta-Analysis: Speech in Parkinson's Disease
authors: Xu, F., Liu, S., Lu, M., & Xu, Z.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs synthesized evidence for LSVT LOUD versus alternative speech interventions and no treatment in Parkinson's disease. Meta-analysis demonstrated significant improvements in vocal intensity for sustained phonation, connected speech, and picture description. Gains were maintained at 24-month follow-up. LSVT LOUD showed superiority over both no-treatment controls and respiratory therapy comparators.
researchFindings: LSVT LOUD produced significant increases in vocal sound pressure level (dB) for sustained phonation, Rainbow Passage reading, monologue, and picture description across 10 RCTs -- effects were robust compared to no treatment and respiratory therapy controls.
Gains in vocal loudness were maintained at 24-month follow-up in studies reporting long-term outcomes, providing strong evidence for durability of LSVT LOUD effects.

Compared to respiratory therapy, LSVT LOUD showed statistically superior improvements in vocal intensity immediately post-treatment, confirming that the loudness-focused behavioral approach adds specific value beyond respiratory support alone.
clinicalApplication: LSVT LOUD is the most evidence-supported behavioral speech-language therapy for hypokinetic dysarthria in Parkinson's disease and should be considered first-line for speech and voice in this population. The LSVT LOUD protocol requires certified training (LSVT Global certification) and follows a strict intensive format: 4 sessions per week for 4 consecutive weeks with daily home practice. The 'Think Loud' carryover principle -- training patients to monitor and self-cue adequate loudness in daily conversation -- is critical for maintenance beyond the treatment period. Consider LSVT LOUD for PD patients at any stage who present with reduced vocal loudness, monotone voice, or impaired speech intelligibility. Evidence is strongest for mild-moderate PD; extrapolation to severe PD requires clinical judgment.

sessionStats.dose: 4 consecutive weeks with daily home practice
sessionStats.bestFit: Parkinson's disease with hypokinetic dysarthria and reduced vocal loudness

bestFitCriteria: Adults with Parkinson's disease and hypokinetic dysarthria presenting with reduced vocal loudness, monotone voice, or reduced speech intelligibility.
Mild to moderate PD (Hoehn and Yahr stages 1-3) represents the most studied population.
Patients must have sufficient cognition to engage in the intensive protocol and apply 'Think Loud' carryover strategies in daily communication.
May also apply to other hypokinetic dysarthria populations (e.g., MSA, PSP) though evidence is primarily for idiopathic PD.

title: Telehealth Versus Face-to-Face Delivery of Speech Language Pathology Services: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Telehealth vs. Face-to-Face SLP Services
authors: Scott, A. M., Clark, J., Cardona, M., Atkins, T., Peiris, R., Greenwood, H., Wenke, R., Cardell, E., & Glasziou, P.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 RCTs compared telehealth (video and phone) to face-to-face SLP service delivery across stuttering, Parkinson's disease, aphasia, voice disorders, speech sound disorders, and post-stroke dysphagia. No significant differences were found between telehealth and face-to-face delivery at any measured time-point up to 18 months, supporting telehealth as a viable equivalent alternative to in-person care.
researchFindings: No significant difference between telehealth and face-to-face delivery for stuttering outcomes (%SS: mean difference 0.1, 95% CI -0.4 to 0.6, p = 0.70), maintained across follow-up periods up to 18 months.

For Parkinson's disease, telehealth produced equivalent improvements in vocal sound pressure levels (SPL) compared to face-to-face LSVT LOUD delivery (MD 0.6, 95% CI -1.2 to 2.5, p = 0.49) -- suggesting LSVT LOUD can be delivered remotely without loss of efficacy.

Four additional trials in speech sound disorder, voice disorder, post-stroke dysphagia, and aphasia also found no significant differences between telehealth and face-to-face service delivery, providing convergent support across SLP practice areas.
clinicalApplication: This meta-analysis provides the strongest available evidence that telehealth SLP services are clinically equivalent to face-to-face delivery across multiple practice areas. For SLPs, the key clinical and practical takeaways are: (1) Telehealth is not a compromise -- it is an evidence-equivalent alternative, which justifies its use for patients with geographic, transportation, or mobility barriers. (2) LSVT LOUD for PD can be delivered via telehealth without measurable loss of outcome -- this is clinically significant given the intensive 4x/week protocol and the mobility challenges of many PD patients. (3) Fluency (Camperdown Program) telehealth delivery is well-supported with outcomes maintained at 18 months. (4) The biggest gap in this evidence base is quality-of-life, patient satisfaction, and economic outcomes -- these dimensions should be documented when delivering telehealth to strengthen the justification. Note: the small number of RCTs (9 total) limits precision; additional high-quality trials are needed to refine subgroup guidance.

sessionStats.frequency: Matches in-person protocol for each condition
sessionStats.sessionLength: Matches in-person protocol for each condition
sessionStats.dose: Matches in-person protocol for each condition
sessionStats.bestFit: Any SLP client with geographic, mobility, or access barriers to in-person care

bestFitCriteria: Patients with geographic or transportation barriers to in-person SLP care.
People who stutter: equivalent outcomes via telehealth including long-term follow-up.
Parkinson's disease: LSVT LOUD telehealth delivery shows equivalent gains to in-person.
Patients must have access to a device with video capability and a stable internet connection.
Aphasia, voice, dysphagia, and speech sound disorder: evidence supports equivalence but based on fewer trials -- monitor outcomes carefully.

title: Evaluation of an Integrated Fluency and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy Intervention for Adolescents and Adults Who Stutter
shortTitle: Integrated Fluency + ACT for Adults Who Stutter (fACTS)
authors: Hart, A. K., Breen, L. J., Hennessey, N. W., & Beilby, J. M.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: This feasibility trial (n=29) evaluated the fACTS Program -- an integrated intervention combining traditional fluency management techniques with Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) for adolescents and adults who stutter. Eight sessions (60-90 min) delivered by certified SLPs produced significant improvements in self-efficacy, psychosocial functioning, psychological flexibility, and observable stuttering behaviors, with all gains maintained at 3 and 6 months post-intervention.
researchFindings: Significant pre-to-post improvements in self-efficacy (communication self-efficacy beliefs), psychosocial impact of stuttering, and psychological flexibility following 8 sessions of the fACTS integrated intervention.
Significant reductions in observable stuttering frequency (stuttered speech behaviors) were also observed, demonstrating that the psychosocial gains were accompanied by direct fluency improvements.
All outcomes -- psychosocial and behavioral -- were maintained at 3-month and 6-month follow-up, suggesting durable effects from a relatively brief 8-session protocol.
clinicalApplication: The fACTS Program represents an important clinical model for SLPs working with people who stutter: rather than targeting speech fluency in isolation, it integrates ACT principles (psychological flexibility, values clarification, acceptance of stuttering) with traditional fluency techniques. This dual focus is particularly valuable because stuttering causes substantial psychosocial burden (anxiety, avoidance, reduced quality of life) that purely fluency-focused approaches often leave unaddressed. Practical implementation: 8 sessions of 60-90 minutes, delivered by a stuttering-trained SLP with basic ACT familiarity. Key ACT components to integrate include: defusion (unhooking from unhelpful thoughts about stuttering), acceptance (allowing stuttering without fighting), values clarification (identifying what matters beyond fluency), and committed action. Important caveat: this is a feasibility trial without a control group -- evidence level is preliminary (Level 2C). A future RCT is needed. However, the 3- and 6-month maintenance data strengthen confidence in clinical utility. This approach is particularly suited to clients who have learned fluency techniques but remain avoidant, anxious, or distressed about their stutter.

sessionStats.dose: 8 sessions total
sessionStats.bestFit: Adolescents and adults who stutter with significant psychosocial impact

bestFitCriteria: Adolescents and adults who stutter experiencing significant psychosocial burden (avoidance, anxiety, reduced quality of life related to stuttering).
Clients who have already tried fluency-focused approaches but continue to experience distress or avoidance behaviors.
Clients with sufficient self-awareness and verbal/cognitive engagement to participate in ACT-based reflection and values work.
SLP delivering the intervention should have familiarity with ACT principles and stuttering treatment -- formal ACT training is recommended but not mandatory.

title: A Systematic Review of Speech-Language Pathology Interventions for Presbyphonia Using the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System
shortTitle: SLP Interventions for Presbyphonia
authors: Saccente-Kennedy, B., Gillies, F., Desjardins, M., Van Stan, J., & Govender, R.
summary: This systematic review applied the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System (RTSS) to characterize and evaluate evidence for SLP voice therapy interventions targeting presbyphonia -- the age-related voice changes caused by vocal fold atrophy and reduced vibratory function, most common in adults over 65. Voice therapy was identified as the preferred first-line treatment, with evidence supporting approaches targeting vocal fold adduction, respiratory support, and resonance. Risk of bias varied across included studies.
researchFindings: Voice therapy with a speech-language pathologist is the preferred first-line treatment for presbyphonia; surgical options (e.g., vocal fold augmentation) are reserved for cases where voice therapy has failed.

RTSS analysis revealed that most SLP interventions for presbyphonia target vocal fold adduction and increased vocal effort/loudness as primary treatment mechanisms -- approaches such as Vocal Function Exercises (VFE) and LSVT LOUD are most commonly applied.

Prevalence of voice disorders in adults >65 years is approximately four times higher than in the general population, making presbyphonia one of the most clinically common voice presentations for SLPs in geriatric and hospital settings.
clinicalApplication: Presbyphonia is the most common voice disorder in adults over 65 and is frequently underdiagnosed and undertreated -- older patients often attribute their voice changes to normal aging and do not seek referral. SLPs should actively screen for presbyphonia in older adult caseloads and advocate for early referral. Voice therapy for presbyphonia typically targets: (1) increased vocal effort and subglottal pressure to compensate for reduced adductory force; (2) respiratory support exercises to improve phonatory efficiency; (3) resonance training to optimize vocal quality with less laryngeal strain. Evidence-supported approaches include Vocal Function Exercises (VFE), LSVT LOUD, and resonant voice therapy. Laryngoscopy prior to treatment is recommended to confirm vocal fold atrophy as the primary etiology and rule out structural pathology (polyps, nodules, malignancy). Voice therapy is particularly effective in mild-moderate presbyphonia; severe atrophy with significant glottal gap may benefit from a combined approach with laryngology (vocal fold augmentation).

sessionStats.dose: 4-8 weeks (varies by intervention)
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults >65 with presbyphonia (vocal fold atrophy, breathy/weak voice)

bestFitCriteria: Adults >65 presenting with breathy, weak, or strained voice, reduced loudness, and voice fatigue consistent with presbyphonia.
Laryngoscopy-confirmed vocal fold atrophy or bowing, with or without incomplete glottal closure.
Mild to moderate severity -- severe glottal gap may require combined SLP and laryngology management.
Exclude concurrent pathology (structural lesions, neurological voice disorders) before attributing to presbyphonia.

title: Dosage, Intensity, and Frequency of Language Therapy for Aphasia: A Systematic Review-Based, Individual Participant Data Network Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Aphasia Therapy Dosage, Intensity, and Frequency (RELEASE)
authors: RELEASE Collaborators (Brady, M. C., et al.)
evidenceType: Systematic review / Individual participant data network meta-analysis
summary: This landmark individual participant data (IPD) network meta-analysis pooled data from 174 studies (3,002 participants) to examine how dosage, intensity, and frequency of SLP language therapy affects outcomes in post-stroke aphasia. Optimal therapy parameters differed significantly by patient age: working-age adults benefited most from moderate-to-high intensity (3-9+ hours/week), while older adults showed greatest gains at lower intensity (up to 2 hours/week). Time post-onset also moderated optimal therapy parameters.
researchFindings: For working-age participants, greatest language gains were associated with moderate-to-high intensity SLP therapy: functional communication improved most at 3-4 hours/week; overall language and auditory comprehension improved most at >9 hours/week.

For older participants (>retirement age), the greatest language gains occurred alongside low-intensity therapy (up to 2 hours/week) except for auditory comprehension, which favored higher dosage -- a clinically critical finding suggesting more is not always better for older adults.

Participants treated within 3 months of stroke onset showed greatest overall language gains at low intensity/moderate total dosage (up to 2 hours/week; 20-50 total hours), with dosage recommendations shifting as time post-onset increases.
clinicalApplication: The RELEASE IPD meta-analysis is the most definitive dataset available to guide aphasia therapy dosage decisions. Key clinical takeaways: (1) Therapy intensity should be individualized by patient age -- working-age adults generally benefit from more intensive therapy, while older adults may do better with lower-intensity, more distributed practice; 'one size fits all' dosage recommendations are not supported. (2) Early post-stroke intervention (within 3 months) is associated with meaningful gains at moderate total dosage (20-50 hours) -- support for intensive early intervention. (3) The field is shifting toward higher-intensity models for working-age adults (3+ hours/week) -- SLPs should advocate for appropriate therapy frequency and duration in treatment plans. (4) Total dosage matters as much as frequency -- accumulating sufficient hours of therapy is important for outcome. This study should be cited when advocating for adequate therapy provision and when tailoring dose to individual patient characteristics.

sessionStats.frequency: Individualized: working-age adults benefit from 3+ hours/week; older adults from up to 2 hours/week
sessionStats.dose: Acute: 20-50 total hours. Chronic: higher total dosage may be needed
sessionStats.bestFit: Post-stroke aphasia across all age groups

bestFitCriteria: Adults with post-stroke aphasia at any severity level and any time post-onset.
Working-age adults (< retirement age): optimal dosage at 3-9+ hours/week depending on language domain.
Older adults (> retirement age): moderate gains at lower intensity (up to 2 hours/week); monitor for fatigue and cognitive capacity.
Acute phase (< 3 months post-stroke): prioritize moderate total dosage (20-50 hours) at manageable intensity.
Use this evidence to advocate for adequate therapy provision and to individualize scheduling decisions.

title: Comparison of the Efficacy and Adverse Effects of Unilateral or Bilateral Botulinum Toxin Injections for Adductor Spasmodic Dysphonia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Botulinum Toxin for Adductor Spasmodic Dysphonia
authors: Park, J., Shim, J., Kim, M., & Choi, S.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 studies (854 patients) compared the efficacy and adverse effects of unilateral versus bilateral botulinum toxin (BoNT) injections for adductor spasmodic dysphonia (ADSD).
