Both approaches demonstrated significant voice improvement, but bilateral injection was associated with a longer duration of vocal improvement. Unilateral injection produced a more favorable adverse effect profile, with less hypophonia. Findings have direct implications for SLP-ENT collaborative management.
researchFindings: Both unilateral and bilateral BoNT injections significantly improved voice quality in adductor spasmodic dysphonia, consistent with long-established evidence for BoNT as the primary medical management of ADSD.

Bilateral BoNT injection was associated with longer duration of vocal improvement between injection cycles compared to unilateral injection -- a clinically meaningful advantage in reducing re-injection frequency.

Unilateral injection produced a more favorable adverse effect profile with reduced incidence and duration of hypophonia (breathy weak voice) post-injection, representing a trade-off between duration of benefit and side effect burden.
clinicalApplication: Botulinum toxin injection is the primary evidence-based medical management for adductor spasmodic dysphonia, and SLPs play a critical role in this condition across multiple touchpoints: (1) Differential diagnosis -- ADSD must be distinguished from muscle tension dysphonia (MTD) and other voice disorders; SLP acoustic/perceptual assessment and voice evaluation are central to this. (2) Pre- and post-injection SLP therapy -- voice therapy is recommended as an adjunct to BoNT to maximize and extend the period of vocal improvement, though optimal protocols remain under-studied. (3) Setting treatment expectations -- patients should understand that BoNT effects are temporary (typically 3-6 months) and hypophonia in the first 1-2 weeks post-injection is expected. (4) The bilateral vs. unilateral decision rests with the laryngologist but SLPs should understand this trade-off: longer benefit (bilateral) vs. less hypophonia (unilateral). ADSD is a neurological voice disorder requiring lifelong management and SLP should remain part of the ongoing care team.

sessionStats.frequency: BoNT injections typically every 3-6 months; SLP voice therapy as adjunct between injections
sessionStats.dose: 4-8 voice therapy sessions per injection cycle
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with confirmed adductor spasmodic dysphonia (laryngeal dystonia)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with a confirmed diagnosis of adductor spasmodic dysphonia (ADSD) established by laryngology evaluation and acoustic/perceptual assessment.
Differential diagnosis of ADSD vs. MTD must be established before BoNT referral -- SLP evaluation is critical in this determination.
Voice therapy as an adjunct to BoNT is appropriate for all ADSD patients to maximize benefit between injection cycles.
Patients who respond poorly to BoNT or who decline injection may be candidates for SLP voice therapy alone, though evidence for voice therapy as a standalone ADSD treatment is limited.

title: Dysphagia Treatments in Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Dysphagia Treatments in Parkinson's Disease
authors: Herd, C. P., Tomlinson, C. L., Deane, K. H. O., Brady, M. C., Smith, C. H., Sackley, C., & Clarke, C. E.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 RCTs (286 participants) evaluated the efficacy of dysphagia treatments in Parkinson's disease. The pooled effect size across all interventions was significant and medium (SMD = 0.58), supporting the overall effectiveness of dysphagia rehabilitation in PD. Interventions included EMST, LSVT LOUD, Lee Silverman treatment, behavioral swallowing therapies, and sensory stimulation approaches.
researchFindings: Pooled effect size across 9 RCTs (286 participants) demonstrated a significant, medium effect of dysphagia treatments in Parkinson's disease compared to control conditions (SMD = 0.58, significant), supporting the clinical utility of SLP-led dysphagia rehabilitation in PD.
EMST (Expiratory Muscle Strength Training) was among the most studied individual interventions and showed positive effects on swallowing physiology and aspiration safety in PD.

Treatment effects were observed across a range of dysphagia outcomes including aspiration measures, swallowing physiology, and patient-reported swallowing difficulty, indicating broad-based benefits rather than narrow effects on single measures.
clinicalApplication: Dysphagia in Parkinson's disease is common (affecting up to 80% of patients at some point in the disease course), underrecognized, and undertreated. This meta-analysis provides important justification for proactive SLP dysphagia assessment and intervention in PD populations. Key clinical guidance: (1) Proactive screening is important -- PD patients often adapt to dysphagia without reporting it, so routine screening (e.g., at motor staging changes) is warranted. (2) EMST has the most individual RCT evidence in PD dysphagia and is directly within SLP scope: the standard protocol is 5 sets x 5 breaths at 75% MEP threshold, 5 days/week for 4-8 weeks. (3) LSVT LOUD also positively impacts swallowing in PD as a secondary benefit of improved respiratory support and laryngeal function. (4) Behavioral strategies (modified postures, diet modification, swallow maneuvers) are appropriate adjuncts at any stage. Given PD is progressive, dysphagia management should be revisited at each significant motor stage change and as part of advance care planning.

sessionStats.frequency: 5x/week for EMST protocols; 2-3x/week for behavioral swallowing therapy
sessionStats.dose: 4-8 weeks per treatment cycle
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with Parkinson's disease presenting with oropharyngeal dysphagia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with Parkinson's disease at any stage who screen positive for dysphagia on clinical assessment or report swallowing difficulty.
EMST is particularly appropriate for PD patients with reduced respiratory support and cough strength contributing to aspiration risk.
Instrumental assessment (FEES or VFSS) recommended to characterize dysphagia physiology and guide specific intervention targets.
Dysphagia management should be part of the broader PD interdisciplinary care team and revisited at each motor staging change.

title: The Impact of Dysphagia Prehabilitation on Swallowing Outcomes Post-Chemoradiation Therapy in Head and Neck Cancer: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: Dysphagia Prehabilitation in Head and Neck Cancer
authors: Novelo, M. N., Guimaraes, A. V., Quon, H., Sun, Y., & Bhatt, A.
summary: This systematic review examined the impact of exercise-based dysphagia prehabilitation (swallowing therapy initiated before chemoradiation for head and neck cancer) on post-treatment swallowing outcomes. Prehabilitation programs included swallowing and jaw exercises, tongue strengthening, and range-of-motion exercises. Results generally supported prehabilitation's ability to reduce post-treatment dysphagia severity and improve swallowing function, though study heterogeneity limited definitive conclusions.
researchFindings: Exercise-based prehabilitation programs initiated before chemoradiation for HNC generally showed favorable effects on post-treatment swallowing outcomes, including reduced diet restriction, improved swallowing function, and reduced penetration-aspiration severity compared to reactive (post-treatment) intervention only.

Prehabilitation targets structurally at-risk swallowing muscles before they sustain radiation-related fibrosis and neuromuscular damage, with the hypothesis that maintaining pre-treatment strength and mobility reduces the severity of treatment-induced dysphagia.

Study heterogeneity in exercise protocols, patient populations (HNC site, stage), and outcome measures limited meta-analytic pooling, but the directional consistency of findings across studies supports clinical implementation of prehabilitation.
clinicalApplication: HNC-related dysphagia (particularly post-chemoradiation dysphagia) is one of the most debilitating and persistent complications of head and neck cancer treatment. SLPs should be involved in care from diagnosis, not just at post-treatment referral. Key clinical guidance: (1) Initiate swallowing exercises before chemoradiation begins -- standard prehabilitation protocols include jaw range-of-motion exercises, tongue base retraction exercises, effortful swallow, and Mendelsohn maneuver practice. (2) The Schwartz protocol and similar pre-treatment swallowing exercise programs are directly SLP-deliverable. (3) Continue exercises through treatment even when it is painful or difficult -- maintaining movement during radiation is critical for preventing fibrosis-related stricture. (4) Document baseline function with FEES or VFSS before treatment to enable meaningful post-treatment comparison. (5) Support completion of oral intake during treatment where medically possible to prevent disuse atrophy of the swallowing mechanism. Tube feeding should be a last resort, not a convenience measure, in this population.

sessionStats.dose: Begin pre-treatment; continue through treatment and into post-treatment recovery
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with head and neck cancer scheduled for chemoradiation or radiation therapy

bestFitCriteria: Adults with HNC (oropharyngeal, oral cavity, laryngeal, hypopharyngeal) scheduled for radiation or chemoradiation therapy.
Prehabilitation is particularly high-priority for patients with large tumor volumes, bilateral neck irradiation, or concurrent chemotherapy -- all associated with highest dysphagia risk.
Baseline FEES or VFSS before treatment strongly recommended to document pre-treatment function.
Patient must be motivated and physically able to complete daily exercise regimen -- caregiver coaching and home program are essential.

title: Systematic Review of Discourse and Social Communication Interventions in Traumatic Brain Injury
shortTitle: Discourse and Social Communication Interventions in TBI
authors: Douglas, J. M., Bracy, C. A., & Snow, P. C.
summary: This systematic review examined discourse and social communication interventions in TBI, searching five electronic databases for interventions published 2012-2021. Discourse approaches were generally more effective for mild-to-moderate TBI, while social communication approaches showed stronger effects for moderate-to-severe TBI. Five treatment components were identified as essential across effective interventions: explicit instruction, feedback, modeling, practice, and real-world generalization support.
researchFindings: Discourse treatment approaches (targeting narrative, procedural, and conversational discourse) were most effective for individuals with mild-to-moderate TBI, with consistent evidence for improvements in discourse informativeness and coherence.
Social communication interventions (targeting pragmatics, partner interaction, and conversational exchange) showed stronger and more consistent effects for individuals with moderate-to-severe TBI.

Five essential treatment components were identified across the most effective interventions: (1) explicit instruction in target skills, (2) feedback on performance, (3) modeling of target behaviors, (4) practice with varied stimuli, and (5) generalization support activities targeting real-world communication.
clinicalApplication: Cognitive-communication deficits -- particularly in discourse and social communication -- are among the most persistent and functionally disabling consequences of TBI, yet they are often underaddressed in rehabilitation programs that prioritize acute cognitive recovery. This review guides SLP intervention selection: (1) For mild-to-moderate TBI: prioritize discourse-level treatments targeting narrative organization, coherence, and informativeness -- Discourse Processing Treatment (DPT) has direct support. (2) For moderate-to-severe TBI: prioritize social communication approaches targeting conversational turn-taking, topic management, and pragmatic appropriateness -- Togher's Communication Partner Training is an evidence-supported model. (3) Across severity levels, ensure all five essential components are present in treatment design: explicit instruction, feedback, modeling, varied practice, and real-world generalization activities. (4) Involve communication partners (family, caregivers, coworkers) in treatment to support generalization -- partner-mediated approaches have consistently strong evidence in TBI. Document functional communication outcomes (discourse sampling, observer-rated conversation) rather than relying solely on standardized cognitive tests.

sessionStats.dose: 8-16 sessions; generalization activities ongoing
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with TBI presenting with discourse and/or social communication deficits

bestFitCriteria: Adults with mild-to-severe TBI who present with discourse deficits (reduced informativeness, coherence, or organization) or social communication impairments (pragmatic errors, conversational breakdown).
Discourse treatment: prioritize for mild-to-moderate TBI with intact or mildly impaired cognitive processing.
Social communication treatment: prioritize for moderate-to-severe TBI; involves partner training as a core component.
Involvement of communication partners (family, caregivers, work colleagues) strongly recommended for generalization.

title: Cognitive Stimulation to Improve Cognitive Functioning in People With Dementia
shortTitle: Cognitive Stimulation Therapy for Dementia (Cochrane)
authors: Woods, B., Rai, H. K., Elliott, E., Hobson, P., Moniz-Cook, E., & Orrell, M.
summary: This Cochrane systematic review (updated 2023) synthesized evidence for cognitive stimulation therapy (CST) for people with mild-to-moderate dementia. Based on 25 included studies, CST produced significant improvements in cognitive functioning, communication, and social interaction, and was recommended in NICE guidelines for dementia care. CST is a structured, person-centred program of themed group activities designed to stimulate thinking and communication.
researchFindings: CST produced significant improvements in cognitive functioning (standardized mean difference ~0.97) and quality of life outcomes in people with mild-to-moderate dementia across 25 studies, representing the largest evidence base for any psychosocial intervention in dementia.

CST significantly improved communication and social interaction outcomes, with participants showing increased engagement, verbal output, and conversational participation during and after the program -- directly relevant to SLP practice.

CST is recommended by NICE (UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) and Alzheimer's Disease International as part of standard dementia care, reflecting its position as the highest-evidenced non-pharmacological intervention for cognition in this population.
clinicalApplication: Cognitive Stimulation Therapy is the most evidence-supported non-pharmacological intervention for dementia and falls squarely within SLP scope of practice. SLPs are well-positioned to lead or co-facilitate CST, given its strong communication and social engagement components. Standard CST consists of 14 structured group sessions (45-60 min) twice weekly over 7 weeks, using themed activities (current affairs, word games, reminiscence, creative activities) to stimulate cognition and communication. Key clinical guidance: (1) CST is appropriate for mild-to-moderate dementia -- screening with MMSE or MoCA to confirm eligibility. (2) Maintenance CST (ongoing weekly sessions following the initial 14-session program) has additional evidence for sustained benefits. (3) Communication facilitation is central to CST -- SLPs can contribute expertise in adapting communication demands, supporting word retrieval, and modifying interaction for participants with aphasia-type presentations in dementia. (4) Individual CST is also available for patients unable to engage in group settings. CST should be part of every dementia-capable SLP's toolkit.

sessionStats.dose: 14 sessions over 7 weeks (initial); ongoing maintenance
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with mild-to-moderate dementia (Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, mixed dementia)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with mild-to-moderate dementia (MMSE 10-24 approximately) including Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, and mixed types.
Sufficient engagement ability to participate in group activities (can be adapted for very mild verbal communication).
Group format (6-8 participants) is standard; individual CST available for those unable to tolerate group settings.
SLP involvement is most valuable for participants with co-occurring language or communication impairments.

title: A Meta-Analysis of Anomia Treatment in Bilingual Aphasia: Within- and Cross-Language Generalization and Predictors of Treatment Outcomes
shortTitle: Anomia Treatment in Bilingual Aphasia
authors: Kambanaros, M., & Grohmann, K. K.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: This meta-analysis investigated anomia treatment efficacy in bilingual and multilingual people with aphasia, examining within-language treatment gains and cross-language generalization (improvement in the untreated language). Results showed significant treatment effects in the treated language, with cross-language generalization evident in some contexts. Treatment duration, phonological treatment components, and baseline comprehension ability predicted outcomes. Findings inform SLP decision-making about language of treatment and generalization expectations in bilingual clients.
researchFindings: Anomia treatment in bilingual aphasia produced significant within-language gains in the treated language, with effect sizes in the moderate-to-large range, confirming that standard anomia approaches (semantic feature analysis, phonological cueing, errorless learning) are effective in bilingual clients.

Cross-language generalization -- improvement in the untreated language following treatment in one language -- was observed across studies, though effect sizes were smaller than within-language gains and more variable.

Treatment duration and provision of phonological treatment components were significant predictors of outcome; stronger single-word comprehension at baseline also predicted better treatment response, informing client selection and treatment planning.
clinicalApplication: SLPs increasingly work with bilingual and multilingual clients with aphasia, yet treatment planning in these cases remains complex due to limited guidance on which language to treat and what to expect for the untreated language. This meta-analysis provides three key clinical takeaways: (1) Anomia treatment works in bilingual aphasia -- SLPs should not withhold or delay treatment due to the client's bilingual status. Use standard evidence-based naming approaches (SFA, phonological cueing, errorless learning) in the client's stronger or most functionally important language first. (2) Cross-language generalization is possible but not guaranteed -- plan treatment goals in both languages from the outset, and document baseline naming in both. (3) Phonological cueing components improve outcomes -- ensure treatment includes phonological support (initial sound cues, rhyming) alongside semantic approaches. Client's pre-treatment single-word comprehension is the strongest predictor of response -- lower comprehension warrants targeting receptive language in parallel. Advocate for bilingual SLP support where available, especially for speakers of languages the primary SLP does not speak.

sessionStats.dose: Varies; longer treatment duration associated with better outcomes
sessionStats.bestFit: Bilingual or multilingual adults with post-stroke aphasia and anomia

bestFitCriteria: Bilingual or multilingual adults with post-stroke or acquired aphasia presenting with anomia in one or more languages.
Treatment language selection should prioritize the client's preferred language, most functionally important language, and available SLP language competency.
Better single-word comprehension at baseline predicts stronger treatment response -- consider targeting comprehension in parallel for clients with lower receptive ability.
Ensure phonological cueing is incorporated into treatment protocol -- phonological components predicted better outcomes in this meta-analysis.

title: Velopharyngeal Insufficiency in Adults With Dysarthria: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: VPI in Adult Dysarthria: Systematic Review
authors: Spencer, K. A.
summary: Systematic review examining velopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI) across adult dysarthria populations, synthesizing evidence on prevalence, assessment methods, and management approaches including prosthetic and behavioral intervention.
researchFindings: VPI is a clinically significant feature of dysarthria across multiple etiologies including ALS, TBI, MS, and Parkinson's disease, with hypernasality affecting intelligibility and voice quality.
Palatal lift prostheses have the strongest evidence for management of VPI in dysarthria, particularly for individuals with flaccid dysarthria and adequate velar tissue movement.
Behavioral voice therapy approaches can complement prosthetic management but alone show limited evidence for correcting VPI at the structural level.
Nasometry and acoustic measures of nasalance are the most commonly used objective assessment tools, though normative data for adult dysarthric populations vary widely.
Surgical referral (e.g., posterior pharyngeal wall augmentation) is considered primarily when prosthetic management is not tolerated or insufficient.
Evidence base is limited by small sample sizes and heterogeneous populations; further RCTs are needed to establish optimal management protocols.
clinicalApplication: Screen for VPI in all clients with dysarthria by listening for hypernasality, nasal emission, and reduced intraoral pressure during plosives and fricatives. Use nasometry or aerodynamic measures to quantify VPI severity when available. Refer to prosthodontist for palatal lift evaluation when VPI significantly impacts intelligibility — particularly in flaccid dysarthria (e.g., ALS, lower motor neuron involvement). Continue behavioral voice and articulation therapy alongside prosthetic management to maximize carryover.

sessionStats.dose: Palatal lift: multiple fitting appointments; behavioral tx: individualized
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with flaccid or mixed dysarthria and hypernasality (ALS, TBI, MS)

bestFitCriteria: Adults with dysarthria secondary to ALS, TBI, MS, or other neurological conditions presenting with hypernasality or nasal emission.
Clients where VPI is reducing speech intelligibility or voice quality despite other treatment approaches.
Clinicians determining whether to pursue prosthetic management, behavioral treatment, or surgical referral for VPI.
Adults who have not had formal VPI assessment and have not been evaluated for palatal lift candidacy.

title: Effectiveness of Constraint-Induced Language Therapy for Aphasia: Evidence From Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
shortTitle: CILT for Aphasia: Umbrella Systematic Review
authors: Raymer, A. M., & Roitsch, J.
summary: Umbrella systematic review synthesizing evidence from existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses on constraint-induced language therapy (CILT) for post-stroke aphasia. CILT incorporates forced verbal use, massed practice, and shaping to drive neuroplastic language recovery.
researchFindings: CILT effectively improves language and functional communication in individuals with post-stroke aphasia, with benefits supported across multiple systematic reviews.
Some reviews report sustained gains from CILT beyond the treatment period, suggesting durable neuroplastic changes.
Generalization to untrained stimuli and connected speech is limited — most gains are seen on trained targets.
The high-intensity, massed practice component of CILT is thought to be a key active ingredient, consistent with neuroplasticity principles.
Constraint component (discouraging gesture/writing) may contribute benefit beyond intensity alone, though disentangling elements is difficult.
CILT may be particularly beneficial for individuals with nonfluent aphasia who retain some residual verbal output to shape.
clinicalApplication: Implement CILT principles by requiring verbal communication attempts during treatment, using shaping techniques to gradually increase response complexity, and discouraging compensatory non-verbal strategies during treatment sessions. Pair with high-intensity scheduling (≥3 hours/week, ≥10 sessions) to leverage neuroplasticity. Program functional targets (e.g., names, frequently used phrases) to maximize ecological validity. For clients who cannot produce verbal output, consider hybrid approaches that incorporate CILT principles with supported communication.

sessionStats.dose: Typically 10–15 sessions over 2–3 weeks
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with post-stroke aphasia retaining some verbal output

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic or subacute post-stroke aphasia who have some residual verbal output.
Clients who have plateaued with traditional low-intensity therapy and may benefit from massed practice.
Individuals where functional verbal communication is the primary treatment goal.
Settings that can accommodate intensive scheduling (rehabilitation programs, intensive outpatient, ICAPs).

title: The Efficacy of the Manual Circumlaryngeal Therapy for Muscle Tension Dysphonia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
shortTitle: Manual Circumlaryngeal Therapy for MTD: Meta-analysis
authors: Barsties v. Latoszek, B., Watts, C. R., Hetjens, S., & Skowronski, T.
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis examining the efficacy of manual circumlaryngeal therapy (MCT) for muscle tension dysphonia (MTD). MCT involves hands-on manual manipulation of the laryngeal and supralaryngeal musculature to reduce excess muscular tension and improve vocal quality.
researchFindings: MCT significantly improved shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR) in individuals with MTD, with these effects maintained after accounting for measurement variability.
Jitter was also significantly reduced following MCT, indicating improvement in cycle-to-cycle frequency stability of the voice.
Effects on fundamental frequency were not consistently verified across studies, suggesting MCT does not reliably alter habitual pitch.
MCT can produce immediate and clinically significant voice improvements, sometimes within a single session.
MCT is a safe, non-invasive technique with no reported adverse effects across included studies.
Variability in MCT technique (Aronson approach, Lieberman approach, etc.) across studies limits direct comparison but all approaches showed benefit.
clinicalApplication: MCT is a first-line technique for functional MTD with high laryngeal position and supralaryngeal tension. Techniques include gentle circular massage of the thyrohyoid space, inferior displacement of the larynx, and reduction of overall laryngeal tension. Prompt the client to phonate (sustain /i/ or /a/) during manipulation to immediately assess change in voice quality. Combine with voice therapy targeting easy onset, resonant voice, and elimination of abusive behaviors. Consider MCT before traditional voice therapy for clients presenting with primary musculoskeletal tension. Can achieve significant vocal improvement in 1–3 sessions when implemented by a trained clinician.

sessionStats.dose: 1–6 sessions (often sufficient with early responders)
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with primary or secondary muscle tension dysphonia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with muscle tension dysphonia (primary or secondary) with elevated laryngeal position, restricted thyrohyoid space, and visible/palpable laryngeal tension.
Clients who have not responded adequately to traditional voice therapy approaches alone.
Voice patients with neck, jaw, or shoulder tension that appears to contribute to dysphonia.
SLPs who have received training in laryngeal manual therapy techniques.

title: Effects of Transcutaneous Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation on Post-Stroke Dysphagia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
shortTitle: NMES for Post-Stroke Dysphagia: Meta-analysis
authors: Wang, Y., Xu, L., Wang, L., Jiang, M., & Zhao, L.
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 46 RCTs (N=3,346) evaluating transcutaneous neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) for post-stroke dysphagia. Findings support NMES combined with standard swallowing therapy as superior to swallowing therapy alone.
researchFindings: NMES combined with routine swallowing therapy (NMES+ST) significantly outperformed swallowing therapy alone across six dysphagia outcome measures: PAS, FOIS, FDS, SSA, VFSS, and WST.
NMES alone was NOT superior to conventional swallowing therapy alone — the adjunctive combination is key to improved outcomes.
Optimal stimulation parameters identified: 25 Hz frequency, 7 mA or 0–15 mA intensity, courses of ≤4 weeks produced the strongest effects.
NMES+ST significantly improved quality of life measures and increased upward movement distance of the hyoid bone during swallowing.
46 RCTs with 3,346 patients were included, representing the largest and most comprehensive meta-analysis on NMES for dysphagia to date.
Subgroup analyses confirmed effectiveness across multiple outcome measures and treatment parameters, supporting clinical generalizability.
clinicalApplication: Use NMES (e.g., VitalStim) as an adjunctive component paired with active swallowing exercises — not as a standalone intervention. Apply transcutaneous electrodes per manufacturer and clinical training protocols. Target treatment courses of ≤4 weeks with NMES+ST combined. Continue traditional swallowing therapy (e.g., effortful swallow, Mendelsohn, postural strategies) alongside every NMES session. Ensure NMES contraindications are screened (pacemaker, metal implants in treatment area, active seizures, altered skin integrity at electrode sites). NMES should be billed and documented as a component of dysphagia treatment, not a passive modality used in isolation.

sessionStats.dose: ≤4 weeks continuous course; typically 20–30 sessions
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with post-stroke oropharyngeal dysphagia, pharyngeal phase impairment

bestFitCriteria: Adults with oropharyngeal dysphagia secondary to stroke with pharyngeal phase weakness.
Clients who have plateaued on standard swallowing therapy and may benefit from adjunctive neurostimulation.
Settings where NMES-certified SLPs and appropriate equipment are available.
Clients without NMES contraindications (no cardiac pacemakers, no metal implants in the cervical region, no seizure disorder, intact skin integrity at electrode sites).

title: Lee Silverman Voice Treatment Compared With Standard NHS Speech and Language Therapy for Dysarthria in Parkinson's Disease: The PD COMM Randomized Controlled Trial
shortTitle: LSVT LOUD vs Standard SLT in Parkinson's: PD COMM RCT
authors: Sackley, C., Patel, S., Hives, L., Bhanu, C., Bradley, E., Noorkoiv, M., et al.
summary: Large multicenter UK RCT (PD COMM) comparing LSVT LOUD, standard NHS speech and language therapy, and no treatment in adults with Parkinson's disease and dysarthria. LSVT LOUD significantly outperformed both standard care and no treatment; standard care showed no benefit over no treatment.
researchFindings: LSVT LOUD significantly reduced the participant-reported impact of voice/speech problems compared to no speech and language therapy.
LSVT LOUD significantly outperformed standard NHS speech and language therapy on the primary voice-related quality of life outcome.
Standard NHS speech and language therapy showed NO statistically significant benefit compared to no speech and language therapy — a major and practice-changing finding.
Benefits of LSVT LOUD were maintained at follow-up, supporting the durability of intensive treatment.
The trial included adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease across multiple NHS speech and language therapy services throughout the UK.
Results reinforce that the intensity and structured protocol of LSVT LOUD are critical active ingredients, not general SLT contact alone.
clinicalApplication: Prioritize LSVT LOUD for individuals with Parkinson's disease-related dysarthria. The 16-session intensive protocol (4 sessions/week for 4 weeks, each 60 min) is key — do not dilute it with a lower-intensity schedule. Emphasize 'THINK LOUD' carry-over for functional communication. The PD COMM trial findings mean that conventional, lower-intensity Parkinson's speech therapy cannot be assumed to be sufficient. If LSVT LOUD is not available, consider at minimum replicating its core elements: loudness focus, high intensity, daily practice homework. Maintenance sessions every 3–6 months support long-term loudness carryover.

sessionStats.dose: 16 sessions over 4 consecutive weeks
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with Parkinson's disease and hypokinetic dysarthria

bestFitCriteria: Adults with Parkinson's disease presenting with hypokinetic dysarthria, reduced loudness, or reduced speech intelligibility.
Individuals who have not yet received intensive voice treatment for Parkinson's disease.
Clients in earlier stages of PD who can tolerate the intensive 4-week schedule and complete daily home practice.
Clinicians selecting between LSVT LOUD and standard speech therapy for a Parkinson's patient — the PD COMM trial provides strong evidence for LSVT LOUD.

title: The Effect of Mobile Application-Based Technology on Post-Stroke Aphasia: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: App-Based Technology for Post-Stroke Aphasia: Systematic Review
authors: Jiang, Z., He, M., Zhang, C., & Chen, X.
summary: Systematic review of 15 studies (including 10 RCTs) examining the effect of mobile application-based technology (tablets, iPads, phones) on post-stroke aphasia outcomes. Findings support app-based therapy as a valuable adjunct for aphasia rehabilitation, particularly for improving language function, naming, and quality of life.
researchFindings: 8 out of 15 studies demonstrated efficacy of mobile application-based therapy in enhancing overall language function for post-stroke aphasia patients.
4 studies indicated positive effects on naming abilities, suggesting app-based approaches can drive lexical-semantic recovery.
3 studies highlighted improvement in communication skills, and 3 in spontaneous speech expression.
2 studies documented improved quality of life for individuals with aphasia using app-based interventions.
App-based therapy enables higher doses of independent practice, addressing a known limitation of clinic-only aphasia treatment.
Apps do not replace face-to-face SLT but serve as effective supplements, allowing individuals to accumulate high-intensity practice outside of sessions.
clinicalApplication: Prescribe app-based aphasia programs (e.g., Constant Therapy, Lingraphica, AphasiaScripts) as between-session home practice to increase treatment intensity. Target naming and word-finding specifically using app-based naming exercises aligned with clinic targets. Set up the app with the client and caregiver in session to ensure independence at home. Monitor progress via built-in app data where available and adjust app targets weekly. Apps are particularly useful for clients with chronic aphasia seeking to maintain or expand gains without daily clinical contact. Ensure the client and communication partner understand the app is supplementing — not replacing — SLP-directed treatment.

sessionStats.frequency: Daily independent practice (supplementing weekly SLT sessions)
sessionStats.dose: Ongoing as adjunct to formal treatment; 4–12 weeks in most studies
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with chronic or subacute post-stroke aphasia with sufficient motor ability to use a touchscreen device

bestFitCriteria: Adults with post-stroke aphasia who are motivated for home practice and have access to a tablet or smartphone.
Clients with intact enough motor control to operate a touchscreen device independently or with caregiver assistance.
Individuals in chronic aphasia seeking to increase treatment intensity beyond weekly clinic sessions.
SLPs looking to augment face-to-face treatment with systematic, data-tracked home practice tools.

title: A Systematic Review of Interventions for Adults Who Stutter
shortTitle: Interventions for Adults Who Stutter: Systematic Review
authors: Brignell, A., Krahe, M., Downes, M., Kefalianos, E., Reilly, S., & Morgan, A. T.
summary: Systematic review examining the evidence for face-to-face interventions, service delivery models, and psychological treatments for adults who stutter. Included 5 RCTs, 4 registered trials, and 3 systematic reviews. Speech restructuring approaches reduced stuttering frequency, and combined approaches incorporating CBT may improve psychosocial outcomes.
researchFindings: Speech restructuring approaches (e.g., prolonged speech, smooth speech, Camperdown Program) reduced stuttering frequency by 50–57% on average across included studies.
No intervention eliminated stuttering to the level of community controls who do not stutter; expectations should be calibrated accordingly.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) combined with speech restructuring may provide additional benefit for psychosocial outcomes (anxiety, avoidance, quality of life).
The Camperdown Program (an RCT-validated protocol) demonstrated significant stuttering reduction using smooth speech syllable-timed speech and problem-solving.
Internet-delivered and group-based treatment formats showed preliminary evidence comparable to individual face-to-face delivery.
Only 5 RCTs met inclusion criteria, highlighting significant gaps in the adult stuttering treatment evidence base.
clinicalApplication: Use evidence-based stuttering restructuring approaches (Camperdown Program, prolonged speech, smooth speech) as the foundation for fluency-focused treatment. Integrate CBT-informed approaches (e.g., acceptance and commitment therapy, desensitization, cognitive restructuring) to address communication anxiety, avoidance, and overall quality of life — particularly for adults where avoidance is a primary presenting concern. Set explicit expectations: the goal is reduced stuttering frequency and improved confidence, not eliminating stuttering entirely. Consider group therapy and self-help support as adjuncts. Telehealth delivery is supported by emerging evidence and may expand access.

sessionStats.dose: 8–20 sessions; maintenance follow-up at 3, 6, 12 months
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults who stutter with moderate to severe stuttering frequency and/or psychosocial impact

bestFitCriteria: Adults who stutter presenting with stuttering frequency that impacts daily communication and occupational or social participation.
Clients with co-occurring communication anxiety, avoidance, or negative self-perception related to stuttering.
SLPs selecting an evidence-based treatment approach for adults who stutter.
Adults who have not received structured stuttering intervention as adults, or who are seeking a refresher with an evidence-based framework.

title: Communication Partner Training With Familiar Partners of People With Aphasia: A Systematic Review and Synthesis of Barriers and Facilitators to Implementation
shortTitle: Communication Partner Training in Aphasia: Systematic Review
authors: Shrubsole, K., Power, E., & Hall, A.
journal: International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders
summary: Systematic review examining communication partner training (CPT) for familiar partners (family members, caregivers) of people with aphasia, with synthesis of barriers and facilitators to real-world implementation. Evidence supports CPT as effective for improving communication activities and participation for both the person with aphasia and their trained partner.
researchFindings: Communication partner training is effective in improving communication activities and participation for trained familiar partners of people with aphasia.
CPT is probably effective in improving communication activities and participation for people with aphasia when interacting with trained communication partners.
Training familiar partners establishes an enriched communication environment, which may enhance neuroplasticity and support community participation long term.
Training that enables family caregivers to maintain their carer role and communication support has been associated with reduced caregiver burden.
Barriers to CPT implementation include partner availability, SLP time constraints, limited resources, and difficulty generalizing strategies beyond training contexts.
Facilitators include structured training programs, video modeling, role-play practice, and booster sessions to support skill retention.
clinicalApplication: Incorporate communication partner training as a routine component of aphasia intervention — not an optional add-on. Teach partners specific Supported Conversation for Adults with Aphasia (SCA) techniques: acknowledging competence, revealing competence through multimodal scaffolding (pictures, writing, gesture), and confirming understanding. Use video modeling and role-play to build partner skills. Provide written resources and practice materials for home use. Conduct at least one session with the partner present in each episode of care. Address caregiver emotional needs and build confidence in communication alongside skill training.

sessionStats.frequency: 1–2 family/partner training sessions per episode of care + ongoing reinforcement
sessionStats.dose: 4–8 structured training sessions; booster sessions at 3–6 months
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with aphasia of any severity who have an available and motivated communication partner

bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia at any stage of recovery who have an available familiar communication partner (family member, caregiver, friend).
Communication partners motivated to learn supported communication strategies and take an active role in aphasia rehabilitation.
Clinicians working with community-dwelling adults with aphasia for whom participation and quality of life are key goals.
Settings providing aphasia group treatment where partner training is feasible as a complementary home-based component.

title: A Systematic Review of Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Programmes — Who Takes Part, What Is Measured, What Are the Outcomes?
shortTitle: Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Programmes: Systematic Review
authors: Monnelly, K., Marshall, J., Cruice, M., & others
summary: Systematic review of 21 studies covering 13 Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Programmes (ICAPs) involving 485 adults aged 18–86 (11–335 months post-stroke). ICAPs combine high-dose individual and group treatment targeting communication across impairment, function, and participation domains. Outcomes generally favored ICAPs for word finding, communication, participation, and QoL.
researchFindings: ICAPs generally improved word finding, functional communication, activity and participation, and communication-related quality of life outcomes for adults with aphasia.
Gains were largely maintained at follow-up, supporting the durability of intensive and comprehensive aphasia treatment.
21 studies covering 13 ICAPs and 485 participants were included; adults ranged from 18–86 years old and 11–335 months post-stroke onset.
ICAPs typically involve 3–5 hours of treatment per day over 2–3 weeks in formats combining individual SLT, group therapy, and self-management practice.
56 different outcome measures were used across studies, highlighting measurement heterogeneity that limits meta-analysis and cross-study comparison.
Individuals at all aphasia severity levels and life stages participated successfully in ICAPs, suggesting broad candidacy.
clinicalApplication: Refer clients with chronic aphasia who have plateaued in traditional low-dose therapy to an Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Programme (ICAP) when available. ICAPs are characterized by: high dose (≥3 hours/day), interdisciplinary group + individual format, targeting impairment AND participation AND quality of life simultaneously, and 2–3 week immersive structure. Communicate ICAP referral pathways in the clinical record and to the client/family. When a formal ICAP is not available, replicate key elements: increase session frequency, add group therapy, incorporate peer support, and target participation-level goals alongside impairment treatment. Outcomes are supported across broad severity range and chronicity.

sessionStats.dose: 2–3 intensive weeks; varies by programme
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with post-stroke aphasia at any chronicity or severity seeking significant functional gains

bestFitCriteria: Adults with post-stroke aphasia who have plateaued in traditional outpatient low-intensity therapy.
Clients who are motivated, medically stable, and can commit to 2–3 weeks of intensive daily treatment.
Individuals where aphasia is significantly limiting participation in life roles and a concentrated intensive effort is desired.
SLPs seeking to refer to an ICAP model or replicate its key components in a modified format within their practice setting.

title: Intensive Speech and Language Therapy in Patients with Chronic Aphasia after Stroke: A Randomised, Open-Label, Blinded-Endpoint, Controlled Trial
shortTitle: Intensive SLT for Chronic Aphasia (Breitenstein 2017)
authors: Breitenstein C, Grewe T, Flöel A, Ziegler W, Springer L, Martus P, Huber W, Willmes K, Ringelstein EB, Haeusler KG, Abel S, Glindemann R, Domahs F, Regenbrecht F, Krupinski JF, Miller N, Billinger M, Knecht S; FCET2EC Study Group
summary: First powered multicenter RCT (n=216) demonstrating that intensive SLT (≥10 hours/week for 3 weeks) produces significantly greater language gains in persons with chronic post-stroke aphasia compared to matched-intensity low-frequency therapy. Gains were maintained at 6-month follow-up.
researchFindings: Intensive SLT (≥10 hrs/week) produced significantly greater improvement in naming ability than less-intensive SLT (3.4 vs. 1.5 correct responses, p=0.003)
Treatment gains were maintained at 6-month follow-up, supporting durability of intensive treatment effects
Effects were independent of time post-stroke onset, severity, lesion site, or age
No increased adverse events were associated with intensive therapy delivery
clinicalApplication: Prioritize intensive scheduling (≥10 hrs/week) when intensive SLT is clinically appropriate for chronic aphasia. Intensive treatment can yield meaningful gains even in individuals with long-standing aphasia (chronic, >6 months post-stroke). Consider dose when planning aphasia treatment programs: intensity appears more impactful than total duration. Supports advocacy for higher-frequency SLP sessions in chronic aphasia.

sessionStats.population: Adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia (>6 months)
sessionStats.duration: 3 weeks (intensive arm)
sessionStats.goals: Naming accuracy, functional communication, language recovery

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic aphasia (>6 months post-stroke) who have plateaued with conventional therapy
Clients who can tolerate intensive scheduling (physically and cognitively)
Situations where concentrated treatment block is possible (e.g., rehabilitation admission, intensive outpatient)

title: New and Emerging Access Technologies for Adults with Complex Communication Needs and Severe Motor Impairments: State of the Science
shortTitle: Emerging AAC Access Technologies for Severe Motor Impairments (Fager 2019)
authors: Fager SK, Beukelman DR, Fried-Oken M, Jakobs T, Baker J
summary: Comprehensive review of emerging and evidence-based AAC access technologies for adults with severe motor impairments, including individuals with ALS, brainstem stroke, and spinal cord injury. Covers eye gaze, brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), switch access, and neural interfaces, with evidence-based recommendations for clinical decision-making.
researchFindings: Eye gaze technology demonstrates reliable access for individuals with ALS and locked-in syndrome, even in late-stage disease
Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) show emerging promise for individuals who cannot use any voluntary movement, though reliability varies across studies
Switch scanning remains the most widely validated access method across a range of motor abilities
Partner-assisted scanning and infrared sensor-based access provide viable alternatives when direct selection is not possible
clinicalApplication: Conduct comprehensive access assessments for adults with severe motor impairments to identify optimal AAC access method. Consider eye gaze technology as a primary access option for clients with reliable eye movements (e.g., ALS, brainstem stroke). Monitor motor changes over time for progressive conditions; re-evaluate access method as motor function changes. Educate clients and families about AAC access options and support training with chosen technology.

sessionStats.population: Adults with severe motor impairments (ALS, brainstem stroke, high cervical SCI, locked-in syndrome)
sessionStats.duration: Ongoing; access needs change with disease progression
sessionStats.goals: Reliable AAC access for functional communication

bestFitCriteria: Adults with severe motor impairments limiting speech and physical access
Individuals with ALS or other progressive neurological conditions approaching or at late-stage disease
Clients with brainstem stroke or high cervical spinal cord injury requiring alternative AAC access

title: Evidence-Based Cognitive Rehabilitation: Systematic Review of the Literature From 2009 Through 2014
shortTitle: Evidence-Based Cognitive Rehabilitation SR 2009–2014 (Cicerone 2019)
authors: Cicerone KD, Goldin Y, Ganci K, Rosenbaum A, Wethe JV, Langenbahn DM, Malec JF, Bergquist TF, Kingsley K, Nagele D, Trexler L, Fraas M, Bogdanova Y, Harley JP
journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
summary: Comprehensive systematic review updating evidence-based recommendations for cognitive rehabilitation in TBI and stroke (covering 2009–2014 literature). Provides practice standards, guidelines, and options across cognitive domains including attention, memory, executive function, social communication, and pragmatics.
researchFindings: Cognitive rehabilitation for attention deficits post-TBI and stroke is supported at the Practice Standard level, particularly attention process training
Meta-memory and prospective memory training demonstrate effectiveness for individuals with mild-to-moderate TBI
Metacognitive strategy instruction for executive function and functional outcomes is supported as a Practice Guideline for TBI
Social communication skills training post-TBI achieves Practice Guideline level support
clinicalApplication: Use attention process training and direct attention training interventions as first-line approaches for attention deficits after TBI/stroke. Implement metacognitive strategy training (e.g., Goal Management Training) for executive function deficits post-TBI. Target prospective memory using external compensatory strategies (alarms, calendars, checklists) and spaced retrieval. Address social communication deficits post-TBI using structured group treatment and communication partner training.

sessionStats.population: Adults with acquired TBI or stroke with cognitive-communication deficits
sessionStats.frequency: Variable based on domain and severity
sessionStats.duration: Varies; typically 6–12 weeks for structured cognitive rehab programs
sessionStats.goals: Attention, memory, executive function, social communication, functional independence

bestFitCriteria: Adults with TBI or stroke presenting with cognitive-communication impairments
Clients with attention, memory, or executive function deficits affecting daily functional communication
Individuals needing evidence-based justification for cognitive rehabilitation treatment planning

title: Effortful Swallow Maneuver in Adults with Dysphagia: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: Effortful Swallow Maneuver Systematic Review (Bahia 2020)
authors: Bahia MM, Lowell SY
summary: Systematic review synthesizing evidence for the effortful swallow maneuver in adults with dysphagia. Examines biomechanical effects (increased hyolaryngeal excursion, tongue base retraction, pharyngeal contraction) and functional outcomes across neurogenic and other etiologies.
researchFindings: Effortful swallow significantly increases tongue base retraction and posterior pharyngeal wall contraction, improving pharyngeal clearance
Hyolaryngeal excursion is enhanced with effortful swallow in healthy adults, with variable effects in neurogenic populations
Evidence supports effortful swallow as a compensatory strategy for reducing pharyngeal residue in neurogenic dysphagia
Therapeutic benefit for long-term use requires further high-quality RCT evidence; most studies are single-session designs
clinicalApplication: Trial effortful swallow maneuver for clients with reduced posterior pharyngeal wall contraction and pharyngeal residue. Teach effortful swallow with clear instruction: 'swallow hard as if squeezing the food down'. Monitor client effort and fatigue; effortful swallow increases muscular demand and may not be appropriate for all populations. Use effortful swallow as compensatory strategy; consider its use during meals in combination with postural strategies as appropriate.

sessionStats.population: Adults with neurogenic or other dysphagia affecting pharyngeal phase
sessionStats.frequency: As part of swallowing treatment sessions; may be trialed per meal
sessionStats.duration: Variable; typically integrated into dysphagia treatment program
sessionStats.goals: Reduce pharyngeal residue, improve bolus clearance, enhance pharyngeal contraction

bestFitCriteria: Adults with pharyngeal residue or reduced posterior pharyngeal wall contraction on MBS/FEES
Neurogenic dysphagia (stroke, TBI, Parkinson's disease) with adequate volitional control
Clients who can follow verbal instruction and self-monitor effort during swallowing

title: Nonpharmacological Interventions for Stuttering in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Nonpharmacological Stuttering Interventions Meta-Analysis (Connery 2021)
authors: Connery A, Galvin R, Cusack T, Staines A
summary: Meta-analysis examining the efficacy of nonpharmacological interventions for stuttering in adults, including speech restructuring, fluency shaping, CBT, stuttering modification, and self-help approaches. Provides pooled effect sizes and evidence grades across outcome categories.
researchFindings: Fluency-shaping interventions (e.g., prolonged speech, breathstream management) showed statistically significant reductions in stuttering frequency post-treatment
CBT and acceptance-based approaches significantly improved quality of life, communication attitudes, and avoidance behaviors
Combined speech restructuring and psychological approaches produced superior outcomes compared to either alone
Maintenance of fluency gains at follow-up varied; psychological approaches demonstrated more durable attitudinal change
clinicalApplication: Offer combined approaches integrating fluency modification techniques with CBT or acceptance-based strategies for adults who stutter. Address psychosocial dimensions of stuttering (avoidance, anxiety, quality of life) as core treatment targets alongside speech modifications. Incorporate self-help and support groups as adjuncts to clinical treatment. Match treatment approach to individual goals: fluency goals vs. acceptance goals vs. both.

sessionStats.population: Adults with developmental stuttering
sessionStats.frequency: Variable; typically 1–2 sessions/week in outpatient setting
sessionStats.duration: Varies widely by approach: 10–20+ sessions typical
sessionStats.goals: Stuttering frequency, communication attitudes, quality of life, avoidance reduction

bestFitCriteria: Adults with developmental stuttering seeking fluency shaping or modification treatment
Clients with significant psychosocial impact of stuttering (anxiety, avoidance, reduced QoL)
Individuals who have not responded to traditional fluency techniques and may benefit from acceptance-based approaches

title: Apraxia of Speech in Adults: An Updated Systematic Review of the Intervention Literature
shortTitle: AOS Treatment Systematic Review Update (Munasinghe 2023)
authors: Munasinghe M, Sullivan AM, Ballard KJ
summary: Comprehensive updated systematic review of intervention research for acquired apraxia of speech (AOS) in adults, covering literature through 2021. Reviews articulatory-kinematic, rate/rhythm, LSVT-based, and multimodal treatment approaches with quality appraisal and clinical recommendations.
researchFindings: Articulatory-kinematic approaches (Sound Production Treatment, Repeated Practice) have the strongest evidence base for AOS, with multiple single-subject experimental design studies supporting efficacy
Rate and rhythm control approaches (metronome, pacing board) demonstrate consistent efficacy for improving intelligibility but may interfere with prosody
Motor learning principles (variable practice, distributed practice, reduced feedback frequency) are increasingly integrated into AOS treatment with positive outcomes
Limited high-quality RCT evidence available; most support comes from single-subject experimental designs
clinicalApplication: Apply articulatory-kinematic approaches (Sound Production Treatment, Motor Learning Guided treatment) as primary interventions for AOS. Integrate motor learning principles: practice variability, clinician feedback fading, distributed practice schedules. Use rate control strategies (pacing board, metronomic pacing) for clients with severely reduced intelligibility. Consider biofeedback (ultrasound, EPG) as adjunct when available to support articulatory precision.

sessionStats.population: Adults with acquired apraxia of speech (post-stroke, TBI, or neurodegenerative onset)
sessionStats.frequency: 3–5 sessions/week for intensive protocols; 1–3/week for maintenance
sessionStats.duration: Typically 8–12 weeks for intensive phase; ongoing for progressive conditions
sessionStats.goals: Articulatory accuracy, speech rate, intelligibility, generalization to conversation

bestFitCriteria: Adults with diagnosed or suspected acquired apraxia of speech
Clients with inconsistent sound production errors, effortful groping, and trial-and-error behavior
AOS with or without co-occurring aphasia or dysarthria

title: Treatment of Vocal Fold Polyps: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Vocal Fold Polyp Treatment Meta-Analysis (Barsties 2023)
authors: Barsties v. Latoszek B, Ulozaitė-Stanienė N, Petrauskas T, Uloza V
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis comparing outcomes of surgical and conservative (voice therapy) treatment for vocal fold polyps. Evaluates acoustic, aerodynamic, and patient-reported outcomes, and assesses predictors of treatment success.
researchFindings: Surgical intervention (microlaryngoscopy) consistently produced significant improvements in Voice Handicap Index (VHI), jitter, shimmer, and HNR across studies
Voice therapy alone demonstrated significant improvement for smaller polyps, particularly sessile polyps; effect sizes were moderate to large
Combined voice therapy plus surgery produced the most comprehensive outcomes, especially for larger or persistent polyps
Vocal hygiene education and voice rest prior to surgery contributed to better post-surgical outcomes
clinicalApplication: Provide voice therapy (vocal hygiene, voice rest, vocal function exercises) as first-line or pre-surgical adjunct for clients with vocal fold polyps. Collaborate with otolaryngology for surgical referral when voice therapy alone is insufficient, particularly for larger or hemorrhagic polyps. Post-surgical voice therapy is recommended to prevent recurrence and optimize voice outcomes. Counsel clients on vocal hygiene, voice rest, and hydration as essential components of polyp management.

sessionStats.population: Adults with diagnosed vocal fold polyp(s)
sessionStats.duration: Typically 4–8 weeks pre-surgery or as primary treatment
sessionStats.environment: Outpatient voice clinic, collaborative ENT setting
sessionStats.goals: Voice quality (VHI, jitter, shimmer), voice hygiene adherence, polyp resolution

bestFitCriteria: Adults with unilateral or bilateral vocal fold polyps confirmed by laryngoscopy
Clients with dysphonia secondary to vocal fold polyp with or without surgical plan
Cases where voice therapy may prevent or delay surgical intervention

title: Pharyngeal Cavity Electrical Stimulation for Post-Stroke Dysphagia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Pharyngeal Electrical Stimulation for Post-Stroke Dysphagia (Liu 2024)
authors: Liu Z, Wang W, Zhong F, Chen W, Wang J
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the efficacy of pharyngeal cavity electrical stimulation (PCES) — delivered via a catheter positioned in the pharynx — for treating post-stroke dysphagia. Pooled analysis of RCTs examining swallowing function outcomes.
researchFindings: PCES significantly improved swallowing function in post-stroke dysphagia compared to sham stimulation across pooled RCT data
Significant reduction in aspiration/penetration on videofluoroscopy or FEES following PCES treatment
Greatest effect sizes observed in subacute stroke patients with moderate-to-severe oropharyngeal dysphagia
Treatment protocols typically involve 3 sessions of 10-minute stimulation delivered on consecutive days
clinicalApplication: Consider PCES as an adjunct treatment option for post-stroke dysphagia in settings where this technology is available. PCES may be particularly beneficial for subacute stroke patients with moderate-to-severe oropharyngeal dysphagia. Advocate for access to PCES (marketed as Phagenyx device in some markets) when other dysphagia interventions have limited response. Combine PCES with behavioral swallowing treatment for comprehensive dysphagia rehabilitation.

sessionStats.population: Adults with post-stroke oropharyngeal dysphagia
sessionStats.frequency: 3 sessions on consecutive days (typical PCES protocol)
sessionStats.duration: 10 minutes per session; effects evaluated over weeks post-treatment
sessionStats.environment: Hospital, medical setting with appropriate equipment
sessionStats.goals: Reduce aspiration/penetration, improve swallowing function, advance diet

bestFitCriteria: Adults with subacute or chronic post-stroke oropharyngeal dysphagia
Clients with persistent dysphagia not adequately managed with behavioral techniques alone
Settings with access to pharyngeal electrical stimulation technology

title: Computerized Cognitive Training for Older Adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment or Dementia: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Computerized Cognitive Training for MCI and Dementia (Wan 2024)
authors: Wan Q, Xu Z, Huo M, Li G, Liu Y, Guo L
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of computerized cognitive training (CCT) programs for older adults with MCI or dementia. Evaluates effects on global cognition, memory, attention, executive function, and language, with subgroup analyses by training characteristics.
researchFindings: CCT produced significant improvements in global cognition, memory, and processing speed in individuals with MCI (pooled effect sizes medium)
Training frequency and duration significantly moderated outcomes: higher-intensity protocols (≥3 sessions/week, ≥8 weeks) showed greatest benefit
Adaptive difficulty CCT programs outperformed fixed-difficulty programs for cognitive gains
Benefits were observed for language and verbal learning measures, relevant to cognitive-communication intervention
clinicalApplication: Incorporate structured computerized cognitive training programs into treatment plans for adults with MCI affecting cognitive-communication. Recommend CCT platforms with adaptive difficulty adjustment for optimal cognitive engagement. Target higher frequency use (≥3 times/week) and longer program duration (≥8 weeks) for meaningful cognitive-communication benefits. Use CCT as adjunct to direct therapy and functional communication strategies; not a standalone replacement for SLP intervention.

sessionStats.population: Older adults with MCI or early-to-moderate dementia
sessionStats.duration: 8+ weeks; ongoing use beneficial for maintenance
sessionStats.goals: Global cognition, memory, processing speed, language, functional communication

bestFitCriteria: Older adults with diagnosed MCI or early dementia affecting cognitive-communication
Clients with access to tablet or computer devices for home-based training
Individuals motivated to engage with technology-based cognitive training

title: Determinants of Clinical Response to Injection Laryngoplasty in Unilateral Vocal Fold Paralysis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Injection Laryngoplasty for UVFP: Outcomes Meta-Analysis (Safia 2024)
authors: Safia A, Abd Elhadi U, Roch M, Kassem K, Safiya R, Zubeidat A, Nofal N, Heib A, Merchavy S, Bishara T
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 82 studies examining injection laryngoplasty (IL) for unilateral vocal fold paralysis (UVFP). Identifies determinants of treatment response including injection material, volume, and timing, with pooled outcomes for voice quality, aerodynamic, and patient-reported measures.
researchFindings: Injection laryngoplasty significantly improved maximum phonation time (MPT), harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR), and Voice Handicap Index (VHI) post-injection across 82 pooled studies
Injection material significantly moderated outcomes: polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) and autologous fat showed superior effects on MPT and vocal quality
Injection volume and timing of intervention were significant predictors of phonatory outcomes in meta-regression
Earlier injection (within 6 months of paralysis onset) was associated with better outcomes for temporary paralysis
clinicalApplication: Educate clients with UVFP on injection laryngoplasty as a first-line procedural intervention for glottic insufficiency and dysphonia. Voice therapy (resonance, projection strategies) can complement injection laryngoplasty to maximize voice outcomes. Timing matters: advocate for timely referral to laryngologist; early injection (within 6 months) is associated with better outcomes. Monitor voice outcomes post-injection; voice therapy should continue post-procedure to reinforce gains.

sessionStats.population: Adults with unilateral vocal fold paralysis (UVFP) causing dysphonia
sessionStats.duration: 4–8 weeks post-injection voice therapy
sessionStats.environment: Outpatient voice clinic; collaboration with ENT/laryngology
sessionStats.goals: MPT, voice quality (VHI), HNR, breathiness, dysphonia grade

bestFitCriteria: Adults with confirmed unilateral vocal fold paralysis causing dysphonia
Clients referred from ENT/laryngology with UVFP who are candidates for or have received injection laryngoplasty
SLP coordinating care with otolaryngology for voice rehabilitation post-injection

title: Effects of Expiratory Muscle Strength Training on Videofluoroscopic Measures of Swallowing: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: EMST Effects on Videofluoroscopic Swallowing Measures (Hegland 2020)
authors: Hegland KW, Bolser DC, Davenport PW
summary: Systematic review examining the effects of expiratory muscle strength training (EMST) on videofluoroscopic (MBS) swallowing measures across multiple neurological populations. Evaluates penetration-aspiration, hyolaryngeal excursion, and pharyngeal swallowing physiology outcomes.
researchFindings: EMST protocols (5x5 breaths/day at 50–75% MEP, 4 weeks) were used across reviewed studies with varied populations including PD, MS, stroke, and aging
Heterogeneous VFS outcomes across studies precluded meta-analysis; several studies showed improvements in Penetration-Aspiration Scale (PAS) scores post-EMST
Improvements in hyolaryngeal excursion and tongue base retraction were reported in some studies, suggesting biomechanical benefits relevant to airway protection
Evidence suggests EMST may improve cough effectiveness and airway clearance complementary to direct swallowing improvement
clinicalApplication: Implement EMST as adjunct treatment to target expiratory muscle weakness contributing to impaired airway protection and swallowing in neurogenic populations. Standard EMST protocol: 5 sets of 5 exhalations against calibrated EMST-150 device at 75% maximal expiratory pressure (MEP), 5 days/week for 4 weeks. Monitor MEP at baseline and weekly; adjust load to 75% MEP weekly to ensure progressive training. Evaluate swallowing outcomes via instrumental assessment (MBS/FEES) to document change in penetration-aspiration and pharyngeal clearance.

sessionStats.population: Adults with neurogenic dysphagia (PD, MS, stroke, ALS, aging)
sessionStats.duration: 4 weeks minimum; may extend for progressive conditions
sessionStats.environment: Home-based training with weekly outpatient check-ins
sessionStats.goals: Expiratory muscle strength, Penetration-Aspiration Scale score, hyolaryngeal excursion, cough effectiveness

bestFitCriteria: Adults with neurogenic dysphagia and suspected expiratory muscle weakness affecting airway protection
Clients with Parkinson's disease, MS, or stroke with aspiration risk related to inadequate cough and airway clearance
Individuals able to use handheld EMST device independently or with caregiver support

title: Communication Partner Training in Aphasia: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: Communication Partner Training in Aphasia SR (Simmons-Mackie 2010)
authors: Simmons-Mackie N, Raymer A, Armstrong E, Holland A, Cherney LR
journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
summary: Landmark systematic review of 31 studies examining communication partner training (CPT) for aphasia. Reviews effects on partners' communication skills, psychosocial adjustment, and quality of life, as well as secondary effects on persons with aphasia. Established evidence base for CPT as a distinct evidence-based approach in aphasia rehabilitation.
researchFindings: Communication partner training produced positive psychosocial outcomes for partners in 21 of 22 studies, including reduced burden and improved confidence
Trained partners demonstrated improved ability to support communication in persons with aphasia in 20+ studies
Persons with aphasia showed secondary benefits from partner training including improved participation and communication effectiveness
Evidence supports CPT as a clinically beneficial, low-cost component of aphasia rehabilitation
clinicalApplication: Include communication partner training (family, caregivers, healthcare workers) as a standard component of aphasia rehabilitation. Train partners to use supported conversation techniques: reduce complexity, use multimodal supports, allow time, verify understanding. Extend partner training beyond spouses to include paid caregivers, volunteers, and community communication partners. Monitor partner confidence and communication quality as outcome measures alongside person-with-aphasia outcomes.

sessionStats.population: Adults with aphasia and their communication partners
sessionStats.frequency: Variable; typically 1–5 training sessions for partners
sessionStats.duration: Partner training may be completed in 4–10 hours; ongoing coaching beneficial
sessionStats.goals: Partner communication skills, person with aphasia participation, caregiver QoL

bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia of any severity who have willing communication partners
Aphasia rehabilitation contexts where family and caregiver involvement is feasible
Individuals transitioning from acute/inpatient rehabilitation to community living

title: Treatment for Acquired Apraxia of Speech: A Systematic Review of Intervention Research Between 2004 and 2012
shortTitle: AOS Intervention Systematic Review 2004–2012 (Ballard 2015)
authors: Ballard KJ, Wambaugh JL, Duffy JR, Layfield C, Maas E, Mauszycki S, McNeil MR
summary: ANCDS-commissioned systematic review of acquired AOS intervention research from 2004–2012. Systematic search of 11 databases identified 215 articles; 26 met inclusion criteria. Reviews articulatory-kinematic, rate/rhythm control, and multimodal approaches, with evidence ratings.
researchFindings: Articulatory-kinematic approaches (Sound Production Treatment, Repeated Practice) had the strongest evidence base: 24 of 26 studies applied these methods
Rate and rhythm control approaches (pacing, metronome, biofeedback) received support across multiple studies with consistent positive outcomes
Evidence quality was predominantly Level V (single-subject experimental design); no Class I RCTs of AOS were identified in this period
Treatment gains were primarily demonstrated for trained items with limited generalization data available
clinicalApplication: Use articulatory-kinematic approaches as the primary evidence-based AOS intervention: Sound Production Treatment (SPT) and Motor Learning Guided (MLG) treatment are well-supported. Apply principles of motor learning: variable practice, distributed schedules, fading feedback to promote generalization. Supplement with rate/rhythm control when intelligibility is severely compromised. Document target behaviors precisely and track generalization probes in clinical practice.

sessionStats.population: Adults with acquired AOS (typically post-stroke or TBI)
sessionStats.duration: 8–12 weeks for a treatment block
sessionStats.goals: Articulatory accuracy on trained sounds/words, intelligibility, speech rate

bestFitCriteria: Adults with confirmed or suspected acquired AOS
Clients demonstrating effortful, groping speech with inconsistent errors on repeated attempts
AOS with or without co-occurring aphasia

title: Comparing the Effectiveness of Cognitive Behavioral Group Therapy and Mindfulness and Acceptance Group Therapy for Adults Who Stutter: A Randomized Clinical Trial
shortTitle: CBT vs. Mindfulness-Acceptance Therapy for Stuttering RCT (2023)
authors: Rahmani M, Yadegari F, Shirazi TS, Asgari A, Khatir MY
summary: RCT (n=36) comparing Cognitive Behavioral Group Therapy + Speech Therapy (CBGT+ST) vs. Mindfulness and Acceptance Group Therapy + Speech Therapy (MAGT+ST) for adults who stutter, assessing fear of negative evaluation and social avoidance outcomes. Both combined approaches demonstrated significant improvements over speech therapy alone.
researchFindings: Both CBGT+ST and MAGT+ST produced significant reductions in social avoidance and distress (SAD) compared to baseline
CBGT+ST significantly reduced fear of negative evaluation (FNE), while MAGT+ST showed non-significant trends
Combined psychosocial and speech therapy approaches outperformed speech therapy alone for psychosocial outcomes
Gains maintained at 6-month follow-up for both combined treatment groups
clinicalApplication: Integrate CBT or mindfulness/acceptance-based techniques into stuttering treatment to target psychosocial impacts. Refer to psychology or use integrated SLP-CBT approaches for clients with significant social anxiety, fear of negative evaluation, or avoidance related to stuttering. Group therapy formats (CBGT or MAGT) may be particularly effective for social communication skill practice and peer support. Address the psychological dimension of stuttering as a co-equal treatment target alongside speech modification techniques.

sessionStats.population: Adults with developmental stuttering and significant psychosocial impact
sessionStats.frequency: Weekly group sessions (combined with speech therapy)
sessionStats.duration: 12–16 weeks typical for combined approach
sessionStats.goals: Fear of negative evaluation, social avoidance, quality of life, communication participation

bestFitCriteria: Adults who stutter with notable social anxiety, fear of negative evaluation, or communication avoidance
Clients who have not achieved psychosocial goals through fluency techniques alone
Individuals interested in acceptance-based or CBT approaches as alternatives or complements to fluency shaping

title: Effects of Transcutaneous Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation on Swallowing Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Transcutaneous NMES for Dysphagia: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (2020)
authors: Li AH, Zhang JM, Xiao AL
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 RCTs/quasi-RCTs examining transcutaneous NMES (e.g., VitalStim) for swallowing disorders. Pooled effect size was significant and moderate overall, with large effects for acquired brain injury and for combined suprahyoid/infrahyoid stimulation.
researchFindings: Pooled effect of NMES + traditional therapy vs. traditional therapy alone: significant moderate effect size (SMD=0.62; 95% CI 0.06–1.17)
Largest effect sizes observed for acquired brain injury (SMD=0.95) and combined suprahyoid+infrahyoid stimulation (SMD=1.4)
Stimulation duration ≤45 minutes per session associated with large, significant effects
No adverse events were reported across included studies; NMES was well tolerated
clinicalApplication: Consider transcutaneous NMES as an adjunct to traditional dysphagia therapy, particularly for acquired brain injury (stroke, TBI). Target combined suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscle groups for optimal swallowing effect. Limit session duration to ≤45 minutes; longer sessions did not show additional benefit. NMES should be delivered alongside behavioral swallowing strategies, not as a standalone replacement for compensatory and rehabilitative approaches.

sessionStats.population: Adults with neurogenic dysphagia (acquired brain injury, stroke, TBI)
sessionStats.frequency: Daily or 5 days/week typical for NMES protocols
sessionStats.duration: 3–4 weeks standard protocol; ≤45 minutes per session
sessionStats.environment: Inpatient, outpatient, or long-term care with certified NMES clinician
sessionStats.goals: Swallowing function improvement, Penetration-Aspiration Scale, FOIS advancement

bestFitCriteria: Adults with neurogenic dysphagia post-stroke or acquired brain injury
Clients who have not adequately responded to behavioral dysphagia treatment alone
Settings with certified NMES practitioners and appropriate equipment

title: Intensive Versus Distributed Aphasia Therapy: A Nonrandomized, Parallel-Group, Dosage-Controlled Study
shortTitle: Intensive vs. Distributed Aphasia Therapy Dosage Study (Dignam 2015)
authors: Dignam JK, Copland DA, McKinnon E, Burfein P, O'Brien K, Farrell A, Rodriguez AD
summary: Dosage-controlled parallel-group study (n=34) comparing intensive (16 hrs/week x 3 weeks) vs. distributed (6 hrs/week x 8 weeks) aphasia therapy, both providing 48 total hours of multimodal treatment (impairment-based, functional, computer, group). Distributed scheduling produced superior language impairment outcomes.
researchFindings: Distributed therapy (6 hrs/week x 8 weeks) produced significantly greater gains on language impairment measures than intensive therapy (16 hrs/week x 3 weeks) despite equal total dose
No significant between-group differences on functional communication or participation measures
Intensive scheduling may produce fatigue or reduced learning efficiency over concentrated short periods
Findings suggest that spaced practice and distributed scheduling may optimize language learning for aphasia
clinicalApplication: When total therapy dose is equivalent, distributed scheduling (lower intensity over longer duration) may yield superior language impairment outcomes for chronic aphasia. Consider spaced practice schedules (e.g., 3x/week over 8 weeks) over highly compressed intensive blocks where possible.
