Distributed scheduling aligns with motor learning principles of spaced practice and may reduce fatigue. Clinical scheduling decisions should also consider client-level factors, access, and goals.

sessionStats.population: Adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia (>3 months)
sessionStats.frequency: Distributed: ~2 hrs/day, 3 days/week; Intensive: ~3 hrs/day, 5 days/week
sessionStats.duration: Total 48 hours; distributed = 8 weeks vs. intensive = 3 weeks
sessionStats.goals: Language impairment, functional communication, participation

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic aphasia who can attend multiple treatment sessions per week over an extended period
Clinicians planning treatment scheduling decisions where total dose is comparable
Aphasia rehabilitation programs comparing short intensive blocks vs. extended outpatient programs

title: Improved Conversation Outcomes After Social Communication Skills Training for People With Traumatic Brain Injury and Their Communication Partners: A Clinical Trial Investigating In-Person and Telehealth Delivery
shortTitle: Social Communication Skills Training for TBI: In-Person vs. Telehealth Trial (Togher 2020)
authors: Togher L, Wiseman-Hakes C, Douglas J, Schultz R, Tate RL, Perdices M, McDonald S, Gillett LE, Power E
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: RCT examining social communication skills training (TBIconneCT program) delivered in-person and via telehealth for individuals with TBI and their communication partners. Demonstrated equivalent outcomes across delivery modes with significant gains in conversation quality and participation.
researchFindings: Both in-person and telehealth delivery of TBIconneCT produced significant improvements in conversation quality as rated by blinded observers
Communication partner involvement in training led to generalized improvements in real-world conversational interaction
Telehealth delivery achieved equivalent clinical outcomes to in-person delivery, expanding access to treatment
Gains in conversation quality were maintained at 3-month follow-up
clinicalApplication: Use structured social communication skills training programs (e.g., TBIconneCT) for adults with TBI with social communication deficits. Include communication partners (family, caregivers) in TBI social communication treatment to promote generalization. Offer telehealth as a clinically valid delivery option for TBI social communication training, particularly for rural or mobility-limited clients. Target specific conversation behaviors: topic management, turn-taking, relevance, asking questions.

sessionStats.population: Adults with moderate-to-severe TBI and social communication deficits
sessionStats.duration: Typically 8–12 weeks for social communication training program
sessionStats.goals: Conversation quality, turn-taking, topic management, partner-rated communication

Clients with communication partners willing to participate in treatment
TBI clients for whom telehealth access may improve treatment engagement and attendance

title: The Effects of Intensive Speech Treatment on Intelligibility in Parkinson's Disease: A Randomised Controlled Trial
shortTitle: Intensive Speech Treatment and Intelligibility in Parkinson's Disease RCT (2020)
authors: Halpern A, Ramig LO, Matos C, Petska-Cable JA, Spielman JL, Pogoda JM, Gilley PM, Sapir S, Bennett JK, McFarland DH
summary: First RCT comparing LSVT LOUD (voice-focused intensive speech treatment) vs. LSVT ARTIC (articulation-focused intensive speech treatment) vs. no treatment (n=64) for hypokinetic dysarthria in Parkinson's disease. LSVT LOUD produced significantly greater improvements in speech intelligibility (transcription accuracy).
researchFindings: LSVT LOUD significantly improved transcription accuracy (speech intelligibility) compared to both LSVT ARTIC and no-treatment control groups
Treatment targeting voice (loudness and vocal function) yielded superior intelligibility gains vs. treatment targeting articulation alone
LSVT LOUD group showed significant improvements in % words transcribed correctly; gains maintained at 6-month follow-up
Results provide first RCT evidence supporting LSVT LOUD as the superior intensive speech treatment for improving intelligibility in PD
clinicalApplication: Use LSVT LOUD as first-line intensive speech treatment for hypokinetic dysarthria in Parkinson's disease to improve intelligibility. Prioritize voice-focused treatment (loudness, vocal effort) over articulation-focused treatment alone based on RCT evidence. Adhere to LSVT LOUD protocol: 4 sessions/week x 4 weeks, targeting maximum phonation time, sustained vowels, reading, and conversation. Teach 'THINK LOUD' carryover strategy for generalization to daily communication.

sessionStats.population: Adults with Parkinson's disease and hypokinetic dysarthria
sessionStats.duration: 4 weeks intensive treatment; carryover exercises ongoing
sessionStats.goals: Speech intelligibility, vocal loudness, communicative participation

bestFitCriteria: Adults with Parkinson's disease presenting with hypokinetic dysarthria (reduced loudness, imprecise articulation)
PD clients with adequate cognition and motivation to participate in intensive 4-week protocol
Clinicians certified in or trained on LSVT LOUD protocol

title: High-Technology Augmentative Communication for Adults with Post-Stroke Aphasia: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: High-Technology AAC for Post-Stroke Aphasia Systematic Review (2017)
authors: Pitt R, Theodoros D, Hill AJ, Russell T
summary: Systematic review synthesizing evidence for high-technology AAC interventions (tablets, speech-generating devices, communication apps) for adults with post-stroke aphasia. Reviews treatment outcomes for functional communication, language recovery, and quality of life, with recommendations for clinical implementation.
researchFindings: High-technology AAC improved functional communication outcomes in adults with post-stroke aphasia across multiple single-case and small group studies
Tablet-based AAC applications (e.g., Lingraphica, Snap Core First) demonstrated feasibility and acceptability in aphasia populations
Speech generating devices (SGDs) supported multimodal communication and reduced communication breakdown
Evidence supports high-tech AAC as a compensatory communication approach alongside, not instead of, impairment-based language therapy
clinicalApplication: Assess for high-technology AAC for adults with aphasia who have persistent communication impairment affecting functional participation. Trial tablet-based AAC apps (e.g., aphasia-specific apps with symbol, photo, and text supports) as part of comprehensive aphasia management. Train both the person with aphasia and communication partners in high-tech AAC device use for maximum benefit. Consider high-tech AAC alongside, not as a replacement for, language therapy; devices support participation while therapy targets impairment.

sessionStats.frequency: Variable; AAC trials and training integrated into SLP sessions

Individuals with aphasia interested in or motivated to use high-technology AAC devices
Clients for whom functional communication is a priority goal alongside or instead of language recovery

title: Three Treatments for Teachers With Voice Disorders: A Randomized Clinical Trial
shortTitle: Three Treatments for Teacher Voice Disorders RCT (Roy 2003)
authors: Roy N, Weinrich B, Gray SD, Tanner K, Stemple JC, Sapienza CM
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: Landmark RCT (n=64 teachers) comparing three voice treatments: voice amplification (VA), resonance therapy (RT), and respiratory muscle training (RMT) for teachers with voice disorders. Resonance therapy and voice amplification produced the greatest improvements in patient-reported voice outcomes.
researchFindings: Resonance therapy significantly improved patient-rated voice quality, handicap, and symptom severity compared to no treatment control
Voice amplification significantly reduced vocal demands and improved perceived vocal effort for teachers during teaching
Respiratory muscle training (RMT/threshold IMT) did not demonstrate significant advantage over control for voice outcomes in this group
Resonance therapy effects were durable at 8-week follow-up, while voice amplification benefits were device-dependent
clinicalApplication: Offer resonance therapy (forward-focused phonation) as a primary evidence-based voice treatment for teachers and other occupational voice users with functional dysphonia. Voice amplification devices can serve as compensatory strategies to reduce phonatory demand for teachers during high-vocal-load periods. Consider respiratory muscle training as adjunct rather than primary treatment for functional voice disorders in vocal professionals. Include vocal hygiene education alongside primary voice treatment for occupational voice users.

sessionStats.population: Adults (teachers) with occupational voice disorders (functional dysphonia)
sessionStats.duration: 8 weeks treatment period
sessionStats.goals: Patient-rated voice quality, vocal handicap, symptom severity, phonatory ease

bestFitCriteria: Adults with functional voice disorders, particularly occupational voice users (teachers, singers, clergy, call center workers)
Clients with muscle tension dysphonia or functional dysphonia without structural pathology
Voice patients seeking evidence-based treatment options including resonance approaches

title: Functional Communication in Individuals with Chronic Severe Aphasia Using Augmentative Communication
shortTitle: AAC for Chronic Severe Aphasia — Functional Communication (2008)
authors: Johnson RK, Hough MS, King KA, Vos P, Jeffs T
summary: Case series examining three adults with chronic non-fluent aphasia who used a dynamic display AAC device (Dialect with Speaking Dynamically Pro) tailored to each participant's skill level. Pre- and post-treatment measures revealed meaningful improvements in functional communication quality and effectiveness across all three participants.
researchFindings: All three adults with chronic non-fluent aphasia demonstrated improvement in quality and effectiveness of communication following AAC device intervention
Two participants showed concurrent improvements in linguistic and cognitive functioning after device use
Dynamic display AAC devices can be successfully customized to the skill level of individuals with severe aphasia using evidence-based protocols
Caregiver (spouse) involvement in AAC training was a key component of successful implementation
clinicalApplication: Trial dynamic display AAC devices for adults with moderate-to-severe chronic aphasia who have limited verbal output. Customize AAC device vocabulary and display complexity to match the individual's linguistic and cognitive skill level. Involve caregivers and communication partners in AAC training from the outset to support carryover to natural settings. Use AAC as a functional communication strategy alongside—not replacing—aphasia treatment targeting language impairment.

sessionStats.population: Adults with chronic non-fluent severe aphasia (post-stroke)
sessionStats.frequency: Sessions integrated around device training protocol
sessionStats.duration: Treatment length variable; pre- and post-treatment assessment conducted
sessionStats.goals: Functional communication, message transmission effectiveness, quality of communication exchanges

bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic non-fluent or severe aphasia with very limited verbal communication
Individuals who have plateaued in language therapy but have functional communication goals
Clients motivated to use technology to support participation in daily communication

title: Augmentative and Alternative Communication Improves Quality of Life in the Early Stages of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
shortTitle: AAC Improves QoL in Early-Stage ALS (2019)
authors: Maresca G, Pranio F, Naro A, De Luca R, Maggio MG, Scarcella I, De Domenico C, Bramanti P, Conti Nibali V, Portaro S, Calabrò RS
summary: Prospective study evaluating low-tech AAC aids in 10 adults with ALS in the early stage of the disease when speech difficulties first emerge. A six-month training program (AAC-intervention + AAC-familiarization phases) demonstrated significant improvements in acceptance of AAC, mood, quality of life, and reduced caregiver burden.
researchFindings: All 10 participants with early-stage ALS showed gradual and significant improvements in mood and quality of life following AAC training
Acceptance of AAC aids improved progressively over the six-month program, highlighting the importance of early and staged introduction
Caregiver burden was significantly reduced following the AAC intervention, benefiting both the patient and care system
AAC introduced proactively in early stages (when some natural speech remains) leads to better long-term uptake than introducing at end-stage
clinicalApplication: Introduce AAC proactively in early ALS when speech is still functional—do not wait for speech to deteriorate significantly. Stage AAC training in phases: initial AAC familiarization, then systematic AAC integration into daily communication. Involve caregivers in all phases of AAC training to reduce caregiver burden and support device use at home. Use low-tech AAC (alphabet boards, communication books) as entry-level tools before progressing to high-tech speech generating devices.

sessionStats.population: Adults with early-stage ALS presenting with dysarthria
sessionStats.duration: 6 months total: 3-month AAC-intervention + 3-month AAC-familiarization
sessionStats.goals: Quality of life, mood, caregiver burden, AAC acceptance and use

bestFitCriteria: Adults with ALS in early stages when dysarthria first presents and natural speech is still partially functional
ALS patients or caregivers motivated to proactively prepare for communication changes
Clients for whom quality of life and caregiver burden are key outcome priorities

title: Intensive Stuttering Modification Therapy: A Multidimensional Assessment of Treatment Outcomes
shortTitle: Intensive Stuttering Modification Therapy Outcomes (2005)
authors: Blomgren M, Roy N, Callister T, Merrill RM
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: Multidimensional treatment outcomes study examining 19 adults who stutter enrolled in a 3-week intensive stuttering modification program (Successful Stuttering Management Program, SSMP). Assessed across 14 fluency and affective measures at baseline, post-treatment, and 6-month follow-up. SSMP produced anxiolytic effects but limited durable reductions in core stuttering frequency.
researchFindings: Statistically significant improvements were observed on 4 of 14 measures immediately post-treatment and at 6-month follow-up
SSMP produced meaningful reductions in stuttering-related anxiety and avoidance behaviors
Core stuttering behaviors (stuttering frequency and severity) showed limited durable improvement at 6-month follow-up
Affective and attitudinal changes (anxiety, attitude toward stuttering) were more durable than behavioral fluency measures
Multidimensional outcomes assessment is essential—stuttering treatment gains in one domain may not reflect gains in others
clinicalApplication: Set realistic expectations with clients about intensive stuttering modification programs: emotional and attitudinal gains may exceed fluency gains. Measure treatment outcomes across multiple domains—fluency frequency, severity, anxiety, avoidance, quality of life—not just disfluency rate. Stuttering modification approaches (SSMP) are particularly appropriate for clients prioritizing reduced fear and avoidance over fluency targets. Plan for long-term follow-up and booster sessions; gains in core stuttering behavior can diminish at 6 months without maintenance.

sessionStats.population: Adults who stutter (moderate-to-severe)
sessionStats.duration: 3-week intensive program (SSMP); 6-month follow-up
sessionStats.goals: Stuttering frequency, severity, anxiety, avoidance, quality of life across 14 measures

bestFitCriteria: Adults who stutter prioritizing reduction in fear, avoidance, and emotional burden over fluency
Clients for whom stuttering-related anxiety and social avoidance are primary barriers
Adults motivated for intensive treatment with availability for multi-week immersive programs

title: The Long Term Effectiveness of Intensive Stuttering Therapy: A Mixed Methods Study
shortTitle: Long-Term Effectiveness of Intensive Stuttering Therapy (2012)
authors: Irani F, Gabel R, Daniels D, Hughes S
summary: Mixed methods study examining client perceptions of a multi-faceted intensive stuttering therapy program and its long-term effectiveness. Qualitative and quantitative data from adults who stuttered captured both objective outcomes and lived experience of treatment, with themes around maintenance, relapse, and psychosocial factors influencing long-term success.
researchFindings: Multi-faceted intensive stuttering therapy produced meaningful gains in both fluency and psychosocial functioning for most participants
Long-term maintenance of treatment gains was variable; participants identified the importance of ongoing practice and support
Client-perceived success was often tied more to quality of life and reduced avoidance than to fluency rates alone
Relapse was commonly reported and linked to high-stress communication situations and reduced practice adherence
Clients valued the psychosocial components of intensive programs as much as or more than the fluency-shaping techniques
clinicalApplication: Address maintenance planning explicitly within intensive stuttering programs—schedule booster sessions and self-monitoring strategies. Use client-perceived outcomes (quality of life, communication confidence) alongside fluency measures to assess long-term treatment success. Prepare clients for expected variability in fluency post-treatment; distinguish lapse from relapse. Incorporate psychosocial support (acceptance, communication confidence) within intensive stuttering treatment to promote durable outcomes.

sessionStats.population: Adults who stutter following intensive multi-faceted treatment program
sessionStats.frequency: Intensive program followed by long-term follow-up (mixed methods data collection)
sessionStats.duration: Long-term follow-up of intensive treatment cohort
sessionStats.goals: Stuttering severity, quality of life, client-perceived success, maintenance, avoidance

bestFitCriteria: Adults who stutter post-intensive treatment requiring maintenance planning
Clients who have completed intensive programs and require ongoing support for relapse prevention
Adults seeking treatment that addresses the psychosocial impact of stuttering in addition to fluency goals

title: Efficacy of the Modifying Phonation Intervals (MPI) Stuttering Treatment Program With Adults Who Stutter
shortTitle: MPI Stuttering Treatment Program Efficacy RCT (2015)
authors: Ingham RJ, Ingham JC, Bothe AK, Wang Y, Kilgo M
summary: RCT comparing the Modifying Phonation Intervals (MPI) stuttering treatment to the standard of care (prolonged speech) in 27 adults who stutter. Both programs used similar infrastructures. At transfer, maintenance, and follow-up, 14 participants who completed treatment achieved speech similar to normally fluent adults, with MPI showing comparable or superior outcomes to prolonged speech.
researchFindings: MPI and prolonged speech treatments both reduced stuttering to near-normal levels in adults who stutter who completed the full program
14 of 27 participants achieved speech indistinguishable from normally fluent adults at transfer and maintenance
MPI treatment was relatively more effective at helping clients identify and change specific speech behaviors associated with treatment success
Both MPI and prolonged speech resulted in improved speech naturalness compared to baseline
The RCT design with active comparator (prolonged speech) provides high-quality evidence for both treatment approaches
clinicalApplication: MPI stuttering treatment is an evidence-based alternative to prolonged speech for adults who stutter, with comparable outcomes at the RCT level. Use MPI when clients benefit from a specific behavioral target (reducing short phonation intervals) as a mechanism for reducing stuttering. Plan for a structured transfer and maintenance phase—both MPI and prolonged speech require active generalization to naturalistic settings. Ensure adequate treatment intensity; not all participants achieved fluency goals, highlighting the importance of individualized dosing.

sessionStats.population: Adults who stutter (moderate-to-severe)
sessionStats.frequency: Intensive treatment schedule (matched infrastructure between MPI and prolonged speech groups)
sessionStats.duration: Full treatment program with transfer, maintenance, and follow-up phases
sessionStats.goals: Stuttering frequency, speech naturalness, phonation interval modification

Clients for whom a specific behavioral mechanism (phonation intervals) may be helpful in achieving fluency
Adults motivated for structured intensive treatment with clear transfer and maintenance phases

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Two Semi-Occluded Vocal Tract Voice Therapy Protocols
shortTitle: Semi-Occluded Vocal Tract RCT: FRT vs. Vocal Function Exercises (2015)
authors: Kapsner-Smith MR, Hunter EJ, Kirkham K, Cox K, Titze IR
summary: RCT comparing two semi-occluded vocal tract (SOVT) treatment protocols—phonation through a flow-resistant tube (FRT) versus Vocal Function Exercises (VFE)—in 20 adults with dysphonia and/or vocal fatigue. Both active treatment conditions produced significant improvements in Voice Handicap Index scores relative to no-treatment control; FRT was non-inferior to VFE.
researchFindings: Both FRT (flow-resistant tube) and VFE (Vocal Function Exercises) produced statistically significant improvements in Voice Handicap Index relative to the no-treatment control group
FRT therapy was non-inferior to the established VFE protocol, supporting its use as an evidence-based treatment option
Semi-occluded vocal tract exercises reduce supraglottic muscle tension and improve vocal efficiency through aerodynamic and resonatory mechanisms
Both treatment groups showed improvement in patient-reported vocal function and dysphonia severity
SOVT exercises are low-risk, low-cost interventions well-suited for home practice
clinicalApplication: Prescribe semi-occluded vocal tract exercises (straw phonation, lip trills, resonance tubes) as evidence-based voice therapy for functional and hyperfunctional dysphonia. Flow-resistant tube exercises are a clinically equivalent alternative to Vocal Function Exercises and may be particularly accessible for home practice. Semi-occluded vocal tract exercises are appropriate for adults with muscle tension dysphonia, vocal fatigue, or functional voice disorders. Provide structured home practice protocols for SOVT exercises; low adverse-event profile makes them safe for independent practice between sessions.

sessionStats.population: Adults with dysphonia and/or vocal fatigue (functional/hyperfunctional)
sessionStats.frequency: Structured treatment sessions over several weeks
sessionStats.duration: Active treatment followed by waitlist/delayed-start control comparison
sessionStats.goals: Voice Handicap Index (VHI) score, dysphonia severity, vocal efficiency

bestFitCriteria: Adults with functional dysphonia, muscle tension dysphonia, or vocal fatigue
Voice patients who would benefit from low-resistance vocal tract exercise (straw phonation, lip trills)
Clients needing a structured home exercise program as part of voice therapy

title: The Effect of SPEAK OUT! and The LOUD Crowd on Dysarthria Due to Parkinson's Disease
shortTitle: SPEAK OUT! and LOUD Crowd for Parkinson's Dysarthria (2020)
authors: Behrman A, Cody J, Elandary S, Flom P, Chitnis S
summary: Pre-post cohort study evaluating 40 individuals with idiopathic Parkinson's disease receiving the SPEAK OUT! program (12 individual sessions, 3x/week, 4 weeks) followed by The LOUD Crowd group maintenance. Significant post-therapy improvements in vocal intensity, frequency variation, cepstral peak prominence, and Voice-Related Quality of Life were maintained at 1-year follow-up for participants engaged in ongoing group sessions.
researchFindings: SPEAK OUT! produced significant improvements in vocal intensity, frequency variation, cepstral peak prominence, and Voice-Related QoL relative to baseline
Treatment gains were maintained at 1-year follow-up, with LOUD Crowd group attendance positively correlated with sustained improvement
SPEAK OUT! leverages intentional, goal-directed basal ganglia-cortical circuits to compensate for automatic speech deficits in PD
Telehealth delivery of SPEAK OUT! produced positive outcomes comparable to in-person delivery in this study
The combination of individual intensive treatment (SPEAK OUT!) and ongoing group maintenance (LOUD Crowd) is critical for long-term outcomes
clinicalApplication: Implement SPEAK OUT! as a structured 12-session individual program for adults with hypokinetic dysarthria due to Parkinson's disease. Transition clients to The LOUD Crowd group maintenance immediately following SPEAK OUT! to support long-term outcomes. Use intentional, goal-directed speech approach: teach clients to 'think loud' and 'speak with intent' rather than relying on automatic habitual speech. Telehealth delivery of SPEAK OUT! is a viable option for clients with limited access to in-person care. Monitor vocal intensity and functional communication at regular intervals to assess maintenance and need for booster sessions.

sessionStats.population: Adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease and hypokinetic dysarthria
sessionStats.duration: 4 weeks individual SPEAK OUT! + ongoing weekly LOUD Crowd maintenance
sessionStats.goals: Vocal intensity, frequency variation, cepstral peak prominence, Voice-Related Quality of Life

bestFitCriteria: Adults with Parkinson's disease presenting with hypokinetic dysarthria (reduced loudness, monotone, rapid rate)
PD clients motivated for an intensive individual program followed by group maintenance
Clients with access to SPEAK OUT!-trained clinicians or telehealth-based delivery

title: Systematic Review of Behavioral Interventions Targeting Social Communication Difficulties After Traumatic Brain Injury
shortTitle: Social Communication Interventions After TBI — Systematic Review (2016)
authors: Finch E, Copley A, Cornwell P, Kelly C
journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
summary: Systematic review of behavioral interventions for social communication difficulties in adults with TBI, searching databases through October 2013. Found that interventions addressing social communication skills for adults with TBI are beneficial regardless of the treatment approach, with the strongest evidence supporting context-sensitive approaches delivered in group-based service models over at least 10 weeks.
researchFindings: Behavioral interventions for social communication in adults with TBI are beneficial regardless of treatment approach (impairment-specific or context-sensitive)
Context-sensitive approaches delivered in group-based models showed the strongest evidence and most durable outcomes
Improvements in social communication were maintained at 3-month follow-up for programs lasting at least 10 weeks
Adults in the chronic phase of TBI can still meaningfully benefit from social communication intervention
Both individual and group formats can be effective; group models offer additional benefits through peer interaction and naturalistic practice
clinicalApplication: Prioritize context-sensitive social communication interventions for adults with TBI—focus on real-world communication scenarios rather than isolated skill drills. Group-based social communication training is particularly effective for adults with TBI; consider group formats for social pragmatics goals. Plan treatment for at least 10 weeks to achieve durable improvements in social communication. Target chronic-phase TBI patients for social communication treatment—significant gains are achievable even years post-injury. Address partner and environmental factors in social communication treatment, not just the individual with TBI.

sessionStats.population: Adults with cognitive-communication disorders secondary to TBI (all severity levels, chronic phase)
sessionStats.frequency: Variable; evidence strongest for programs with sufficient dosage over 10+ weeks
sessionStats.duration: Minimum 10 weeks for durable outcomes per systematic review findings
sessionStats.goals: Social communication, pragmatic skills, conversational partner interaction, community participation

bestFitCriteria: Adults with TBI presenting with social communication difficulties (pragmatic impairment, discourse deficits, reduced social participation)
Clients in chronic phase of TBI seeking meaningful gains in community participation
Adults with TBI who would benefit from group-based social communication intervention

title: Expiratory Muscle Strength Training for Therapy of Pharyngeal Dysphagia in Parkinson's Disease
shortTitle: EMST for Pharyngeal Dysphagia in Parkinson's Disease RCT (2021)
authors: Claus I, Muhle P, Czechowski J, Ahring S, Labeit B, Suntrup-Krueger S, Wiendl H, Dziewas R, Warnecke T
summary: Double-blind, sham-controlled RCT of 50 adults with Parkinson's disease and pharyngeal dysphagia randomized to 4 weeks of active EMST (n=25) or sham EMST (n=25). Active EMST produced significant reduction in pharyngeal residue and overall dysphagia severity, with improvements sustained at 3-month follow-up, providing Level 1b evidence for EMST as a dysphagia intervention in PD.
researchFindings: 4 weeks of active EMST significantly reduced overall dysphagia severity in adults with Parkinson's disease compared to sham training
The primary mechanism of benefit was reduction in pharyngeal residue—a significant VFSS measure distinguishing active from sham groups
Treatment effects were sustained at 3-month follow-up, indicating durable swallowing improvements beyond the active training period
Sham EMST showed no significant benefit, confirming that device load (resistance) is the active therapeutic component
Double-blind, sham-controlled design provides the highest level of evidence for EMST in PD-related dysphagia
clinicalApplication: Prescribe EMST as an evidence-based swallowing intervention for adults with Parkinson's disease and pharyngeal dysphagia. Use EMST at 75% of maximum expiratory pressure (MEP) with a structured 4-week program of 5 sets of 5 repetitions, 5 days per week. Target pharyngeal residue as a key outcome—EMST's primary benefit in PD is reducing post-swallow pharyngeal pooling. Plan for reassessment at 3 months post-treatment; sustained gains justify EMST as a stand-alone maintenance program. Sham EMST can be useful as a placebo comparator in clinical research; active loading is required for therapeutic benefit.

sessionStats.population: Adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease and pharyngeal dysphagia
sessionStats.frequency: 5 sets × 5 repetitions, 5 days per week (home-based program)
sessionStats.duration: 4 weeks active EMST training; 3-month follow-up assessment
sessionStats.environment: Home-based EMST device use with clinical monitoring
sessionStats.goals: Overall dysphagia severity, pharyngeal residue (VFSS), penetration-aspiration scale

bestFitCriteria: Adults with Parkinson's disease and confirmed pharyngeal dysphagia on instrumental assessment
PD patients with pharyngeal residue as the primary swallowing impairment
Clients motivated for a structured home exercise program targeting respiratory-swallowing coordination

title: Clinical Focus on Prosodic, Discursive and Pragmatic Treatment for Right Hemisphere Damaged Adults: What's Right?
shortTitle: Prosodic, Discursive and Pragmatic Treatment for Right Hemisphere Damage (2011)
authors: Ferré P, Fonseca RP, Ska B, Joanette Y
summary: Clinical review synthesizing evidence for prosodic, discursive, and pragmatic intervention for adults with right hemisphere brain damage (RHD). At least 50% of individuals with RHD display impairments in prosody, discourse, pragmatics, or lexical semantics. The review identifies structured intervention principles and a clinical framework for targeting these communication deficits in SLP practice.
researchFindings: At least 50% of adults with right hemisphere damage display impairments in prosody, discourse, pragmatics, or lexical semantics affecting functional communication
Controlled treatment evidence for RHD communication is most developed for aprosodia; emerging evidence supports structured intervention for discourse and pragmatics
A structured intervention framework addressing prosodic, discursive, and pragmatic components can be incorporated into SLP clinical practice
Both impairment-specific and participation-focused approaches can be adapted for adults with RHD communication deficits
Partner education and environmental modification are important complements to individual treatment for RHD pragmatic impairments
clinicalApplication: Screen all adults with right hemisphere stroke for prosodic, discourse, and pragmatic communication deficits—these are frequently missed in standard aphasia testing. Target prosody (emotional prosody comprehension and expression), discourse organization, and pragmatic appropriateness as distinct clinical goals for RHD. Use structured conversational interaction tasks and role-play to address pragmatic deficits in naturalistic communication contexts. Educate communication partners about RHD-related communication changes (tangential speech, poor topic maintenance, reduced humor comprehension). Adapt aphasia and cognitive rehabilitation principles to address the unique communication profile of adults with right hemisphere damage.

sessionStats.population: Adults with right hemisphere stroke or brain damage
sessionStats.frequency: Variable; no single frequency established; treatment integrated with overall post-stroke rehabilitation
sessionStats.duration: Ongoing; RHD communication deficits often persist into chronic phase
sessionStats.goals: Prosody comprehension/production, discourse coherence, pragmatic communication, partner interaction

bestFitCriteria: Adults with right hemisphere stroke or acquired brain injury presenting with communication difficulties not captured by standard aphasia testing
Clients with pragmatic communication deficits (tangential speech, poor topic maintenance, difficulty with indirect speech acts) following RHD
Adults with RHD for whom social communication and participation are priority goals

title: A Treatment for Apraxia of Speech in Adults
shortTitle: Eight-Step Continuum for AOS
authors: Rosenbek, J. C., Lemme, M. L., Ahern, M. B., Harris, E. H., & Wertz, R. T.
journal: Journal of Speech and Hearing Disorders
evidenceType: Case series with treatment protocol description
researchFindings: Eight progressive steps systematically fade auditory and visual cuing from maximum support (simultaneous imitation with the clinician) to fully independent production.
Integral stimulation — the clinician saying "Watch me, listen to me" before modeling — provides simultaneous auditory and visual input for the client to imitate at each step before cuing is faded.
Target words and phrases are selected for functional relevance and appropriate phonetic complexity; targets are worked from simpler to more complex phonemic sequences.
Criterion is typically 80–90% accuracy across three consecutive sessions at a given step before advancing to the next level of the hierarchy.
The hierarchy is not strictly linear — clinicians can return to earlier steps when accuracy drops, maintaining a mostly successful practice schedule that aligns with motor learning principles.
This cueing-fade paradigm directly parallels motor learning principles: fading extrinsic feedback supports long-term retention and self-monitoring capacity.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with acquired apraxia of speech following stroke, TBI, or other neurological event.
Clients with AOS across severity levels — step selection determines appropriate entry point into the hierarchy.
Clients who respond to imitation and auditory/visual models — integral stimulation depends on intact auditory and visual processing.
Cases where DTTC, RASP, or MSTP are planned — the Eight-Step Continuum provides the cueing structure underlying those protocols.
summary: The foundational paper introducing the Eight-Step Continuum for acquired apraxia of speech — a hierarchical integral stimulation approach that systematically fades auditory and visual cuing from simultaneous imitation to spontaneous production.
clinicalApplication: The Eight-Step Continuum is the backbone of integral stimulation-based AOS therapy and remains among the most widely applied clinical frameworks decades after publication. Use it to structure session targets: select a functionally meaningful word or phrase and move through steps from simultaneous imitation (Step 1) toward spontaneous production in connected speech (Step 8), targeting 80–90% accuracy before progressing. When accuracy drops, step back rather than abandoning the target — maintaining a high success rate during practice supports motor learning. Combine with Maas et al. (2008) motor learning principles: vary practice targets within sessions, reduce feedback systematically as accuracy improves, and target minimum 100 trials per session. This approach is the structural foundation for DTTC (Dynamic Temporal and Tactile Cueing) and RASP, both of which extend these cueing principles with additional sensorimotor input.

sessionStats.dose: 100–200 trials per session; 80% accuracy criterion per step before advancing
sessionStats.bestFit: Acquired AOS of any severity; most effective with adequate trial volume and systematic feedback fading

title: Treatment Efficacy: Dysarthria
shortTitle: Treatment Efficacy in Dysarthria
authors: Yorkston, K. M.
journal: Journal of Speech and Hearing Research
researchFindings: Evidence supports behavioral speech treatment for dysarthria across a range of neurological diagnoses including Parkinson's disease, TBI, stroke, and ALS.

The SLP's role encompasses four key functions: participation in differential diagnosis, provision of behavioral speech treatment, staging treatment appropriateness over time, and timely education about communication alternatives.

Treatment staging is critical in progressive conditions — the same intervention approach is not appropriate across all disease stages; behavioral treatment may be indicated early, shifting to AAC strategies as communication deteriorates.
Rate control treatment shows consistent evidence for improving intelligibility in dysarthria across multiple etiologies.
Behavioral treatment for Parkinson's disease dysarthria (loudness and rate approaches) produces measurable gains in intelligibility and communication function.
For ALS, staging of communication treatment is essential — early AAC introduction while speech remains functional improves long-term communication outcomes.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with dysarthria of any etiology requiring treatment planning, staging decisions, or payer justification.
Patients with progressive neurological conditions (ALS, Parkinson's, MS) where staging is required to time interventions appropriately.
SLPs documenting medical necessity for dysarthria treatment for payers, medical teams, or interdisciplinary rounds.
Cases requiring AAC pre-planning in the context of a progressive dysarthria diagnosis.
summary: Foundational efficacy review synthesizing evidence for dysarthria treatment across the most common neurological diagnoses and defining the SLP's roles in diagnosis, staging, and intervention throughout the disease course.
clinicalApplication: This review establishes the clinical framework still used for dysarthria management today: stage the client, then match the intervention to the stage. For progressive conditions like ALS, introduce AAC planning early — do not wait until speech becomes unintelligible, because the patient needs to participate in AAC system design while insight and motor control are preserved. For stable or improving conditions (post-TBI, post-stroke), behavioral approaches targeting intelligibility, rate, loudness, and respiratory support are evidence-supported. Use differential staging documentation in your reports: identify where the client sits on the continuum from "optimize natural speech" to "natural speech insufficient as primary communication." This staging rationale justifies AAC consultation before it is urgently needed and frames SLP services as proactive management rather than reactive response.

sessionStats.frequency: Varies by etiology and disease stage
sessionStats.bestFit: All dysarthria etiologies — provides the staging and evidence framework for treatment planning

title: Comparison of Clinic, Home, and Deferred Language Treatment for Aphasia: A Veterans Administration Cooperative Study
shortTitle: VA Cooperative Study: SLP vs. Home vs. Deferred Aphasia Treatment
authors: Wertz, R. T., Weiss, D. G., Aten, J. L., Brookshire, R. H., García-Buñuel, L., Holland, A. L., Kurtzke, J. F., LaPointe, L. L., Milianti, F. J., Brannegan, R., Greenbaum, H., Marshall, R. C., Vogel, D., Carter, J., Barnes, N. S., & Goodman, R.
researchFindings: 121 participants with aphasia were randomized across multiple VA centers to clinic treatment (by SLP), home treatment (by trained volunteer), or deferred treatment followed by SLP treatment.
Clinic treatment by SLPs produced significantly greater language improvement than volunteer-delivered home treatment, despite equivalent hours of treatment exposure.
Deferred treatment participants showed significantly less improvement during the no-treatment phase, with gains accelerating markedly once SLP treatment began.
The superiority of clinic treatment over home volunteer treatment demonstrates that professional SLP expertise — not merely exposure to language stimulation — drives meaningful aphasia recovery.
All groups ultimately improved, but the rate and extent of improvement was significantly greater in the SLP-treated condition.
This large, multi-site RCT was among the first of its scale in aphasia research and remains a cornerstone of the aphasia treatment evidence base.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with acquired aphasia of any severity requiring professional SLP services — the primary citation for medical necessity.
Cases where insurance or payer authorization for SLP services is being challenged.
Settings where volunteer or caregiver substitution for formal SLP is proposed — this RCT demonstrates that professional expertise is not replaceable.
Patients in the first year post-onset where active treatment has the greatest documented impact.
summary: Landmark VA cooperative RCT demonstrating that SLP-provided clinic treatment significantly outperformed volunteer-delivered home treatment and deferred treatment for aphasia — establishing the medical necessity of professional speech-language intervention.
clinicalApplication: The Wertz et al. VA study is the definitive evidence that SLP-delivered treatment for aphasia is superior to volunteer-based or deferred approaches. Use this citation when: (1) documenting medical necessity for aphasia treatment against payer denials; (2) educating family members who assume that conversational practice at home is equivalent to formal SLP intervention; (3) advocating for professional staffing rather than volunteer-supported programs as a substitute for SLP services. Pair with Robey 1998 (meta-analysis confirming aphasia treatment effect sizes), Bhogal 2003 (demonstrating dose-response relationship), and Brady et al. 2016 Cochrane review for a comprehensive, multi-level evidence stack supporting aphasia treatment authorization.

sessionStats.dose: 12 weeks of active treatment; studied across clinic, home volunteer, and deferred conditions
sessionStats.bestFit: Any adult with post-stroke or acquired aphasia requiring professional SLP intervention

title: Melodic Intonation Therapy for Aphasia
shortTitle: Melodic Intonation Therapy (Original 1973)
authors: Albert, M. L., Sparks, R. W., & Helm, N. A.
evidenceType: Original case series describing novel treatment
researchFindings: MIT was developed based on the clinical observation that some patients with severe nonfluent aphasia could sing words they were unable to speak, suggesting right-hemisphere involvement in musical-linguistic processing.
The technique exaggerates the natural melodic and rhythmic contour of speech into a simple two-note sung pattern, combined with continuous left-hand tapping to reinforce rhythm.
Three treated patients with severe nonfluent aphasia demonstrated meaningful gains in verbal production, with one patient progressing to functional conversational speech.

The right-hemisphere recruitment hypothesis proposes that intact right-hemisphere language homologs — typically underdeveloped for speech production — can be activated by the melodic and rhythmic structure of MIT.

Patient selection criteria identified in this foundational paper include: nonfluent aphasia with severely limited verbal output, relatively preserved auditory comprehension, poor repetition, right-handedness, and high motivation.
MIT is explicitly not recommended for fluent aphasia types, patients with right-hemisphere damage, or globally aphasic patients with severely impaired comprehension.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic nonfluent aphasia (Broca's or similar) with severely limited verbal output and at least functional auditory comprehension.
Right-handed adults with left hemisphere damage — MIT mechanism depends on intact right-hemisphere networks.
Clients who demonstrate at least a minimal response to melodic or sung cuing during informal probing.
Cases where standard language stimulation approaches have plateaued and an alternative right-hemisphere approach is clinically indicated.
summary: The original 1973 paper introducing Melodic Intonation Therapy — the landmark approach using melodic contour, rhythm, and left-hand tapping to facilitate verbal production in nonfluent aphasia by recruiting intact right-hemisphere language networks.
clinicalApplication: This foundational paper establishes the theoretical rationale and patient selection criteria for MIT that remain clinically standard today. MIT is indicated for adults with chronic nonfluent aphasia who have: very limited verbal output, relatively preserved auditory comprehension, and at least some response to sung or melodic cuing on informal probing. The three-level protocol described in the companion 1974 Sparks et al. paper begins with high-frequency, high-utility phrases (requests, greetings, daily expressions) sung in simple melodic contour with left-hand tapping, progressing through fading melodic support toward natural prosody. The hand-tapping component is not optional — it is a specified element of the protocol targeting right-hemisphere sensorimotor activation through contralateral hand control. When selecting candidates, note that the target population is severely nonfluent, not simply hesitant or apraxic — MIT was designed for patients with markedly limited spontaneous verbal output.

sessionStats.dose: Minimum 15–20 sessions; advance through MIT levels based on 80% accuracy criterion
sessionStats.bestFit: Chronic nonfluent aphasia with severely limited verbal output and relatively preserved auditory comprehension

title: Stuttering: A Review of Research Findings and Theories Circa 1982
shortTitle: Stuttering: Review of Research Findings and Theories
authors: Andrews, G., Craig, A., Feyer, A. M., Hoddinott, S., Howie, P., & Neilson, M.
journal: Journal of Speech and Hearing Disorders
researchFindings: Prevalence of stuttering in the general population is approximately 1%, with a 3:1 male-to-female ratio; onset typically occurs between ages 2–5 years.
Genetic factors play a meaningful role in stuttering risk — first-degree relatives of people who stutter have elevated rates, with concordance higher in monozygotic than dizygotic twins.
Natural recovery from stuttering occurs in approximately 80% of those who stutter in childhood, typically before or during early adolescence, with persistence more likely in males.
Behavioral treatments — including fluency shaping and stuttering modification approaches — produce significant reductions in stuttering frequency, but long-term maintenance is variable.
Fear, anxiety, and avoidance behaviors are not causes of stuttering but develop as secondary responses to the experience of stuttering; these must be addressed in comprehensive treatment.
No pharmacological or surgical treatment demonstrated consistent efficacy for stuttering at the time of this review.
bestFitCriteria: Adults who stutter presenting for evaluation where psychoeducation about stuttering etiology is a treatment component.
Clinicians needing foundational evidence to explain the neurological and genetic basis of stuttering to clients, families, or interdisciplinary teams.
Cases where avoidance behaviors, anxiety, or social withdrawal are secondary features requiring integrated behavioral and psychosocial intervention.
Clients or families who attribute stuttering to psychological causes or believe it could be "cured" with willpower.
summary: Comprehensive 1983 synthesis of stuttering research across epidemiology, etiology, genetics, assessment, and treatment — the foundational review framing the scientific basis of stuttering management still referenced in contemporary practice.
clinicalApplication: This foundational review frames the multidimensional nature of stuttering that continues to guide evidence-based practice. The most clinically important takeaways: (1) stuttering has a strong genetic and neurological basis — it is not caused by anxiety, poor parenting, or psychological weakness; (2) the high natural recovery rate in childhood (~80%) has major implications for when and how to intervene in young children; (3) treatment for adults needs to address both the core stuttering behavior AND the avoidance, anxiety, and negative self-perception that have developed secondarily. Use this review in psychoeducation with clients and families when misattributions about stuttering causation are present. The distinction between fluency shaping (training new speech patterns) and stuttering modification (changing relationship with stuttering) is foundational for clinical decision-making about which approach matches the individual client's goals and values.

sessionStats.bestFit: Adults who stutter seeking foundational understanding of stuttering etiology, epidemiology, and treatment rationale

title: Laryngeal Adduction in Resonant Voice
shortTitle: Laryngeal Adduction in Resonant Voice
authors: Verdolini, K., Druker, D. G., Palmer, P. M., & Samawi, H.
researchFindings: Resonant voice is produced with a barely adducted or abducted laryngeal configuration — significantly different from the pressed phonation characteristic of hyperfunctional voice disorders.
Electroglottographic (EGG) closed quotient (CQ) for resonant voice falls between 0.5 and 0.6, objectively distinguishing it from pressed voice (high CQ) and breathy voice (low CQ).
Both speakers with healthy larynges and those with vocal nodules produced resonant voice with this barely-adducted configuration, demonstrating feasibility even in dysphonic speakers.
Biomechanically, the barely-adducted configuration produces efficient voicing while minimizing vocal fold collision forces — protecting tissue and reducing the biological cost of phonation.
Resonant voice was reliably distinguished from pressed and breathy voice types using EGG CQ, providing an objective measurement tool for clinical monitoring of treatment progress.
The EGG CQ finding supports the LMRVT clinical goal of training the "Goldilocks zone" of adduction: enough contact for efficient voicing, not so much as to produce tissue trauma.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with hyperfunctional voice disorders where reducing laryngeal adduction force is a primary treatment goal.
Patients with vocal nodules or contact granulomas resulting from excessive vocal fold collision during phonation.
Clinicians using LMRVT or other resonant voice approaches who need the biomechanical rationale for the technique.
High vocal demand users (teachers, singers, performers) where tissue-efficient phonation is essential for long-term vocal health.
summary: Established the biomechanical basis of resonant voice therapy, demonstrating that resonant voice is produced with barely adducted vocal folds — providing the theoretical foundation for LMRVT and all resonant voice-based clinical approaches.
clinicalApplication: This paper provides the biomechanical rationale for Lessac-Madsen Resonant Voice Therapy (LMRVT) and all resonant voice-based approaches. When training resonant voice, you are training a specific laryngeal configuration — not simply "forward resonance" as a perceptual sensation, but an actual measurable change in vocal fold adduction. The EGG CQ metric (0.5–0.6) provides a physiological training target, and EGG biofeedback can be incorporated into treatment to help clients find and stabilize this configuration. For clients with hyperfunctional dysphonia, vocal nodules, or contact granulomas — conditions characterized by excessive adduction force — resonant voice reduces tissue trauma by lowering medial compression while maintaining voicing. Teach clients to recognize resonant voice through tactile and kinesthetic cues (buzzing sensation forward in the face, easy onset, minimal laryngeal tension) before relying on auditory monitoring alone. This is the foundational science underlying LMRVT's "easy-onset, forward-placed" phonation training.

sessionStats.dose: Clinical protocols from the LMRVT program; foundational mechanism paper
sessionStats.bestFit: Hyperfunctional voice disorders, vocal nodules, contact granulomas, muscle tension dysphonia

title: Noninvasive Approaches to Deglutitive Aspiration
shortTitle: Noninvasive Compensatory Strategies for Dysphagia
authors: Logemann, J. A.
evidenceType: Expert review with clinical evidence summary
researchFindings: Chin-down posture narrows the entrance to the airway and widens the valleculae, reducing aspiration risk for clients with delayed pharyngeal swallow onset or reduced anterior laryngeal movement.
Head rotation toward the damaged side in unilateral pharyngeal weakness closes the damaged side and directs bolus flow through the stronger contralateral pharyngeal channel.
Head tilt toward the stronger side uses gravity to direct bolus flow through the better-functioning side in unilateral oral or pharyngeal dysfunction.
Bolus modifications — thickened liquids, altered textures, reduced volume — can directly reduce aspiration risk by slowing transit and improving oral bolus control.
Thermal-tactile stimulation (cold, sour, carbonated boluses) can facilitate swallow initiation in clients with delayed pharyngeal swallow trigger.
Supraglottic swallow maneuver (voluntary breath hold before and during swallow, followed by cough) protects the airway through volitional glottic closure independent of reflexive laryngeal elevation.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with dysphagia and documented aspiration where immediate compensatory management is needed while rehabilitative approaches are initiated.
Patients for whom rehabilitative exercises alone cannot maintain safe oral intake — compensatory strategies bridge functional eating.
Cases where caregiver and nursing training in compensatory techniques is required to maintain safety across all meal contexts.
Patients with progressive conditions (ALS, Parkinson's, dementia) where compensation is the primary long-term management strategy.
summary: Foundational review outlining the evidence for noninvasive compensatory strategies to reduce or eliminate aspiration in dysphagia — including postural techniques, bolus modifications, sensory enhancement, and behavioral swallow maneuvers.
clinicalApplication: This review is the foundational reference for compensatory dysphagia management. Always match the strategy to the specific physiological deficit identified on instrumental imaging: chin tuck for delayed swallow trigger or reduced laryngeal elevation; head rotation for unilateral pharyngeal paresis; head tilt for unilateral oral stage deficits; thickened liquids for reduced lingual control or delayed trigger causing thin liquid aspiration. Compensatory strategies reduce aspiration during use but do not change underlying physiology — always pair with rehabilitative exercises targeting the mechanism (Mendelsohn maneuver, EMST, Shaker, MDTP) wherever possible. Confirm strategy effectiveness with instrumental assessment (MBSS or FEES) — a strategy that appears effective clinically may not eliminate aspiration on imaging, and some strategies that reduce penetration may worsen residue. Document which strategies were trialed on imaging and the physiological rationale for each assignment.

sessionStats.frequency: Applied at every meal; must generalize to all eating contexts
sessionStats.sessionLength: Instruction and practice integrated into meal contexts and caregiver training
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with dysphagia and documented aspiration where compensatory management is indicated pending or alongside rehabilitation

title: Discourse-Level Communication Success in Aphasia: Unveiling Its Significance Through Observers' Ratings
shortTitle: Discourse-Level Communication Success in Aphasia
authors: Ramage, A. E., Rowe, A. L., & Greenslade, K. J.
researchFindings: Observers rating communication success in aphasia prioritized overall message transmission and functional effectiveness above linguistic form or accuracy.

Discourse-level communication ratings captured aspects of real-world communication that standardized language tests and single-word measures systematically miss — including gesture, prosody, and multimodal compensation.

Communication success varied meaningfully across discourse elicitation tasks, supporting multi-genre sampling (procedural, narrative, conversational) rather than a single task for clinical assessment.

Linguistic accuracy (correct information units, grammatical completeness) did not fully predict observer-rated communication success — compensatory communication strategies contribute meaningfully to perceived effectiveness.
Findings support a shift toward functional communication outcome measures: treatment and assessment should target real-world message exchange, not only linguistic accuracy at the impairment level.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia where functional communication at the discourse and conversational level is a treatment goal alongside impairment-focused work.
Clinicians seeking to expand assessment beyond standardized naming tests to include connected speech sampling and observer-rated functional outcomes.
Patients for whom compensatory communication strategies (gesture, drawing, writing, AAC) should be formally validated as effective communication.
Settings requiring participation-based outcome measurement for program evaluation, insurance justification, or quality reporting.
summary: Demonstrates that naive observers rate communication success in aphasia based on functional message transmission — not linguistic accuracy — supporting real-world communication effectiveness as a primary treatment and outcome target.
clinicalApplication: This study reinforces that communication success is about message delivery, not linguistic perfection — a finding that directly supports life participation frameworks in aphasia care. When setting treatment goals, include discourse-level outcome measures alongside word retrieval and sentence production targets. Use multimodal communication assessment tasks that reflect real communication contexts — conversation, procedural description, narrative retell — and train clients to use gesture, drawing, writing, and AAC as legitimate communication tools within those contexts. When documenting goals for payers, frame outcomes in terms of functional communication success: "client will convey daily care needs using verbal and gestural communication in 4/5 opportunities" rather than purely impairment-level linguistic targets. Assessment batteries should routinely include connected speech samples across multiple task types — not only confrontation naming tasks.

sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with aphasia of any type where discourse-level functional communication effectiveness is a treatment and outcome priority

title: A Combined Speech-Language and Counseling Intervention for Primary Progressive Aphasia: Acceptability, Feasibility, and Preliminary Outcomes
shortTitle: Combined SLP and Counseling for PPA
authors: Mendez, K. S., Evans, W. S., Wauters, L. D., Dutcher, C. D., Philburn, C., & Henry, M. L.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
evidenceType: Feasibility study with preliminary outcome data
researchFindings: The combined SLP-counseling intervention was rated as highly acceptable by participants with PPA and their care partners across multiple dimensions of acceptability including relevance, burden, and value.

Both the SLP component (language function maintenance, AAC preparation) and the counseling component (emotional adjustment, grief processing, identity) were valued — participants did not want either eliminated.
Preliminary outcomes showed maintenance or improvement in trained language targets and care partner-reported functional communication.

Participants reported that integrated counseling helped them process the emotional experience of a progressive communication diagnosis without feeling abandoned or unsupported by their healthcare team.
The combined approach aligns with emerging models of comprehensive care for progressive neurological conditions where psychosocial adjustment is inseparable from communication management.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with any PPA variant for whom psychosocial adjustment to progressive communication loss is an explicit component of care.
Care partners who are distressed, uncertain about their role, or needing structured guidance on supporting communication at home.
Clinicians in PPA specialty programs or neurology clinics wanting to integrate counseling-informed practice into SLP sessions.
Settings where psychology or social work access is limited — this study supports SLPs providing integrated supportive communication within their scope of practice.
summary: Documents the acceptability, feasibility, and preliminary outcomes of a combined speech-language therapy and counseling intervention for PPA — establishing that integrating psychosocial support with language treatment is both feasible and strongly valued by participants.
clinicalApplication: This study makes the case that SLP treatment for PPA should not be narrowly focused on language targets alone. The person with PPA is experiencing progressive loss of a core human capacity, and integrating psychosocial support is both clinically appropriate and actively desired by clients and families. In practice, build explicit space in PPA sessions for emotional processing: acknowledge grief, address identity concerns related to communication change, and involve care partners as active participants in goal setting and session discussion. You do not need to be a licensed counselor to hold supportive conversations — but knowing when to refer to psychology or social work is part of competent PPA care. Pair language treatment (word-finding maintenance, script training, proactive AAC planning) with explicit counseling integration: check in emotionally at session start, normalize grief responses, and help clients articulate what communication means to them personally as a guide for goal-setting priorities.

sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with any PPA variant, particularly early-to-mid stage where psychosocial adjustment to a progressive diagnosis is ongoing

title: Communication Partner Training in Aphasia: An Updated Systematic Review
shortTitle: Communication Partner Training in Aphasia: Systematic Review
authors: Simmons-Mackie, N., Raymer, A., & Cherney, L. R.
journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
researchFindings: Twenty-five articles met inclusion criteria for this updated systematic review, a substantial expansion from the original 2009 review of 13 articles.
Communication partner training (CPT) was probably effective for improving communication participation and functional communication in adults with chronic aphasia.
Outcomes extended beyond communication impairment to include psychosocial adjustment, quality of life, and communication burden reduction for communication partners themselves.
CPT approaches varied widely — from formal Supported Conversation for Adults with Aphasia (SCA) to informal coaching, video-based feedback, and group partner training programs.
Training communication partners improved both the partner's communication strategies AND the aphasia patient's participation — benefits were documented in both members of the dyad.
Structured feedback components (active coaching with modeling, practice, and reflection) were associated with stronger outcomes than information-only sessions.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic aphasia of any severity who have a regular communication partner willing to participate in training.
Family members or caregivers reporting communication frustration, withdrawal, or reduced participation in the person with aphasia.
Patients with chronic aphasia who have plateaued in impairment-level treatment but whose functional communication could improve through better partner support.
Discharge planning for transition home — CPT ensures communication partners are equipped to maintain treatment progress and support ongoing participation.
summary: Updated systematic review of 25 studies concluding that communication partner training is probably effective for improving functional communication and participation for people with chronic aphasia — establishing partner training as a distinct evidence-based component of comprehensive aphasia care.
clinicalApplication: Communication partner training should be a standard component of aphasia rehabilitation — not an optional supplement. This systematic review gives you the evidence to justify including family members, caregivers, and significant communication partners in formal treatment sessions. Effective approaches include: Supported Conversation for Adults with Aphasia (SCA) — teaching partners to acknowledge competence and reveal competence through natural conversation facilitators; video-based partner feedback sessions reviewing interaction patterns; and group partner training combining instruction, practice, and reflection. Do not rely on information pamphlets or brief verbal instructions alone — active coaching with modeling and feedback is what drives meaningful partner behavior change. Bill CPT as patient treatment time when the partner is being trained specifically to serve the patient's identified communication needs. Document the functional communication goals the partner training directly supports.

sessionStats.frequency: 4–12 training sessions depending on approach and partner need
sessionStats.dose: Structured coaching with practice and feedback; more intensive training produces stronger outcomes than information alone
sessionStats.bestFit: Any adult with chronic aphasia who has a willing, consistent communication partner (family, caregiver, coworker)

title: Effect of Verb Network Strengthening Treatment (VNeST) in Persons With Aphasia: Extension and Replication of Previous Findings
shortTitle: VNeST: Verb Network Strengthening Treatment
authors: Edmonds, L. A., Mammino, K., & Ojeda, J.
researchFindings: VNeST produced significant improvements in verb retrieval, sentence production, and discourse measures in 11 participants with aphasia due to stroke using a multiple baseline design.
Generalization to untrained items and connected speech was documented — a critical advantage over item-specific naming approaches that do not generalize beyond trained targets.

VNeST targets verb-centered semantic networks by training clients to generate agent and patient thematic roles for each target verb, strengthening verb-argument structure at the lexical-semantic level.
Improvements in picture naming and discourse production co-occurred, suggesting that strengthening verb networks has cascading effects on sentence-level and discourse-level production.
Results replicated and extended earlier VNeST findings (Edmonds et al. 2009) with a larger, more diagnostically diverse participant group.
VNeST is particularly suited for clients with agrammatic or nonfluent aphasia who produce predominantly nouns with reduced verb retrieval and simplified, telegraphic sentence production.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with nonfluent or agrammatic aphasia with reduced verb retrieval and telegraphic or simplified sentence structure.
Clients who have made gains in noun retrieval (via SFA or similar) but remain limited in sentence production and discourse.
Patients for whom generalization beyond trained items is a primary goal — VNeST demonstrates broader generalization than most targeted naming approaches.
Group aphasia treatment settings where verb-centered semantic discussion can be leveraged across multiple participants simultaneously.
summary: Extension and replication study demonstrating that VNeST — targeting verbs and their thematic agent-patient roles — produces generalized gains in naming, sentence production, and discourse that extend beyond trained items in adults with aphasia.
clinicalApplication: VNeST is one of the strongest generalization-producing aphasia treatments currently available. Unlike noun-focused word retrieval approaches (SFA, anagram treatments), VNeST targets verbs — the structural core of sentences — and produces broader improvements that carry over to discourse. The protocol: select a target verb (e.g., "examine") and train the client to generate agents who perform the action (doctor, nurse, student) and patients who receive it (patient, test, sample) through systematic semantic questioning. Practice naming, generating sentence frames, and elaborating with additional details. The verb-centered approach directly addresses agrammatism, telegraphic speech, and reduced sentence elaboration — common presenting features in Broca's and transcortical motor aphasia. Combine with ORLA or discourse-level practice for maximum generalization. VNeST works particularly well in group formats where multiple participants contribute agents and patients for each target verb, creating rich semantic discussion.

sessionStats.dose: 2–4 verbs targeted per session; daily home practice with verb-cuing cards
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with aphasia with reduced verb retrieval, agrammatism, or simplified sentence production

title: The Influence of Food Texture and Liquid Consistency Modification on Swallowing Physiology and Function: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: Texture and Liquid Modification for Swallowing: Systematic Review
authors: Steele, C. M., Alsanei, W. A., Ayanikalath, S., Barbon, C. E., Chen, J., Cichero, J. A. Y., Coutts, K., Dantas, R. O., Duivestein, J., Giosa, L., Hanson, B., Lam, P., Lecko, C., Leigh, C., Nagy, A., Namasivayam, A. M., Nascimento, W. V., Odendaal, I., Smith, C. H., & Wang, H.
researchFindings: Thicker liquids consistently reduce the risk of penetration and aspiration — the biomechanical effect of slowing liquid transit gives the pharyngeal swallow additional time to prepare for airway protection.

However, thickened liquids are associated with significantly increased pharyngeal residue post-swallow, which creates its own aspiration risk if residue is aspirated on subsequent swallows or respiration.

Harder and more adhesive food textures require greater oral processing effort; reduced lingual strength or coordination can lead to premature posterior spillage and aspiration risk with harder textures.

No single texture or consistency modification eliminates all swallowing risk — there is an inherent clinical trade-off between reducing aspiration and increasing residue that must be managed individually.

Standardization of texture terminology is critical for patient safety — inconsistent terminology across facilities leads to inappropriate texture assignments when patients transfer between care settings.
Individual swallowing physiology matters more than group-level texture recommendations — instrumental assessment is needed to verify which modifications are effective for each patient.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with dysphagia and documented aspiration of thin liquids on instrumental assessment.
Patients for whom liquid or food texture modification is being prescribed as a primary or adjunctive management strategy.
Clinical decision-making requiring explicit analysis of the trade-off between reduced aspiration and increased residue.
Settings transitioning to IDDSI terminology — this systematic review provides the evidence underlying the IDDSI framework.
summary: Systematic review establishing that thickened liquids reduce aspiration risk but increase pharyngeal residue — providing the clinical evidence base for the trade-off analysis required in all liquid texture modification decisions.
clinicalApplication: The key clinical lesson from this systematic review: thickened liquids are not a risk-free intervention. While they reduce aspiration, they increase residue — and in some patients (those with reduced cough effectiveness or impaired airway clearance), residue may pose a greater clinical risk than the aspiration the thickening was meant to prevent. Always verify texture modification effectiveness with instrumental assessment (MBSS or FEES) rather than assuming that thickening will automatically make swallowing safer. When prescribing modified textures, use IDDSI terminology: Thin (Level 0), Slightly Thick (Level 1), Mildly Thick (Level 2), Moderately Thick (Level 3), Extremely Thick (Level 4); Puréed (Level 4), Minced & Moist (Level 5), Soft & Bite-Sized (Level 6), Regular (Level 7). Document the physiological basis for texture assignment explicitly — "nectar-thick per MBSS demonstrating reduced aspiration with modified liquid consistency at IDDSI Level 2" is the clinical standard.

sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with dysphagia where texture or liquid consistency modification is being considered or prescribed as part of the management plan

title: A Systematic Review of Voice Therapy: What "Effectiveness" Really Implies
shortTitle: Voice Therapy Effectiveness: Systematic Review
authors: Desjardins, M., Halstead, L., Cooke, M., & Bonilha, H. S.
researchFindings: Direct behavioral voice therapy provided by SLPs produced significant improvements across perceptual, acoustic, and patient-reported voice outcomes compared to no treatment or indirect interventions.
Effects were demonstrated across multiple voice disorder etiologies including functional dysphonia, vocal nodules, muscle tension dysphonia, and neurological voice disorders.
Homework compliance — client practice of assigned vocal exercises and hygiene behaviors outside of sessions — was identified as a critical factor predicting treatment effectiveness.
Voice therapy effects were maintained at follow-up assessments, suggesting durable vocal behavior change rather than transient, session-dependent improvements.
Indirect approaches alone (vocal hygiene education only, without direct behavioral exercises) were significantly less effective than direct behavioral voice therapy for most voice disorders.
The review identified a need for more standardized, validated outcome measures in voice research — perceptual, acoustic, aerodynamic, and quality-of-life measures should be used consistently.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with dysphonia of any etiology seeking behavioral voice treatment by an SLP.
Patients with vocal nodules, contact granulomas, muscle tension dysphonia, or functional dysphonia requiring direct behavioral intervention.
Professional voice users (teachers, singers, performers) needing evidence-based rationale for behavioral voice therapy.
Cases requiring documentation of voice therapy efficacy for insurance prior authorization or appeals.
summary: Systematic review establishing that direct behavioral voice therapy by SLPs significantly improves voice outcomes for dysphonia compared to no treatment — with homework compliance identified as a critical driver of treatment effectiveness.
clinicalApplication: This systematic review confirms that direct voice therapy — targeting specific vocal behaviors through exercises and feedback — is the evidence-based standard for dysphonia treatment. Vocal hygiene education alone is insufficient for most patients; it must be paired with active behavioral intervention. The homework compliance finding has direct clinical implications: structure home practice as a specific, manageable daily assignment (e.g., "5 minutes of resonant voice exercises twice daily") and build compliance monitoring into every session. Patients who practice consistently between sessions improve faster and more durably than those relying on in-session practice alone. When selecting a voice therapy approach, match to the patient's diagnosis and goals: LMRVT or resonant voice exercises for hyperfunctional disorders; Vocal Function Exercises (Stemple) for fatigue and professional voice users; LSVT LOUD for hypokinetic dysphonia. Document both in-session behavioral targets and the home practice plan in the plan of care.

sessionStats.dose: Daily home practice is a predictor of outcomes — homework compliance must be monitored and supported
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with dysphonia of any etiology — functional, organic, neurological, or psychogenic

title: Melodic Intonation Therapy in Chronic Aphasia: Evidence from a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
shortTitle: MIT for Chronic Aphasia: Pilot RCT
authors: van der Meulen, I., van de Sandt-Koenderman, W. M. E., Heijenbrok-Kal, M. H., Visch-Brink, E. G., & Ribbers, G. M.
researchFindings: In a multicenter waiting-list RCT, 27 participants with chronic nonfluent aphasia were randomized to MIT treatment (n=16) or waiting-list control (n=11).
MIT produced significant improvement in repetition of both trained and untrained utterances compared to the waiting-list control — demonstrating treatment-specific effects.
Generalization of repetition gains to untrained items was documented, indicating that MIT produced broader language learning rather than item-specific memorization.
Moderate-to-large effect sizes were observed in the treatment group on the primary repetition outcome measures.
The MIT group demonstrated maintained improvement at follow-up relative to the control group, suggesting durable rather than transient effects.

This pilot RCT represents a significant methodological advance over earlier uncontrolled MIT case series, providing a controlled evidence base for a treatment with strong clinical tradition but previously limited Level 1 evidence.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic (post-acute, 6+ months post-onset) nonfluent aphasia with severely limited verbal output.
Patients in the chronic phase where payers or referrers question whether treatment is still evidence-supported.
Cases where standard aphasia treatment has plateaued and a right-hemisphere alternative approach is clinically indicated.
