Settings where intensive delivery (4–5x/week blocks) is achievable — the RCT protocol used intensive scheduling.
summary: Pilot RCT demonstrating that MIT significantly improves repetition in chronic nonfluent aphasia compared to a waiting-list control — providing the first controlled randomized evidence base supporting MIT effectiveness in the chronic phase.
clinicalApplication: This is the strongest controlled trial evidence for MIT specifically in chronic nonfluent aphasia — a population for whom evidence of continued treatment response has historically been limited. Use this study when justifying MIT for patients in the chronic phase (post-acute): payers sometimes question the evidence base for treatment in chronic aphasia, and this RCT directly addresses that concern. Combine with Albert et al. (1973) for the foundational rationale, Sparks et al. (1974) for the detailed protocol, and Tarng et al. (2022) systematic review for a complete evidence stack. When implementing MIT, ensure: (1) adequate intensity — at least 3–4 sessions per week; (2) appropriate patient selection — nonfluent, preserved comprehension, right-handed, intact right hemisphere; (3) systematic progression through MIT levels with accuracy criteria before advancing. The generalization to untrained items found in this RCT suggests MIT engages broader learning mechanisms beyond drill-based repetition.

sessionStats.dose: 6 weeks of intensive treatment; daily practice of trained phrases between sessions
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with chronic nonfluent aphasia with severely limited verbal output and intact right hemisphere

title: Development of International Terminology and Definitions for Texture-Modified Foods and Thickened Fluids Used in Dysphagia Management: The IDDSI Framework
shortTitle: The IDDSI Framework for Dysphagia Diet Standardization
authors: Cichero, J. A. Y., Lam, P., Steele, C. M., Hanson, B., Chen, J., Dantas, R. O., Duivestein, J., Kayashita, J., Lecko, C., Murray, J., Pillay, M., Riquelme, L., & Stanschus, S.
evidenceType: Consensus-based framework development with systematic evidence review
researchFindings: Prior to IDDSI, texture and consistency terminology varied substantially across countries, hospitals, and care settings — creating patient safety risks at care transitions when the same modification level was named differently.

The IDDSI framework establishes 8 levels (0–7) defined by numbers, text descriptors, color codes, precise definitions, and standardized measurement methods applicable across all cultures and care settings.
Drink/fluid levels (0–4): Thin, Slightly Thick, Mildly Thick, Moderately Thick, Extremely Thick; Food levels (3–7): Liquidised, Puréed, Minced & Moist, Soft & Bite-Sized, Regular/Easy to Chew.

IDDSI was developed through an international, multidisciplinary consensus process incorporating systematic review of existing terminology, SLP expertise, dietetics, nursing, food science, and patient/caregiver input.
Simple, reproducible test methods (fork drip test, spoon tilt test, syringe flow test) can verify IDDSI level compliance without specialized equipment at the point of care.
IDDSI has been adopted as the standard by ASHA, Speech Pathology Australia, RCSLT, and health authorities in more than 40 countries.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with dysphagia requiring texture-modified foods or thickened fluids as part of the management plan.
Care transitions (acute to SNF, hospital to home) where consistent texture terminology is required for patient safety.
Settings establishing or updating dysphagia diet protocols — IDDSI is the evidence-based international standard.
Training programs for nursing, dietary, food service, and caregiver staff on diet modification standards and verification.
summary: The paper establishing the International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative (IDDSI) framework — the globally adopted 8-level classification system for texture-modified foods and thickened fluids that replaced inconsistent national terminology and is now the international clinical standard.
clinicalApplication: IDDSI is the clinical standard for communicating diet modifications in dysphagia care. Every SLP managing dysphagia should be fluent in IDDSI levels and specify prescriptions using IDDSI terminology: "IDDSI Level 6 (Soft & Bite-Sized) foods and IDDSI Level 2 (Mildly Thick) liquids" rather than vague terms like "soft diet with nectar-thick liquids." Use IDDSI test methods to verify that food preparation at your facility actually meets the prescribed level — preparation methods vary widely and visual inspection alone is unreliable. Train nursing, dietary, and caregiver staff in IDDSI levels and verification methods. When writing MBSS or FEES reports, document bolus trials and outcomes by IDDSI level number and name for clear communication to all care providers. IDDSI Level 0 (Thin) covers all unmodified liquids; do not default to facility-specific terminology when IDDSI is the adopted standard.

sessionStats.bestFit: All adults with dysphagia requiring texture-modified foods or thickened fluids — IDDSI is the communication standard for all diet prescriptions

title: The Efficacy of Group Communication Treatment in Adults With Chronic Aphasia
shortTitle: Group Communication Treatment in Chronic Aphasia: RCT
authors: Elman, R. J., & Bernstein-Ellis, E.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
researchFindings: Twenty-four participants with chronic aphasia were randomly assigned to immediate treatment or deferred treatment groups; all participants ultimately received treatment.
The treatment group received 5 hours per week of group communication treatment for 4 months, provided by an SLP with a functional communication exchange focus.
Treatment group participants showed significantly greater improvement on language measures (PICA) compared to the deferred group during the active treatment phase.
Both groups ultimately improved, but earlier treatment produced faster and more substantial gains — demonstrating the clinical cost of deferring treatment in chronic aphasia.
Psychosocial outcomes including communication confidence and participation were also reported as improved in the treatment group.
This is among the first RCTs specifically examining group communication treatment as a distinct, evidence-based service model for chronic aphasia.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with chronic aphasia who can participate in group communication exchange based on functional comprehension.
Patients transitioning from individual to group treatment as communication goals shift toward functional exchange and community participation.
Settings where group aphasia programs are established or being developed — this RCT provides Level 1b evidence justifying group SLP services.
Cases where insurance authorization for group treatment requires evidence — cite as Level 1b evidence for group aphasia intervention.
summary: RCT demonstrating that 5 hours per week of group communication treatment for adults with chronic aphasia produced significant language and communication gains compared to deferred treatment — establishing group SLP treatment as evidence-based.
clinicalApplication: This RCT is your primary citation when justifying group aphasia treatment as a medically necessary, evidence-based service — not a social activity or maintenance program. Group aphasia treatment works: it produces measurable language gains in chronic aphasia when delivered by an SLP with a functional communication focus. The 5-hours-per-week dose in this study is high by many clinical standards — communicate to administrators that low-intensity group participation (1 hour per week) will produce fewer measurable gains than the study dose. Document group treatment as active SLP intervention with specific, measurable communication goals — not as supportive socialization. Use alongside Simmons-Mackie et al. (2016) partner training, Brady et al. (2016) Cochrane review, and Bhogal et al. (2003) intensity evidence to build a comprehensive multi-level evidence stack supporting aphasia services across individual, group, and partner training formats.

sessionStats.frequency: 5 hours/week in study (higher dose = greater gains); minimum 2–3 group sessions/week in practice
sessionStats.dose: 4 months of active group treatment in study; dose-response relationship suggests more treatment time is better
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with chronic aphasia of any severity appropriate for group participation

title: Aphasia Rehabilitation Resulting from Melodic Intonation Therapy
shortTitle: MIT: Aphasia Rehabilitation Results and Protocol (1974)
authors: Sparks, R., Helm, N., & Albert, M.
evidenceType: Case series with detailed treatment protocol description
researchFindings: Eight severely nonfluent, right-handed aphasic patients with left hemisphere damage were treated with MIT — all demonstrated meaningful gains in verbal production.

The complete three-level MIT protocol is described: Level I (intoning phrases simultaneously with clinician using two-note melody and left-hand tapping), Level II (fading clinician support with client continuing alone), Level III (client produces targets with natural prosody and reduced melodic cuing).

Patient selection criteria are refined from Albert et al. 1973: ideal candidates have severely limited verbal output, relatively preserved auditory comprehension, poor articulation, right-handedness, left hemisphere lesion, and high motivation.

MIT is explicitly not indicated for globally aphasic patients with severely impaired comprehension, fluent aphasia types, patients with right hemisphere damage, and patients with severe oral apraxia limiting even simultaneous imitation.

Right-hemisphere recruitment is elaborated as the proposed neural mechanism: intact right-hemisphere language homologs are activated by melodic and rhythmic structure, allowing verbal production to be rerouted through undamaged tissue.

The left-hand tapping element is emphasized as a specific and essential protocol component — not decorative — designed to activate right-hemisphere sensorimotor networks through contralateral hand control.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with severely nonfluent aphasia (Broca's or similar profile) with markedly limited verbal output and relatively preserved auditory comprehension.
Right-handed adults with left hemisphere damage — MIT mechanism requires intact right-hemisphere language networks.
Clinicians implementing MIT who need the original protocol hierarchy, level descriptions, and advancement criteria.
Cases where auditory-motor coupling through melodic and rhythmic structure may access verbal production that standard stimulation approaches have not unlocked.
summary: The 1974 expansion of Melodic Intonation Therapy presenting the complete three-level protocol, eight treated cases, and refined patient selection criteria — the definitive clinical protocol reference alongside the original 1973 Albert et al. paper.
clinicalApplication: This 1974 paper is the definitive protocol description for MIT and should be read alongside the original 1973 Albert et al. letter. It provides the full three-level treatment hierarchy with explicit criteria for advancing across levels — the practical implementation guide for MIT. Clinically: start target selection with high-frequency, high-utility phrases at Level I; the hand-tapping component is not optional; progress to Level III by systematically fading the melodic contour toward natural prosody; when clients spontaneously produce MIT-trained phrases in conversation, that represents protocol completion for that target. Patient selection: the ideal candidate is severely nonfluent (markedly limited spontaneous output — not simply hesitant or apraxic), has preserved comprehension, is right-handed, has left hemisphere lesion, intact right hemisphere, and can imitate at least minimally. Probe imitation ability informally before committing to MIT — if simultaneous production is not achievable even with maximum support, MIT may not be appropriate.

sessionStats.dose: Advance through MIT levels based on 80% accuracy criterion; minimum 15–20 sessions per target batch
sessionStats.bestFit: Chronic, severely nonfluent aphasia in right-handed adults with left hemisphere lesion and preserved comprehension

title: What People With Aphasia Want: Their Goals According to the ICF
shortTitle: What People With Aphasia Want: Goals by ICF Domain
authors: Worrall, L., Sherratt, S., Rogers, P., Howe, T., Hersh, D., Ferguson, A., & Davidson, B.
researchFindings: Fifty people with aphasia articulated their goals for therapy across semi-structured interviews; goals were systematically coded using the WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF).

The majority of goals fell at the Activity and Participation level of the ICF — people with aphasia primarily want to communicate in real-world contexts, maintain relationships, and participate in meaningful life roles.

Impairment-level goals (improving specific linguistic skills like naming or sentence production) were less frequently cited and were typically instrumental to broader participation goals rather than ends in themselves.

Frequently expressed goals included: resuming conversations with family and friends, returning to valued roles (worker, volunteer, community member), accessing news and information, and resuming recreational activities.
Environmental goals were prominent — many participants wanted changes in how communication partners and settings accommodated their aphasia, not only changes in their own linguistic abilities.
Misalignment between clinician-generated goals and client-generated goals has direct implications for therapeutic engagement, motivation, and perceived treatment relevance.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia at any stage during goal-setting or plan-of-care revision conversations.
SLPs seeking evidence to justify or adopt a client-centered, life participation approach to aphasia goal-setting.
Cases where family or referrers push for exclusively impairment-level goals — this study demonstrates that clients themselves prioritize participation.
Program development for community aphasia groups or outpatient services targeting sustained communication participation.
summary: Qualitative study mapping the self-reported goals of 50 adults with aphasia onto the ICF framework — finding that people with aphasia overwhelmingly prioritize participation-level and quality-of-life goals above impairment-level outcomes.
clinicalApplication: This study fundamentally supports the Life Participation Approach to Aphasia (LPAA): people with aphasia don't primarily want better naming scores — they want to talk to their family again, rejoin their book club, return to work, or access news. Start every goal-setting conversation with participation-level questions: "What do you most want to be able to do that you can't do right now?" Then write goals that reflect those participation priorities, using impairment-level work as the mechanism to achieve them. Frame goals for insurance in ICF participation terms paired with linguistic targets: "Client will produce 5-word requests with minimal prompting to communicate daily needs during morning care routine" rather than "Client will produce 5-word sentences." This study gives you direct patient-level evidence that the life participation model is what people with aphasia actually want — a powerful argument when advocating for functional, participation-based goals with administrators, referrers, or payers who favor purely impairment-level metrics.

sessionStats.bestFit: All adults with aphasia — particularly those in chronic stages where participation-focused goal-setting is most clinically meaningful

title: Writing Treatment for Severe Aphasia: Who Benefits?
shortTitle: Writing Treatment for Severe Aphasia
authors: Beeson, P. M., Rising, K., Kim, E. S., & Rapcsak, S. Z.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
researchFindings: Writing treatment produced meaningful gains in written naming accuracy in several participants with severe aphasia — gains that were maintained at follow-up assessment.

Better preserved graphemic knowledge (the ability to produce letters) at baseline was the strongest predictor of treatment response — participants with some residual letter production showed the greatest gains.
Improvements in writing generalized to untrained items in some participants, suggesting engagement of broader orthographic processing networks beyond item-specific memorization.
Written naming improved even in participants whose verbal naming remained severely limited, establishing that written and spoken naming routes can be differentially targeted and strengthened.
Improved written naming expanded functional communication in daily life for participants who achieved gains — creating a multimodal communication option where verbal output was insufficient.
Treatment response varied considerably across participants, underscoring the importance of baseline graphemic assessment before committing to writing as a primary treatment approach.
bestFitCriteria: Adults with severe aphasia and severely limited verbal output who retain some residual letter writing or copying ability.
Patients for whom multimodal communication is a goal — written naming as an alternative channel alongside verbal, gestural, and AAC approaches.
Clients with nonfluent or global aphasia where writing may access orthographic routes relatively independently of severely impaired verbal production.
Cases where family and caregiver training in supporting written communication is part of the functional communication goal.
summary: Identifies which adults with severe aphasia benefit from writing treatment, demonstrating that residual graphemic ability predicts treatment response and that improved written naming creates a functional multimodal communication channel when verbal output is severely limited.
clinicalApplication: Writing treatment is an underutilized option for adults with severe aphasia who cannot rely on verbal output as the primary communication channel. If a client can produce some letters — even with errors — a structured writing treatment (copy-and-recall training, anagram and copy treatment) may open a functional written communication channel. Before beginning: assess baseline graphemic ability — can the client copy letters? Write any letters from memory? Recognize correct versus incorrect spellings of familiar words? Even partial ability suggests potential benefit. Target functionally meaningful words first: names of family members, daily care needs, frequently used verbs. Pair written production with other AAC supports — a communication book combining written words with picture symbols gives the client a comprehensive multimodal approach. Successfully writing a key word to convey a message is a real, clinically significant gain — document these functional communication outcomes explicitly in your progress notes. Combine with SFA or VNeST when lexical-semantic access limitations affect both written and verbal naming.

sessionStats.dose: Copy-and-recall training: 15–20 trials per target word per session; daily home practice with written word cards and cuing hierarchy
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with severe aphasia and some residual graphemic ability for whom multimodal communication is a goal

title: Electrical Stimulation for Swallowing Disorders Caused by Stroke
shortTitle: NMES for Post-Stroke Dysphagia
authors: Freed, M. L., Freed, L., Chatburn, R. L., & Christian, M.
summary: RCT comparing neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES/VitalStim) to thermal-tactile stimulation for dysphagia in stroke survivors — foundational study establishing NMES as a treatment modality for pharyngeal dysphagia.
researchFindings: 63% of the NMES group achieved normal swallowing function versus 23% in the thermal-tactile stimulation group — a statistically significant difference.
Dysphagia Outcome and Severity Scale (DOSS) scores improved significantly more in the NMES group across the 12-session treatment protocol.
NMES was applied externally to the anterior neck over the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles during active swallowing attempts.
Improvements were maintained at 6-month follow-up, suggesting durable changes in neuromuscular function rather than temporary compensation.
Treatment was delivered intensively (5 days/week) and both groups demonstrated some improvement, indicating task-specific swallowing practice contributes regardless of modality.
clinicalApplication: NMES (VitalStim) remains one of the most debated modalities in dysphagia rehabilitation. This foundational RCT established its efficacy for post-stroke pharyngeal dysphagia, but subsequent research has produced mixed results. Use NMES as an adjunct — not a standalone — combined with active swallowing tasks and traditional dysphagia therapy. Patient selection matters: best evidence supports pharyngeal-stage dysphagia in stroke with adequate sensation and cortical drive. Avoid in patients with pacemakers, active cancer over the treatment area, or impaired sensation. Document baseline function with DOSS or MBSImP, set electrode placement based on anatomy, and re-assess every 4–6 sessions. The Steele et al. (2015) IDDSI framework and Logemann aspiration risk work pair well with NMES to guide diet level decisions alongside active treatment.

sessionStats.dose: 30–60 min NMES per session; 12–20 sessions typical protocol
sessionStats.bestFit: Post-stroke pharyngeal dysphagia with adequate sensation and cortical drive

bestFitCriteria: Adults with pharyngeal-stage dysphagia following stroke or other neurological event.
Patients with documented aspiration or penetration on instrumental assessment (MBSS or FEES).
Adequate cutaneous sensation over the anterior neck for electrode placement.
Absence of contraindications: pacemaker, active malignancy over treatment site, seizure disorder.
Patients who can participate actively in swallowing tasks during stimulation.

title: Evidence-Based Cognitive Rehabilitation: Recommendations for Clinical Practice
shortTitle: Evidence-Based Cognitive Rehabilitation (2000)
authors: Cicerone, K. D., Dahlberg, C., Kalmar, K., Langenbahn, D. M., Malec, J. F., Bergquist, T. F., Morse, P. A., Giacino, J. T., Harley, J. P., Harrington, D. E., Herzog, J., Kneipp, S., Laatsch, L., & Morse, P. A.
journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
summary: Landmark systematic review establishing the evidence base for cognitive rehabilitation across attention, memory, language, visuospatial, and executive functions — the foundational reference for evidence-based cognitive-communication treatment following TBI and stroke.
researchFindings: Attention training for mild TBI and stroke received strong (Practice Standard) recommendation based on consistent RCT evidence across multiple studies.
Visuospatial rehabilitation post-right hemisphere stroke received Practice Standard recommendation; interventions targeting scanning and compensation were most supported.
Cognitive-linguistic deficits post-stroke (language, memory, pragmatics) received Practice Guideline recommendations with moderate evidence.
Executive function and problem-solving interventions received Practice Guideline support, particularly metacognitive strategy training in post-acute TBI.
Compensatory memory strategy training — particularly external aids and errorless learning — received Practice Guideline support for moderate-to-severe TBI.
This review was updated in 2005 and 2011 (Cicerone et al.) with expanded evidence; the 2000 version established the tiered Practice Standard/Guideline/Option framework still used today.
clinicalApplication: This is the first major systematic review to grade cognitive rehabilitation evidence using a tiered framework — Practice Standard (strong RCT support), Practice Guideline (Class II evidence), Practice Option (expert consensus). For cognitive-communication SLP practice: prioritize attention training (scanning, sustained/divided attention) for early post-acute care; use external compensatory strategies (notebooks, smartphones, alarms) for memory deficits with strong evidence support; address executive function through metacognitive strategy instruction and task-specific training rather than non-contextual drills. Pair with Sohlberg & Mateer APT-3 for attention and the Cicerone 2011 update for the most current evidence base. Document functional goals aligned with ICF participation domains — the review emphasizes participation-level outcomes as targets, not cognitive scores alone.

sessionStats.dose: Domain-specific; attention training 20–30 sessions; memory strategy training 12–20 sessions
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with acquired cognitive-communication deficits from TBI or stroke in post-acute or outpatient settings

bestFitCriteria: Adults with cognitive-communication impairments following traumatic brain injury (mild to severe).
Post-stroke adults with cognitive-linguistic deficits affecting memory, attention, or executive function.
Clinicians designing cognitive rehabilitation programs who need a tiered evidence framework.
Cases where attention, visuospatial, memory, or executive function is the primary treatment target.
Settings requiring documentation of evidence level for insurance justification or program development.

title: The Role of Semantic Complexity in Treatment of Naming Deficits: Training Semantic Categories in Fluent Aphasia by Abstractness and Typicality
shortTitle: Semantic Complexity in Naming Treatment
authors: Kiran, S., & Thompson, C. K.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
evidenceType: Experimental single-subject design with multiple baselines
summary: Demonstrates that training atypical (harder) exemplars within a semantic category produces greater generalization to untrained items than training typical (easier) exemplars — establishing the Complexity Account of Treatment Efficacy (CATE) for anomia therapy.
researchFindings: Training atypical category members (e.g., penguin as a bird) resulted in generalization to untrained typical members (e.g., robin, eagle) but not vice versa.
Training typical exemplars produced little generalization to atypical items, suggesting the semantic network is best reorganized from its less-established edges.
The Complexity Account of Treatment Efficacy (CATE) predicts that treatment of more complex, marked items will generalize to simpler, more typical items within the same category.
Results held across participants with fluent aphasia, supporting the principle across different aphasia subtypes.
Semantic feature training focused on both shared category features and distinguishing features, aligning with the semantic feature analysis approach.
clinicalApplication: Apply CATE by selecting atypical exemplars (unusual items within a category) as treatment targets rather than the most common or easily named items. For a patient targeting animal naming, train penguin and platypus before robin and dog — generalization is more likely to flow from complex to simple than the reverse. Pair with Semantic Feature Analysis (Boyle 2004) and VNeST (Edmonds 2014) for a comprehensive naming treatment protocol. Use baseline probes across both trained and untrained exemplars to document generalization — this is how the evidence is measured and how you'll justify treatment decisions. CATE applies beyond naming to syntax (Thompson 2003 TUF) and other language domains, making it a core theoretical framework for evidence-based aphasia treatment planning.

sessionStats.dose: Target 2–3 atypical exemplars per category; probe generalization weekly
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with fluent or nonfluent aphasia and word-finding deficits; any anomia treatment program

bestFitCriteria: Adults with aphasia and anomia as a primary treatment target.
Clients where naming generalization (trained to untrained items) is a therapy goal.
Clinicians using Semantic Feature Analysis who want to optimize target selection.
Cases where treatment efficiency is prioritized — CATE maximizes generalization per hour of treatment.
Fluent aphasia presentations including Wernicke's, anomic, or conduction aphasia.

title: Swallowing Disorders in Closed Head Trauma Patients
shortTitle: Swallowing Disorders in TBI
authors: Lazarus, C., & Logemann, J. A.
journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
summary: Foundational study characterizing the nature and frequency of swallowing disorders in closed head trauma patients via videofluoroscopy — establishing that TBI-related dysphagia is common, multistage, and distinct in profile from stroke-related dysphagia.
researchFindings: Swallowing disorders were present in the majority of closed head trauma patients assessed, with oral-stage and pharyngeal-stage abnormalities frequently co-occurring.
Aspiration was documented in a significant proportion of TBI patients, often occurring silently (without cough or behavioral indication).
Common dysphagia profiles included delayed pharyngeal swallow, reduced tongue control, and impaired laryngeal closure — patterns differing from typical post-stroke presentations.
Reduced oral transit time and disorganized oral bolus management were frequently observed, reflecting the diffuse cortical and subcortical involvement typical of closed head injury.
Cognitive and behavioral factors (impulsivity, distractibility, reduced self-monitoring) were identified as contributors to dysphagia risk beyond the physiological swallowing abnormalities.
clinicalApplication: In TBI populations, do not rely solely on clinical observation or behavioral signs to rule out aspiration — instrumental assessment (FEES or MBSS) is essential given the high rate of silent aspiration documented in this foundational study. Factor in cognitive status when designing dysphagia management: impulsivity, reduced self-monitoring, and agitation can undermine even physiologically intact swallowing. Compensatory strategies may need to be simplified or externally cued given TBI-related executive and memory deficits. Coordinate with the medical team on level of consciousness, medication effects on swallowing, and tracheostomy status. Reassess frequently — TBI dysphagia often improves with neurological recovery and should not be treated as static.

sessionStats.dose: Individualized based on severity; re-assess every 4–6 weeks
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with closed head TBI in acute, subacute, or inpatient rehab settings

bestFitCriteria: Adults with closed head traumatic brain injury and suspected or confirmed dysphagia.
TBI patients who have failed clinical swallowing evaluation and require instrumental workup.
Patients with cognitive impairment complicating dysphagia management (impulsivity, reduced self-monitoring).
Inpatient rehabilitation or acute care settings where TBI dysphagia protocols are being developed.
Cases where aspiration pneumonia history or recurring respiratory events warrant dysphagia screening.

title: Management of Oral-Pharyngeal Dysphagia Symptoms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
shortTitle: ALS Oral-Pharyngeal Dysphagia Management
authors: Strand, E. A., Miller, R. M., Yorkston, K. M., & Hillel, A. D.
summary: Describes the clinical course of oral-pharyngeal dysphagia in ALS patients and proposes a staged management framework — foundational for understanding how dysphagia progresses in ALS and how intervention should evolve with disease stage.
researchFindings: Dysphagia in ALS follows a predictable progressive course tied to upper and lower motor neuron involvement, with distinct oral and pharyngeal presentations depending on the predominant UMN vs. LMN profile.
Early ALS dysphagia often presents as prolonged meal times and fatigue during eating, with pharyngeal dysphagia and aspiration risk increasing as disease progresses.
Diet modification (texture and liquid alteration) remains the most consistent intervention across disease stages, but must be titrated to avoid caloric restriction.

Compensatory strategies (chin tuck, head rotation, small bolus volumes, altered positioning) may provide short-term benefit in early-to-mid-stage disease but lose efficacy as pharyngeal weakness progresses.
Gastrostomy tube (PEG) placement should be discussed proactively — ideally while FVC remains above 50% — not reactively after severe aspiration or weight loss.
Patients and families require ongoing counseling about the progressive nature of swallowing decline and the relationship between dysphagia management, nutrition, and quality of life.
clinicalApplication: In ALS dysphagia management, adopt a proactive staging approach: early = compensatory strategies and dietary counseling; middle = texture modification, caloric supplementation, fatigue management; late = PEG discussion, palliative eating goals, comfort feeding. The critical clinical window for PEG referral is before respiratory function drops below 50% FVC — raise this with the ALS clinic team early and often, not reactively. Use the ALSFRS-R bulbar subscale alongside your own dysphagia assessment to track progression. Diet modification conversations must weigh aspiration risk against quality of life — many ALS patients choose to accept some aspiration risk to continue oral eating. Always involve the patient's goals in these decisions. Coordinate with palliative care and the ALS multidisciplinary team.

sessionStats.frequency: Monthly in early-mid stage; more frequent as disease progresses
sessionStats.dose: Reassessment-focused; treatment is largely compensatory and counseling-based
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with bulbar or mixed ALS at any disease stage

bestFitCriteria: Adults diagnosed with ALS (bulbar-onset or with bulbar involvement in limb-onset disease).
Patients with progressive weight loss, prolonged mealtimes, or reported choking/aspiration episodes.
ALS clinic settings where SLP coordinates with neurology, nutrition, pulmonology, and palliative care.
Families and care partners requiring counseling on evolving dysphagia management and PEG decision-making.
Cases where instrumental swallowing assessment is needed to guide diet level and aspiration risk.

title: Comparing Differences in the Effects of Mendelsohn Maneuver, Head Rotation, and Effortful Swallow on Swallowing Mechanics in Normal Adults
shortTitle: Swallowing Maneuvers Evidence
authors: McCullough, G. H., Huddleston, F. C., & Prigge, K. E.
summary: Compares the biomechanical effects of three widely-used compensatory swallowing maneuvers — Mendelsohn, head rotation, and effortful swallow — on swallowing physiology in normal adults, providing the evidence base for selecting maneuvers for specific dysphagia profiles.
researchFindings: The Mendelsohn maneuver significantly increased UES opening duration and the extent of hyoid and laryngeal elevation compared to no-maneuver baseline.
Head rotation toward the weaker side redirected bolus flow toward the stronger piriform sinus and reduced residue on the rotated side, consistent with its use in unilateral pharyngeal weakness.
The effortful swallow increased tongue base retraction and posterior pharyngeal wall pressure, but did not significantly alter UES opening in normal adults.
No single maneuver improved all physiological parameters simultaneously; maneuver selection should be based on the specific biomechanical deficit identified on instrumental assessment.
Participant fatigue and compliance affected maneuver performance — clinicians must verify correct execution before assuming therapeutic benefit.
clinicalApplication: Match maneuver to mechanism: Mendelsohn for reduced UES opening or insufficient laryngeal elevation; head rotation for unilateral pharyngeal weakness (rotate toward weak side to direct bolus to the stronger side); effortful swallow for reduced tongue base retraction and posterior pharyngeal wall contact. Do not prescribe maneuvers based on diagnosis alone — use MBSS or FEES to identify the specific physiological breakdown and then select the maneuver that directly addresses it. Teach maneuvers during instrumental assessment where possible so you can confirm they produce the intended change. Reassess maneuver effectiveness as the patient's swallowing function changes. Educate patients that these are effortful techniques requiring conscious application — carryover to automatic eating requires consistent practice.

sessionStats.dose: 10–20 trials per maneuver per session; individualized to fatigue tolerance
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with documented pharyngeal dysphagia on instrumental assessment, particularly reduced UES opening or unilateral pharyngeal weakness

bestFitCriteria: Adults with pharyngeal-stage dysphagia identified on videofluoroscopy or FEES.
Patients with documented reduced UES opening (Mendelsohn), unilateral pharyngeal weakness (head rotation), or reduced tongue base retraction (effortful swallow).
Cognitively intact adults who can learn and consistently apply effortful techniques during eating.
Situations where diet modification alone is insufficient and behavioral technique training is warranted.
Post-instrumental assessment where specific physiological targets for maneuver training have been identified.

title: Evidence-Based Medicine and Practice Guidelines: Application to the Field of Speech-Language Pathology
shortTitle: EBP Guidelines in SLP
authors: Yorkston, K. M., Spencer, K. A., Duffy, J. R., Beukelman, D. R., Golper, L. A., Miller, R. M., Strand, E. A., & Sullivan, M.
summary: Tutorial translating the evidence-based medicine framework into speech-language pathology practice — describing how to appraise, interpret, and apply research evidence in clinical decision-making across motor speech, dysphagia, and related SLP domains.
researchFindings: EBM's hierarchy of evidence (RCTs > cohort studies > case series > expert opinion) was adapted for SLP, where RCTs are rare but high-quality single-subject experimental designs provide meaningful evidence.

Practice guidelines require explicit methodology: systematic literature search, defined inclusion criteria, graded evidence levels, and transparent expert consensus processes for lower-evidence areas.

The article distinguishes Practice Standards (strong RCT support), Practice Guidelines (moderate cohort support), and Practice Options (expert consensus / case series) — a tiered framework adopted by ASHA.
Clinical expertise and patient values are identified as co-equal components of EBP alongside research evidence — not subordinate to it.
Barriers to EBP adoption in SLP include small sample sizes, heterogeneous populations, and outcome measurement challenges — methodological issues, not absence of evidence.
clinicalApplication: Use this paper as a conceptual anchor for understanding the levels of evidence across SLP literature. When documenting clinical rationale, reference the evidence tier: Standard (Level I RCT), Guideline (Level II cohort), or Option (Level III case series / expert opinion). This is particularly important when communicating with medical teams, writing insurance justifications, or presenting treatment plans to supervisors. It also reframes weak evidence — a well-designed single-subject study is not anecdote; it is empirical evidence appropriate to the clinical complexity of SLP populations. Pair with Dollaghan (2004, 2007) for a deeper operationalization of EBP and Threats (2006) for ICF-based goal-setting within an EBP framework.

sessionStats.dose: N/A
sessionStats.bestFit: SLPs applying EBP in any clinical domain; supervisors, CFs, and academic settings

bestFitCriteria: Clinicians seeking to understand how to appraise and apply research evidence in SLP practice.
Settings requiring documentation of evidence levels for treatment justification.
Clinical fellowship supervisors and academic educators teaching EBP principles.
Situations where treatment decisions must be explained to medical teams, payers, or families.
Any SLP working in motor speech, dysphagia, or cognitive-communication who wants a methodological foundation for clinical reasoning.

title: Inferencing Processes After Right Hemisphere Brain Damage: Maintenance of Inferences
shortTitle: Right Hemisphere Inferencing Deficits
authors: Blake, M. L.
journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
summary: Examines inferencing deficits following right hemisphere brain damage (RHD) — demonstrating that difficulty maintaining and revising inferences during discourse comprehension is a core feature of RHD communication, beyond simple literal comprehension.
researchFindings: Adults with RHD showed deficits in maintaining elaborative inferences (world-knowledge-based conclusions drawn during text comprehension) over time, even when initial inference generation was intact.

RHD participants had difficulty revising incorrect inferences when contradictory information was introduced later in discourse — suggesting a perseveration or suppression deficit rather than a failure to generate inferences.
Performance differences were evident on indirect measures (reading time, priming tasks) as well as explicit comprehension tasks, suggesting the deficit is not purely metalinguistic.
These findings support the Suppression Deficit Hypothesis — RHD disrupts the ability to suppress contextually inappropriate interpretations, leading to overreliance on salient or literal meanings.
Inferencing deficits contribute to the pragmatic comprehension impairments observed clinically, including difficulty with indirect requests, humor, sarcasm, and narrative coherence.
clinicalApplication: When assessing adults with RHD, include inferencing tasks beyond literal comprehension: test understanding of implied meanings, humor, sarcasm, idioms, and indirect requests. Deficits often emerge on discourse-level tasks when sentence-level comprehension appears intact. For treatment, use structured discourse activities targeting the client's ability to generate, maintain, and revise inferences — for example, open-ended story completion, prediction tasks, and error detection in incongruent stories. Togher (2013), Turkstra (2015), and Tompkins are key companion references for the broader RHD communication profile. Remember that RHD communication deficits are frequently underdiagnosed because clients may pass traditional aphasia screeners; always assess discourse and pragmatics.

sessionStats.dose: Discourse-based tasks; 10–15 trials per session across inferencing types
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with RHD and pragmatic/discourse comprehension deficits passing basic aphasia screens

bestFitCriteria: Adults with right hemisphere brain damage (stroke, TBI) and reported communication difficulties despite intact sentence-level language.
Patients whose family members report conversational breakdowns, difficulty with humor, or social communication changes.
Clinicians assessing RHD and needing to differentiate pragmatic from linguistic impairments.
Settings where discourse and inferencing assessment (not just aphasia batteries) is available.
Post-acute or outpatient settings where higher-level cognitive-communication goals are appropriate.

title: Speech and Language Therapy Versus Placebo or No Intervention for Speech Problems in Parkinson's Disease
shortTitle: SLT for Parkinson's Speech — Cochrane Review
authors: Herd, C. P., Tomlinson, C. L., Deane, K. H. O., Brady, M. C., Smith, C. H., Sackley, C. M., & Clarke, C. E.
summary: Cochrane review comparing SLT interventions (primarily LSVT LOUD) to placebo or no treatment for speech and voice problems in Parkinson's disease — finding significant treatment effects on vocal loudness and intelligibility that support the use of SLT for PD speech.
researchFindings: SLT (primarily LSVT LOUD) produced significant improvements in vocal intensity and functional speech loudness compared to no treatment or placebo in adults with PD.
Intelligibility improved significantly in the treatment groups, with effects documented across both self-report and listener-based outcome measures.
Benefits were demonstrated in the short term (immediately post-treatment); evidence for long-term maintenance was more limited and called for further study.

LSVT LOUD was the most frequently studied intervention, providing the strongest individual evidence base; other approaches (Lee Silverman generics, respiratory training, oromotor exercises) had weaker evidence.
The review highlighted methodological heterogeneity and small sample sizes as limitations but concluded the overall direction of evidence supported SLT for PD speech.
clinicalApplication: This Cochrane review is the highest-level evidence supporting SLT for Parkinson's speech and is your go-to citation when justifying treatment for hypokinetic dysarthria. LSVT LOUD — the most-studied protocol — targets vocal loudness as the entry point for broader speech improvement, leveraging the PD speaker's ability to recalibrate internal sensory targets for loudness ('think loud'). If LSVT certification is not available, intensive approaches using similar principles (high repetition, loudness calibration, minimal feedback delay) can be used with reference to the Ramig et al. RCT evidence. Reassessment of loudness (dB SPL) and intelligibility at baseline and post-treatment is essential for documenting change. Coordinate with the neurology team around medication timing — speech function often varies with on/off cycles in advanced PD.

sessionStats.dose: 16 sessions over 4 weeks (LSVT standard); home practice daily
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with Parkinson's disease and hypokinetic dysarthria with reduced vocal loudness and intelligibility

bestFitCriteria: Adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease and hypokinetic dysarthria (reduced loudness, monotone, imprecise articulation).
PD patients with self-reported or partner-reported communication difficulty in daily life.
Clients early enough in disease progression to engage in intensive treatment (adequate cognition and motivation).
Clinicians needing highest-level evidence to support SLT referral or insurance justification for PD communication treatment.
Settings where LSVT LOUD or equivalent intensive loudness-focused protocols can be delivered.

title: A Systematic Review of the Use of Telehealth in Speech, Language and Hearing Sciences
shortTitle: Telehealth in SLP — Systematic Review
authors: Molini-Avejonas, D. R., Rondon-Melo, S., de la Higuera Amato, C. A., & Samelli, A. G.
summary: Systematic review of telehealth applications across speech, language, and hearing sciences — finding that telepractice produces equivalent outcomes to in-person delivery across a range of SLP clinical areas, supporting its use as a valid service delivery model.
researchFindings: Telehealth interventions across aphasia, fluency, voice, dysarthria, and hearing demonstrated equivalent outcomes to in-person treatment in the majority of studies reviewed.
Assessment via telehealth yielded comparable reliability and validity to face-to-face assessment for most speech and language domains evaluated.
Patient satisfaction with telehealth services was consistently high, particularly among clients with mobility limitations, rural access challenges, or caregiver constraints.
Aphasia treatment and fluency interventions had the strongest evidence base for telehealth delivery; dysphagia teletherapy had more limited evidence but was emerging.
Technical barriers (internet connectivity, equipment), assessment standardization, and regulatory/licensure issues were identified as ongoing implementation challenges.
clinicalApplication: Telehealth is a clinically supported service delivery model, not a second-tier option. For aphasia and fluency, the evidence for equivalence to in-person treatment is strongest — use this review to justify teletherapy referrals and reimbursement requests. For swallowing, telehealth assessment requires additional validation, though behavioral teletherapy for compensatory strategies is increasingly supported. Best practices: ensure adequate bandwidth and device quality; conduct tech checks before first sessions; adapt materials for screen-sharing; build informal observation time to compensate for reduced physical proximity. Document the telehealth modality in session notes per ASHA and payer requirements. In rural, underserved, or mobility-limited populations, telehealth may be the primary access point for SLP services — this review provides the evidence base to advocate for its expansion.

sessionStats.frequency: Equivalent to in-person frequency recommendations per area
sessionStats.sessionLength: 45–60 min (slightly shorter to reduce screen fatigue)
sessionStats.dose: Evidence equivalent to in-person; adjust for tech and access factors
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with aphasia, fluency disorders, or voice disorders with geographic, mobility, or scheduling barriers to in-person care

bestFitCriteria: Adults requiring SLP services who face geographic, transportation, or mobility barriers to in-person care.
Aphasia and fluency clients where telehealth equivalence evidence is strongest.
Settings developing or justifying a telepractice program for speech-language services.
Clinicians seeking evidence to support reimbursement for telehealth SLP services.
Patients in rural or underserved areas where in-person SLP access is limited.

title: Dysphagia and Diets in Skilled Nursing Facilities When Patient's Health Status Changes: The Role of Imaging
shortTitle: Dysphagia and Diet Changes in SNFs: Role of Imaging
authors: Bice, E., Martin-Harris, B., & Brodsky, M. B.
journal: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association
summary: Retrospective review examining clinical decision-making for swallowing in skilled nursing facilities, specifically when patients' health status changes. Argues that a new instrumental assessment is required any time medical status changes—not just at admission.
researchFindings: Only 33% of SNF patients recommended for FEES actually demonstrated dysphagia on imaging.
Only 4% of patients ultimately required continued alternative nutrition after instrumental assessment.
Many patients were kept on unnecessarily restricted diets without updated imaging following health status changes.
A new instrumental assessment is clinically required to inform diet decisions whenever medical status changes significantly.
Relying solely on clinical swallow evaluation at health status change is insufficient to ensure accurate diet recommendations.
clinicalApplication: In SNF settings, do not assume a patient's dysphagia status remains stable when their medical condition changes. Request updated instrumental assessment (FEES or VFSS) before modifying or maintaining diet restrictions. This study supports advocating for timely imaging access in long-term care and challenges the practice of indefinite diet restrictions without re-evaluation.

sessionStats.frequency: As indicated by health status change
sessionStats.dose: Re-evaluate with imaging at each significant status change
sessionStats.bestFit: Adult dysphagia in SNF/long-term care

bestFitCriteria: Adults with dysphagia residing in skilled nursing facilities.
Patients whose medical status has changed since last swallowing evaluation.
SLPs making diet modification decisions in long-term care.
Advocating for FEES program implementation in SNF settings.

title: Safety of FEES Performed by Speech-Language Pathologists and Physicians: Evidence Supporting Task Sharing from a Retrospective Observational Study of 964 Consecutive Examinations
shortTitle: Safety of FEES Performed by SLPs vs. Physicians
authors: Various (PMC12567526)
summary: Large retrospective observational study examining the safety of FEES performed by SLPs compared to physicians across 964 consecutive examinations. Supports SLP-performed FEES as safe and comparable to physician-performed procedures.
researchFindings: No statistically significant differences in complication rates were found based on examiner professional background (SLP vs. physician).
No significant differences were found based on level of endoscopic experience.
Appropriately trained SLPs can safely perform FEES with a complication profile comparable to that reported internationally.
Task-sharing of FEES between SLPs and physicians is supported by this evidence base.
The study adds to the growing literature supporting SLP-performed FEES within appropriate training frameworks.
clinicalApplication: Use this evidence to support SLP-performed FEES programs in your facility. When advocating for SLP scope in instrumental assessment, this study demonstrates that trained SLPs perform FEES as safely as physicians. Supports workforce efficiency and improved patient access to timely swallowing imaging.

sessionStats.dose: Single instrumental session per evaluation
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with dysphagia requiring instrumental assessment

bestFitCriteria: SLPs seeking to establish or expand a FEES program.
Adults requiring instrumental swallowing assessment.
Facilities where physician-only FEES creates access barriers.
Advocating for SLP scope of practice in instrumental assessment.

title: Analysis of Patients' Dietary Status/Restrictions Following Instrumental Swallow Evaluations in Skilled Nursing Facilities
shortTitle: Dietary Status After Instrumental Evals in SNFs
authors: Various (PMC11893628)
summary: Examines dietary status and restrictions for patients following instrumental swallow evaluations in skilled nursing facilities, analyzing patterns of diet liberalization or restriction post-VFSS/FEES.
researchFindings: Instrumental swallow evaluation frequently results in diet liberalization rather than restriction in SNF populations.
Many patients in SNFs are maintained on unnecessarily restrictive diets without current imaging evidence.
Access to instrumental assessment in SNF settings improves the accuracy of diet recommendations.
Clinical swallow evaluation alone may over-restrict diets compared to findings on imaging.
Findings support routine use of instrumental assessment in SNF populations with dysphagia.
clinicalApplication: Advocate for instrumental swallowing assessment access in SNF settings. When patients are placed on modified diets based on clinical exam alone, instrumental follow-up may reveal that liberalization is appropriate. This supports quality of life, nutritional status, and patient-centered care in long-term care settings.

sessionStats.dose: Single evaluation with follow-up as needed
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with dysphagia in SNF settings

bestFitCriteria: Adults with dysphagia in skilled nursing or long-term care settings.
Patients on modified diets without recent instrumental confirmation.
SLPs advocating for imaging access in SNF settings.
Quality improvement efforts targeting diet appropriateness in long-term care.

title: Using and Modifying Standardized Restorative Treatments in Aphasia: Clinician Perspectives
shortTitle: Modifying Standardized Aphasia Treatments: Clinician Views
authors: McMaster, E., et al.
summary: Investigates which standardized aphasia treatments clinicians use most frequently, how and why they modify them, and what sources guide their modifications.
researchFindings: Semantic Feature Analysis (SFA) and Verb Network Strengthening Treatment (VNeST) were the most frequently used standardized aphasia treatments.
Clinicians regularly modify standardized protocols to fit individual client needs, goals, and contexts.
Little published research describes how clinicians modify protocols or which sources guide those modifications.
Clinicians reported using client characteristics, treatment response, and clinical experience as primary guides for modification.
Treatment individualization is a common and necessary practice in aphasia therapy, but the evidence base for specific modifications remains limited.
clinicalApplication: SFA and VNeST are your most evidence-supported starting points for naming/word retrieval treatment in aphasia. When individualizing, document your rationale clearly. This study validates the clinical need for treatment adaptation, but encourages SLPs to evaluate client response systematically when deviating from standardized protocols.

sessionStats.dose: Individualized based on protocol and client response
sessionStats.bestFit: Anomia, fluent and nonfluent aphasia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with post-stroke or acquired aphasia presenting with word retrieval deficits.
Clinicians selecting or adapting standardized aphasia treatment protocols.
SLPs using SFA or VNeST and considering protocol modifications.
Program evaluation or quality improvement in aphasia rehabilitation settings.

title: Neurologic Music Therapy for Non-Fluent Aphasia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
shortTitle: Neurologic Music Therapy for Non-Fluent Aphasia: Systematic Review
authors: Hong, I. S., et al.
evidenceType: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs examining neurologic music therapy (NMT) techniques—including melodic intonation therapy and rhythmic speech cueing—for non-fluent aphasia.
researchFindings: Neurologic music therapy (NMT) techniques demonstrated significant positive effects on language outcomes in non-fluent aphasia.
Melodic intonation therapy and rhythmic speech cueing showed the strongest evidence within NMT approaches.
NMT was associated with improvements in verbal fluency, naming, and repetition in Broca's aphasia.
RCT-level evidence supports NMT as an adjunctive treatment for non-fluent aphasia.
The efficacy of NMT for non-fluent aphasia is widely accepted by the rehabilitation medical community.
clinicalApplication: Neurologic music therapy—particularly melodic intonation therapy and rhythmic speech cueing—has RCT-level support for non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia. Consider NMT as a complement to traditional language therapy, especially for patients with severe non-fluency who are not responsive to standard verbal approaches.

sessionStats.dose: Varies by protocol; intensive approaches show stronger effects
sessionStats.bestFit: Non-fluent aphasia, Broca's aphasia, severe aphasia

bestFitCriteria: Adults with non-fluent or Broca's aphasia post-stroke.
Patients with severe aphasia who show limited response to traditional verbal approaches.
Clinicians interested in melodic intonation or music-based language treatment.
Settings where adjunctive music-based therapy is feasible.

title: Voice Outcomes in Patients With Laryngopharyngeal Reflux: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Voice Outcomes in Laryngopharyngeal Reflux: Meta-Analysis
authors: Various (PMC12441754)
summary: PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis examining voice outcomes across pharmacological, behavioral, and diagnostic approaches for laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR). Covers 2000–2024.
researchFindings: Behavioral interventions (e.g., voice therapy, LSVT) demonstrated robust efficacy for voice outcomes in LPR patients (ES=0.60).
Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) showed negligible effects on voice outcomes (ES = -0.15).
Adjunctive rikkunshito significantly improved outcomes in refractory LPR cases (ES=0.82).
Voice therapy addressing muscle tension and laryngeal hygiene is more effective than medication alone for voice complaints in LPR.
Acoustic voice analysis reliably detects changes in LPR patients, with 27 of 33 studies confirming reproducible acoustic voice changes.
clinicalApplication: For patients with voice complaints secondary to LPR, behavioral voice therapy is more effective than PPIs alone. Prioritize voice hygiene, manual circumlaryngeal techniques for muscle tension, and resonant voice approaches. Coordinate with ENT regarding medical management, but advocate for concurrent voice therapy rather than waiting for reflux resolution before initiating treatment.

sessionStats.dose: 6–8 sessions with home practice
sessionStats.bestFit: LPR-related dysphonia, muscle tension dysphonia with reflux

bestFitCriteria: Adults with voice complaints attributed to laryngopharyngeal reflux.
Patients who have not responded to PPI therapy alone.
Muscle tension dysphonia with suspected reflux component.
Multidisciplinary voice clinic patients with ENT/GI referral.

title: Communication Patterns and Characteristics of Family Caregivers and Persons Living With Dementia: Secondary Analysis of Video Observation
shortTitle: Caregiver Communication Patterns in Dementia
authors: Various (PMC10955794)
evidenceType: Secondary analysis of video observation data
summary: Secondary analysis of video-observed interactions between family caregivers and persons living with dementia. Examines how caregiver burden, depression, and communication competence relate to interaction quality.
researchFindings: Caregiver burden, depression, and competence in managing burden are significantly related to communication patterns with persons living with dementia.
Higher caregiver burden was associated with less person-centered communication.
Persons with dementia were more communicatively engaged when caregivers used supportive, patient-centered strategies.
Video observation revealed that many problematic interactions stem from caregiver stress rather than intentional communication failures.
Findings support the need for SLP involvement in caregiver communication training, not just patient-directed treatment.
clinicalApplication: When working with patients with dementia, routinely assess and address family caregiver communication competence and burden. Provide communication partner training targeting specific interaction strategies (open-ended questions, validation, reduced rate). Screening for caregiver depression may be relevant to treatment planning, as it directly impacts communication quality.

sessionStats.frequency: As part of family training component
sessionStats.dose: Ongoing caregiver support integrated with patient treatment
sessionStats.bestFit: Family caregivers of adults with dementia

bestFitCriteria: Family caregivers of adults living with dementia at any stage.
SLPs providing communication partner training in home or community settings.
Patients with dementia whose primary communication partners are family members.
Memory care or home health settings.

title: The Effectiveness and Characteristics of Communication Partner Training Programs for Families of People With Dementia: A Systematic Review
shortTitle: Communication Partner Training in Dementia: Systematic Review
authors: Various (PMC10949353)
summary: Systematic review of communication partner training (CPT) programs for family members of people with dementia. Examines program characteristics, outcomes, and the evidence base for CPT as an essential component of dementia care.
researchFindings: Communication partner training is essential in dementia care and demonstrates positive outcomes for both caregivers and persons with dementia.
CPT programs that include both skill-building and emotional support components show stronger outcomes.
Programs targeting specific communication strategies (e.g., simplifying language, using visual cues) are more effective than general education alone.
CPT can reduce caregiver burden and improve quality of interactions in persons with dementia.
SLP-led CPT programs are effective and address a gap in dementia care that medication and medical management cannot fill.
clinicalApplication: Incorporate structured communication partner training as a standard component of dementia treatment, not an add-on. Teach specific strategies: speak slowly, use short sentences, avoid corrections, provide visual cues, allow extra processing time. Program should include both a skill-building component (practice) and emotional support/counseling. CPT is reimbursable when integrated into the treatment plan.

sessionStats.dose: 4–8 sessions; ongoing reinforcement
sessionStats.bestFit: Family caregivers and care partners of adults with dementia

bestFitCriteria: Family members or paid caregivers of adults with dementia at any stage.
SLPs establishing dementia care programs.
Memory care units or home health settings.
Situations where caregiver communication is a barrier to quality interaction.

title: How People Living With Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Use Personalized Automatic Speech Recognition Technology to Support Communication
shortTitle: Personalized ASR Technology in ALS Communication
authors: Various (PMC12379579)
summary: Examines how individuals living with ALS use personalized automatic speech recognition (ASR) technology to maintain communication as speech deteriorates. Explores user experiences, barriers, and facilitators to AAC technology adoption.
researchFindings: Personalized ASR technology supports continued natural-sounding communication for people with ALS as speech intelligibility declines.
Early adoption of voice banking and ASR technology is critical before speech deterioration reduces voice recording quality.
Users reported that personalized ASR felt more natural and person-centered than generic text-to-speech voices.
Barriers to adoption include technological complexity, limited SLP guidance, and cost.
Integration of ASR technology with existing AAC devices improved functional communication outcomes.
clinicalApplication: Introduce voice banking and personalized ASR options early in the disease course—before speech deterioration limits recording quality. Services like ModelTalker, VocaliD, and ALS-specific voice preservation programs allow patients to capture their natural voice. SLPs should guide ALS patients through technology options proactively and monitor communication needs at each visit as disease progresses.

sessionStats.dose: Initiate voice banking early; reassess at each follow-up
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with ALS or progressive motor neuron disease

IDDSI-standardized diet levels improve consistency of diet modification across settings.

Communication partner training and augmentative communication strategies are increasingly important as disease progresses.

title: Interventions for Postextubation Dysphagia in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

Early initiation of swallowing therapy (within 48 hours of extubation) was associated with better outcomes.
No serious adverse events attributable to swallowing therapy were reported across studies.

Implement structured swallowing exercises targeting lingual strength, laryngeal elevation, and pharyngeal contraction. NMES (e.g., VitalStim) may be added as an adjunct to traditional therapy. Advocate for early SLP consultation post-extubation in ICU settings — waiting until oral intake is initiated increases aspiration pneumonia risk. Track return to oral diet, aspiration events, and time to decannulation as primary outcome metrics.

Treatment adherence and patient satisfaction were high in the telehealth format.

Neurostimulation (pharyngeal electrical stimulation, tDCS, rTMS) may promote neuroplasticity in the sensorimotor swallowing network.
Evidence supports individualized, multimodal treatment combining rehabilitation, dietary management, and adjunctive strategies.

Track aspiration pneumonia events, nutritional status, and return to full oral intake as primary outcomes across all phases of recovery.

title: A Systematic Review of Dysphonia in Multiple Sclerosis
shortTitle: Dysphonia in Multiple Sclerosis: Systematic Review
authors: Authors from Journal of Voice (2025)
summary: Comprehensive systematic review of 58 studies (from 1,140 screened) characterizing dysphonia in multiple sclerosis across self-reported, perceptual, acoustic, aerodynamic, and laryngoscopic domains; breathiness and increased jitter were the most consistent findings versus controls.
researchFindings: 58 studies included from 1,140 identified; covers vocal self-perception, perceptual assessment, acoustics, aerodynamics, and laryngoscopy.
People with MS report voice impact on quality of life and communicative participation significantly more than controls.
Auditory-perceptual assessment revealed increased breathiness, harshness, and overall dysphonia severity versus healthy controls.
Acoustic measures: increased jitter and shimmer, reduced harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR) were the most consistently significant findings.
Aerodynamic findings included reduced maximum phonation time and reduced subglottal pressure support.
Laryngoscopy revealed vocal fold bowing, incomplete glottal closure, and adductor spasms in subsets of patients.
clinicalApplication: When evaluating voice in adults with MS, conduct a comprehensive assessment: patient-reported measures (VHI, V-RQOL), perceptual ratings (CAPE-V, GRBAS), acoustic analysis (jitter, shimmer, HNR, MPT), and laryngoscopic referral to characterize the dysphonia subtype. MS dysphonia may present as spastic, flaccid, ataxic, or mixed depending on lesion location — treatment targets differ accordingly. Address breath support for reduced subglottal pressure, coordination exercises for ataxic components, and voice conservation strategies for fatigue-related deterioration. LSVT-LOUD has emerging evidence for neurological voice disorders including MS.

sessionStats.frequency: 1–2x/week; reassess with MS relapse or EDSS change
sessionStats.dose: 8–12 sessions; ongoing monitoring as disease progresses
sessionStats.bestFit: Adults with multiple sclerosis presenting with voice complaints affecting communication or quality of life

bestFitCriteria: Adults diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (any type: RRMS, SPMS, PPMS).
Reporting voice-related quality-of-life impact (VHI >18) or functional communication difficulty.
Voice complaints including reduced loudness, breathiness, harshness, or phonatory fatigue.
Differentiating MS-related dysphonia from reflux, infection, or structural vocal fold pathology.
Pre-treatment baseline assessment for tracking voice changes with MS disease progression.

title: Prevalence of Dysphagia in Patients With Multiple Sclerosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Dysphagia Prevalence in Multiple Sclerosis: Meta-Analysis
authors: Authors from Multiple Sclerosis and Related Disorders (2023)
summary: Meta-analysis of 54 studies (N=11,266 MS patients) establishing 45% overall dysphagia prevalence; objective assessment detects dysphagia in up to 58% — far exceeding self-reported rates — underscoring the need for routine SLP screening in all MS patients.
researchFindings: 54 studies included; N=11,266 MS cases; overall dysphagia prevalence 44.8% (95% CI 40.4–49.2%).
Prevalence via subjective methods (self-report) was 37%; objective assessment detected 58%.
Dysphagia severity correlated with MS disease duration, number of relapses, and respiratory function.
Decreased pharyngeal peristalsis and delayed swallowing reflex were the most common physiological findings.
Dysphagia in MS strongly linked to aspiration risk, malnutrition, and reduced quality of life.
Significant underreporting by patients underscores the need for routine SLP screening — self-report alone misses more than 1 in 5 cases.
clinicalApplication: Routine SLP dysphagia screening should be integrated into MS care across all disease phases. Use validated MS-specific tools (e.g., DYMUS questionnaire) at regular follow-up visits. When screening is positive, conduct formal clinical swallowing evaluation and consider VFSS or FEES to characterize the physiological deficit. Treatment targets include pharyngeal contraction, timing of swallowing reflex, airway protection, and compensatory strategies. Counsel patients and caregivers on safe swallowing, appropriate diet texture per IDDSI, and increased aspiration risk during MS fatigue periods or relapse.

title: Prevalence of Dysarthria in the Multiple Sclerosis Population: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
shortTitle: Dysarthria Prevalence in Multiple Sclerosis: Meta-Analysis
authors: Authors from Multiple Sclerosis and Related Disorders (2025)
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis quantifying dysarthria prevalence and characteristics in the MS population; findings establish motor speech assessment as a critical component of comprehensive MS clinical care.
researchFindings: Meta-analysis quantifying dysarthria prevalence across MS subtypes and disability levels.
MS dysarthria presents as spastic, ataxic, or mixed (spastic-ataxic) depending on lesion distribution.
Speech characteristics include imprecise articulation, harsh/strained voice quality, hypernasality, and irregular articulatory breakdowns.
Dysarthria prevalence increases with disease progression, EDSS disability score, and disease duration.
Self-reported speech difficulties underestimate objective dysarthria prevalence — formal SLP assessment is required.
Motor speech disorders in MS significantly impact communicative participation, employment, and social engagement.
clinicalApplication: When evaluating motor speech in adults with MS, conduct a standardized motor speech examination (Mayo Clinic motor speech battery or equivalent) to characterize the dysarthria subtype. Use the Assessment of Intelligibility of Dysarthric Speech (AIDS) or Dysarthria Impact Profile for functional measurement. Treat according to the predominant subtype: for spastic components, support articulatory effort reduction and rate control; for ataxic components, target rhythmic pacing and articulatory precision. Introduce rate reduction strategies, contrastive stress drills, and AAC backup systems proactively — especially for periods of MS fatigue or relapse. Reassess motor speech status at each clinical visit.
